The memorial service at Frogmore recalls to our minds the greatness of the debt which we owe to Queen Victoria, who although she came to the throne in cir- cumstances of exceptional difficulty, yet succeeded in changing for the better all the traditions of monarchy in Britain, and afforded to all her subjects reason for congratulation that we have, in this country no Salic law. It would be gross ingratitude to-depreciate in any way the efforts of King Edward to devote himself to the welfare of his people, but there can be no doubt that his present Majesty owes much to the example of his revered mother, and that he is the better King on that account. When he came to the throne, he recog- nised that his ideal should be that of walking in his mother's footsteps, and it is because he has performed the promise to do so, which he made to his Privy Coun- cil that he has stimulated the loyalty and evoked the affection of his subjects. Great preparations have to be made for Royal visits such as the King and Queen are paying to the Duke and Duchess of Devonshire at Chatsworth. The suites of apartments used by their Majesties have to be entirely redecorated, and refurnished, even though they may have been closed and unused since a previous visit from the Sovereign. Then there are the police arrangements which have to be made days beforehand, and the Post Office has to provide special telegraphic facilities, though a private telegraphist always'accompanies the King wherever his Majesty may be. Not only the list of guests, but the menus, and the programme of each days' events have first to be submitted to the King, and invitations to thehouse party are issued in his Majesty's name, and have the same force as a Royal command. It is intended to greatly increase the number of women in the nursing service at the various military hospitals. That is the principal feature in the re- organization of the Army Nursing Staff, which is being carried out under the direction of Miss Sidney Browne, the matron-in-chief. Miss Browne has been in the Army service for nearly 20 years, and after serving in Egypt she was in the hospitals in South Africa, through the recent war. The new system is first to be tried at the Herbert Military Hospital at Woolwich, which Queen Victoria visited shortly before her death. The orderlies of the Army Medical Corps will still be employed, but the responsibility for the care of the patients will be vested in the matron, and her staff of nurses. Inaddi- tion to the regular staff of each hospital, there will be organized a number of special nurses,. who couldbe sent in an emergency to any district or country, where their services were needed. The arrangements for the emigration of women to South Africa are making satisfactory progress, from the point of view of those who have this movement in hand, though it will not help us to solve the domestic servant-girl difficulty in this country. Under the , care of the Expansion Committee of the Emigration Assoc- elation, about fifty girls are now leaving every week, and reports from the colonies generally speak of them as doing well. The girls remain under Government protection for one year, situations being found for them, and the cost of sending them out, which amounts to about .£l2, is deducted in monthly instalments from their earnings. Since five o'clock tea has been turned into a luxuri- ous repast, many women find it more convenient to receive their visitors at one or other of the fashionable tea houses. It used to be a simple and homely social function, but now the French cook, the confectioner and the fruiterer are all called in to supply the rarest and most appetising delicacies and the cutting of the sandwiches is made almost a matter of art. Whether this tends to improve a pleasant sociable institution may perhaps be doubted,though with such a meal, it is only fitting that conversation should be the happiest and brightest kind. The chief objection however to these luxurious " Five o'clocks "taken out of doors is, that they tend to make one somewhat indifferent about the home dinner. Within reason, one can, now-a-days, please oneself as to the arrangement of one's tresses. For the moment, fringes are out of favour, but if they prove becoming, or are required to hide a high or receding forehead,then they should be worn. Queen Alexandra still remains faithful to the high, closely-curled fringe that so well becomes her,and the Princess of Wales also prefers this style of coiffure to any other. The secret of successful hairdressing is to make it accord with one's height,style and features. If the face is narrow, the prevailing fashion of dressing the hair low and priffiing it out at the sides, is vet y suitable, but if the head is somewhat 'fiat on the top, then the hair should be raisel by means of a rounded cushion, and if the ears are not pretty they should be hidden beneath soft loops of hair. The efforts of Lady Warwick and Lady Dudley to reintroduce the long curls of the sixties, nestling on the neck, have not, so far, been successful. These ladies, it will be remem- bered, appeared at the Coronation wearing their half so dressed, and in each instance the style proved particu- larly becoming. The bell-shaped sleeve is doomed, together with the sleevelet that accompanies it. The woman who has to ring many changes with one costume, will regret this decree, on the part of Dame Fashion, for the dainty sleevelet—to match the front and collar band—has proved of the greatest service to her. The new Cavalier cuffs however,will afford the home worker considerable scope in the way of "schemes." These cuffs are, in -many instances, turned back, almost to the elbow, and stiffened. Sleeves, tightly fitting from the shoulder, and pouched between the elbow and wrist, are still correct, the deep wristlet matching the collar band, and front. The chiffon hat or toque reigns supreme at the moment. No one cares to indulge in felt, now the early spring is close at hand, and it is too soon to be wearing straw, hence the popularity of chiffon head- gear. This nicked, pleated, gathered or tucked, requires little trimming, a feather aigrette being the favourite addition. Regarding shape, the turban prevails, slightly tilted on one side. The overmantel is distinctly out of date, but when a room is small it is better to be behind the times, and permit it to remain. When such a consideration is unnecessary, a picture in the place of the overmantel is to be preferred. There is always a suspicion of vulgarity about a display of looking glass in living TOOMS. "From Behind the Arms" (T. Fisher Unwin) proves to boa thrilling story of eighteenth century adventure. It may truly be said that this book does not contain one dull page. All the machinery cf medimval romance isset in motion, trap doors, sliding panels, etc. ; but eventually the villains are unmasked, and the path is made smooth for the lovely andheadstrong heroine, and the charming M. de Sivrac. APPLES IN JELLY.—POOI, core and quarter some firm apples, cook so as not to break them. Dissolve a jelly square, lemon flavour, and pour a little in a mould. When set place on it a layer of apples, then moire jelly, and so on till the mould is full. Turn out when set, and garnish, if possible, with pyramids of whipped cream.

.ere lay conspicuousty by Ins plate a pate purple missive, re-addressed from the Cottage, much scented with violets, quaint of form, and texture, the latest extravagance of Regent -s reet stationery, bearing "Violette" in deep purple letters across the nap. Percy took it. no with a frown. ' As he read it, the frown deepened, lie thrust it into his pocket, and looked up to meet, Mrs. Lowther', eyes, full of haughty inquiry. Ire coloured furiously, indignant that his private • correspondence should be criticiv.d.
said Mrs

"Evelyn is brealfa.,ting in her room," Lowther. "She is Dot very wet i this morning Percy was startled, but did not connect her absence with the letter, for she had been coletand ill-at-ease last night, and he had not been permitted to have a moment with her alone. After a very constrained meal he demanded an explanation. "All things considered it is best you and she should not meet again until. things are settled," said Mrs. Lowther. "We will write to you." "But they are settled," cried the exasperated over. "We love each other and we cannot give Jach other up. You were quite satisfied yesterday-- or Mr. Lowther was—promised to be so." "Hardly. We contented to no engagement. We must have breathing time. Evelyn wishes it, too." "Evelyn ? " incredniously. . "I will bring you a written expression of her wish if you require it." "Good Heavens! I require nothing, A want nothing, I understand nothing. A written expression ! I shall go crazy." Mrs. Lowther was silent and looked rigid. Percy remembered that he must not insult his intended mother-in=law by accusing her of imprisoning her daughter.- Then the dog-cart came round. He was too much dazed by the unexpected- ness of the situation to delay for protest. Indeed, the trap brought opportunity to escape and consider what to do next.

At the station the Clives' omnibus was waiting. Happy new guests were arriving who would be near Evelyn while he was far away. It was . hard beyond endurance, 'absurd, preposterous. It was more—it was impossible. Another omnibus was waiting, labelled The Black Lion. That was a nice little inn •a mile from Longwood. He dis- missed the Longwood dog-cart and servants, and as soon as they were out of sight hd astonished the porters and Mrs. Clive's servants by ordering his luggage to be put on the Black Lion omnibus. te walked on to the inn, too impatient to wait with the omnibus for the train. _

He was determined on going back to Longwood and having it out with Mrs. Lowther and -Evelyn. Then he remembered they were going out to luncheon at a great distance, and could not return until shortly before dinner. Dinner! They were dining at the Bishop's. That meant a rush through dressily. and another long drive. No use to go so soon. 'He must wait for morning. Time hung heavily on his hands, though he had much to ponder and plan, besides a telegram to send and a long letter to write to the same address. The aain had brought some rather pleasant fellows to the Black Lion on fishing intent, and the hours wore through ; even the sleepless night hours. Morning found him where night left him, determined on seeing Evelyn and her mother. Now it was Evelyn who must be first. He dared not go until their breakfast-hour was past, but eleven o'clock found him outside an ivy-hung wall which separated the Longwood domain from the higt road. A few steps further on was the lodge., pointing out the half-mile of avenue which lay between hint and his love.

He was divided from her by less than he reckoned—only by those bricks and that mantle of ivy. She was in the garden behind the wall, inspectinc, the progress of some cherished fruit- crop. He could not in any case have heard her soft footsteps, nor was she likely to recognise his manly tread. Just as they met, though parted like Pyramus and Thisbe by the wall (only more so by their mutual unconsciousness), the noise of wheels rushed upon the sweet country silence. "Well, Percy, this is a stroke of luck!" cried a girl's ringing voice that might have been heard over a stampede of cavalry and a rampart of granite wall. He started and turned to see a high, shabby gig driven by a rustic servant, at whose side sat a charming young lady in the most bewitching of travelling costumes, a sailor . hat on her shining hair, her blue eyes sparkling in the morning sun- shine brimful of laughter. " Violette !" he exclaimed. brought you here?" There was considerable vexation in his tone, but no one being in sight it did not occur to either of them to lower their voices. Neither heard the pause, the catching of breath that was nearly a groan on the other side of the wall. - "I had your odious wire, putting me off en some miserable pretext. See here, I'll get down. We will converse quietly on terra firnia ; much more privately than in an inn where walls have ears. Has this wall ears, do you suppose? You look uneasy enough. This youth may drive about for half-an-hour.. I was sick of waiting for you, so as this place is not so far off the road to Ireland came on, and the Scotts will pick me up at Monkchester. I meant to carry you on with us to Ireland—we are going to Ireland—but I came on here on my own first, for two's company and four's none under the circumstances. I was on my way to find you at—Longwood, isn't it? What a gaol of a house But this place is much better. I have only an hour between trains, so we must make the most of each other, lest you dare not come on to Ireland at present." She was climbing down while she chattered, and stopped only to astonish the groom and discomfit Percy by bestowing on the latter a very audible kiss. "But, Violette, it is not proper to come like this," he expostulated. "You must think more of how things look." "Proper! Look!" she cried, laughing, in her clear, penetrating tones. The gig had disappeared round a turning and they watked together very slowly under the green wall. "As if there could be a question of proprieties between you and me, you dear, silly old thing! And there is nobody to see. I rather wish there were. It is such fun com- promising you as I did the other day, coming out of your chambers. How Captain Jones stared! Why turn? Oh, I see. The lodge. Would it be shocked? Isn't it fun ? Don't you love these impromptu meetings far better than my coming to your chambers? Suppose I lose my train and have to stop here with you ? That would be deliciously imrromptu. How shocked you look Don't be fri ht:med. I am going to talk business. We mi at not waste any more time. I am positively _ .
"What on earth has

thirsting for you, Yet you cruelly ask me to wait -a whole day alone in London, after promising so faithfully to come to me yesterday. Writing is no good I can never tell you half thilt is in my heart though I write every day—more, sometimes, I: fear. Oh, Percy. I cannot live unless you stick to me. The loneliness is awful and you leave me so much. I am, afraid, too, that your letters have been noticed, and however should I get along without them? How much longer is this suspense to go on? I cannot bear it. lam sometimes half- crazy. You are all the comfort and support I have in the world, and you are so much away. Must you really go to Trentmore ? " "You are goini, to Ireland." "I wouldn't if would come to London. It is quiet there now, far emptier than the country. We could talk'all day in peace." They walked slowly along under the wall, not noticing that it presently ended and was replaced a thick hedge. Evelyn followed their voices and saw them through the hedge, dimly, but sufficiently to see Violette clinging to Percy's arm and looking up appealingly into his face. She dared not follow along the hedge, but waited behind this end of the wall in anguish, feeling as if every thorn in the hedge, through which she could faintly and intermittently discern their figures, were piercing her like Philomel to the heart. Her mind was too dull for active thought. She could only suffer. • They turned and their voices became audible again.

"Oh, Percy, you have given me hope at last. I will do my best to worry no more about gossip. I won't even listen to it. I trust you entirely. I know you .would not deceive me. I will snap my fingers at the enemy's wiles. It is perfectly dreadful what bother cdnes of one person being short of money and another haVing so much, and how marriage must be profaned and love made to play second fiddle, or made a cli,alc for mercenary designs. But that trouble is all settled and done with, and I trust implicitly to your word that I may shut my ears to talk and forgive everything magnanimously—for you know everytiing is not quite explained away—and w 3 shall live happy ever alter. A woman ha 4 to put up with things and forgive and trust, hasn't she? You will see whlt a good wife I shall ma' e —gentle, patient, trustful, a perfect Griselda, even if you do—" The rest was silence till the gig drove up. Then there were sounds of mounting and adieux, and Evelyn's strained ears were positive there was another kiss, though the performance ,was removed

A sad home-coming was that of a Devon girl, whose story the " Western Times" prints. "1 was obliged to give up my situation and come home," said Annie Martin, Langford House, S. Wonford, near Exeter. "Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people gave me back my health and strength, which other remedies failed to benefit, even partially." The change in her fortune has been as complete as it is happy. Formerly despondent and tnable to work, she is now both well and happy. And the fate she has escaped ' a most distressing - It was

Her saa ret,trit : changing traiw. feared that she would have to undergo an operation. "After eating," she, said, •• I felt such distressing, stabbing pains in my back that my friends feared I had sustained an internal injury and would have to be operated upon." But the cause was anwmia—poorness of blood—for which, as in the happy case of Miss Martin; Dr. Williams' pink pills are a noble remedy. "I had lost all colour, said she, "became gradually weak, and had no appetite for food. My feet swelled and I had always cold hands and feet, while violent palpitation of the heart seized me on taking the least exertion, until I became a conTlete " But hearing so much talk in S. Wonford, of the wonderful cures wrought by Dr. Williams' pink pills, I -resolved to give them a trial. I had not taken a whole box before I already felt brighter in spirits, and after continuing them a little longer my appetite came back, the colour returned to my cheeks,and before long I was quite well. I never felt better in my life than Ido to-clay." _ _ _

A pale cheek, dull eyes, poor complexion, lost vitality, breathlessness and palpitating heart all show poor blood. The condition is dangerous ; it leads to con- sumption: too dangerous to neglect; too dangerous to play with, with substitutes. The pills that cure it, are the genuine Dr. Williams', and they alone. Do not risk your life with purgatives or substitutes but if you experience any diL:Ctilty in obtaining the genuine pills send two shillings and ninepence for one box (or thir- teen and nine for six) to Dr. Williams' company, Holborn-viadust, London. Rheumatism, paralysis, St. Vitus dance, and other diseases of blood and nerves bave been cured by the same means. 0 Miss Martin had come home an invalid. She was able go away again strong and happy, admired by all her lends. -

div.head: VIOLETTE.
div.p: VIOLETTE.
BY ELSPETH CURRIE.
Author of "The Poyntz-Percivals," "As Gold in the Furnace," "A Breath of Slander," "Queen Isabel," "Nell Garland's Marriage," "A. Country-House Tragedy," &c.
She was so sweet, and. it was hard to part, for

• they had found each other only a fortnight ago, and up to the happy day of the Clives' garden- party their lives lay barren, bleak, and waste behind. But it could not be helped. There were still persons and duties left in the outer world, who insisted on forcing themselves into the Eden

that was the only real aid worthy world. Late as life had been in coming, they had made the most of their time. She had fallen in love with him with quite Shaksperean promptitude the very moment his eyes, from the other side of the Clives's lawn, had told her of his admiration. Now, it was the last afternoon of his visit to the Olives; and he had seized it, his first opportunity, to reveal his passion and his hope. They had fewer opportuni- ties than country neighbourhood usually offers, fo her mother disliked his hostess, a faded garrison beauty, too fruch addicted to faded flirtation to please a very rigid county matron. It was sharp work, but time pressed. "You will write to me every day," said Percy, tenderly. "Writing is no use," lamented Evelyn; "you „ -. .

must not Co. Why, should you? Everything is changed now. Why, we hardly know each other!" "I know you by heart, sweet; I read your inmost soul the first moment I looked into your heavenly eyes. Don't you feel that you know me as well as if we had been together always?" "Yes—of course "—hesitating. ."Do you doubt me ? " he asked, hurt. "N—no. But—are you sure you never cared for anybody but me ? " "Sure and certain, my own." "You seem to want so much to be in London, and leave me."
"Want to be there! I go like a prisoner to the condemned cell; bat I can't help myself. A man has business to consider, dearest. I shall think of

you all the time, every minute of it, and live upon your letters till we meet again. I must give you my address-" He felt in his pocket and drew out a letter. He took it from the envelope and replaced it in his pocket, ran a pencil through his own address, and wrote above it, "200 A Jermyn-street, S. W." Then be doubled the envelope up and gave it to Evelyn, who tucked it mechanically into her bodice. She had noticed that it was a pale purple envelope, that it smelt of violets and was addressed in a big, fashionable feminine hand; but he had so folded it that neither noticed the name " Violette " embossed in violet letters upon the flap. She knew

that after a flying visit to town, be was going to the Talboys', at Trentmore, and she supposed vaguely, half-consciously, that the letter was foona Mrs. Talboys. "I don't believe you need really go," she pro- tested, petulantly. , "Really, I am engaged—have promised—" "It will be so dreary here while you are keeping your engagements in London." "London is empty just now." "Then why go?" "Business, business." "Men always say it is business." He was a little bit shocked. He had not expected such cynicism from his country maid. "I assure you, it really is business," he said, rather stiffly. "Won't it put off?" "No. She is very urgent—and I promised----* "She? A woman! And you said it was business." "Women have business now and then." She frowned and was silent. The frown was pretty enough to see on a brow so fair, but ,the trouble in her blue eyes troubled him. He said, quickly: "She is a relative—a sort of—in fact, my grand- mother." He laughed, and there was something it. his laugh that annoyed her; as if there were a joke she must not share. "Your grandmother? What is there funny in that?" "A good deal—as you happen to look at it." "You spoke as if you were not quite sure what relation she is." "You little goose! If you read trange meanings into my words, where shall we be ? I aisure you, I am going to town to see my grandmother about some, family business. Can't you trust me, Evelyn, even though we have known each other only two little weeks, as other people reckon time ? It seems to me I was not born till a fortnight ago." "It is so strange," she murmured. - "A fortnight ago I had not seen you, yet I had lived nineteen whole years. What stupid years they were!" "Were they so stupid? What about Sir Harry Nevill ? How dare I leave you, Evelyn? He is a powerful rival, a far better match than I am; and little birds have whispered to me." She flushed angrily. "He is nothing to me. Can't you trust me? You expect me to trust you." Half-an-hour later he was pleading his cause with her father, while she told her story to her considerably startled mother. Mrs. Lowther meant to be kind and just, but nobody could deny that things had been settled very hastily. Mr. Lowther insisted upon Percy's coming next day to Long- wood to stop the night and talk matters over. business or no business. What business could NA more urgent than his marriage, since he admitted he had no pecuniary expectations from his grand- mother. He hesitated. Well, her business must be postponed for a day, though two days later he was due at the Talboys', in Yorkshire. The Lowthers knew the Talboys' by name and repute,which was point in Percy's favour; but, then, they also.knew Mrs. Clive, and it was impossible to look with immediate favour on a person introduced by Mrs. Clive. He telegraphed to put off his business appointment for one day; and on the following afternoon left Mrs. Clive's charming cottage for the statelier halls of Longwood. Mr. Lowther found him satisfactory enough, but Mrs. Lowther still demurred. "So far, we 'have only his own account of himself," she said. "Of course, there must be no formal engagement till we know him a little better ; but I see no ground of objection s. far. He seems to have plenty of money, and he answered all I asked him most satisfactorily and frankly. He is a nice, manly young fellow." "That horrid Mrs. Clive " groaned his wife. He lauhed. "Mrs. Clive may have deccnt friends." "Very likely his money doesn't exist." "Of course, we must have proof of it; but it is the best of proof that be is quite indifferent to . . _ .

the fact of Evelyn having none.- Well, let it rez.: for the present. Surelyl have Evelyn's happiness as much at heart as you have? If anything objec- tionable turns up, there is an end of it; but I won't have the girl thwarted without reason, or even made unhappy." "I don't think she is very happy," said Mrs. Lowther, uneasily. "She is a different girl to-day from what she was last night. She looks worried and depressed." Percy also found Evelyn pale and depressed. "Mamma is so provoking," she replied to her lover's anxious questioning. "She says we must know eaCh other better before we can be really engaged." She could not bring herself to ask him who was Violette who wrote to him on scented paper? She had tried honourably not to wonder, not even to think of it; but she had thought and wondered all night. He had no sisters. Mrs. Olive's name was Daisy. The post-mark was not Trentmore, but London, W. Was Violette the "relative " who had summoned him So imperiously to town? She could not imagine a grandmother haviljg such a name as Vioiette, or even Violet. Was this "grandmother" a blind to conceal a charminc, cousin ? She could not ask him, for that would be acting on information he had given her uncon- sciolsly, by accident. It would seem as mean as if she had opened a letter.

She copies the address that night and tore up thP envelope, just as her mother came into the rooa, There was no fire in which to burn the fragments. "Who writes to you on such vulgar paper?" asked MINI. 'Lowther, sniffing with her aristocratic nose at the strong scent.

"Nobody," Evelyn replied, with a deep blush. The blush and the reply mtarally diew Mrs. Lowth«,r's eyes to the fragments, on one of which she could distinctly "—cy Leigh, Esq." Ne7t morning, when Percy appeared at the bret,!f ,st-table, Mr. Lowther had just distributed the contents of the post-bag. Evelyn was not present. "Theres only ..one letter for you," his host informed him. ffruflly and (mite eratuitonsly. for

to the doubtfulness of dlstnnee. I.,en terrcr ,cized her lest Percy should find her, now he Isas set at liberty and she fled across the garden and oler the park and hid herself in a plantation.

Percy went down the avenue to the house. He was positive he saw Mrs. Lowther at a window, but he was told she was not at home; nor was Miss Lowther at home. Mr. Lowther was attending a magistrates' meeting. He gave the man a sovereign. "Perhaps you will find Miss Lowther at home if you inquire again," he suggested. No; Miss Lowther really was out, no one knew where. Percy returned to his inn and wrote a nott to her, whiuli he sent by messenger. In'an hour he had his answer.

"Mrs. Lowther is informed by her daughter thr4 there is no engagement whatever between her an Mr. Leigh, as Mr. Leigh seems to imagine, an 4 that she cannot receive or reply to any fetter Mr. Leigh may address to her. Mrs. Lowther begs sbi may hear nothing further on the subject." His own letter was enclosed, unopened.

"I think I will go to Ireland with Violette," ho ',old himself half-an-hour later, having found he had just lost the chance of catching the next London train. He thought she might comfort him. She certainly owed him some such service; and she might be able to solve the mystery. Women must understand one another better than simple men can hope to understand them. - If ever a girl had looked loving and true it was Evelyn; if ever a girl had looked simple and unworldly, it wal Evelyn. If ever the course of true love had promised to run smooth, it was the course of his love. How'could such changes have taken place so quickly? Mrs. Lowther had been uncordial, but she was only one of the parties concerned; her husband had been most cordial. Evelyn certainly seemed inclined to be jealous ; but then, he was entirely unconscious of ever having given her the slightest reason for jealousy, and surely she could not have changed her mind for no sort of reasonable reason.
"Out in the sun again, Evelyn," said her mother when she went into the house. "What a

complexion!" "Oh, my complexion doesn't matter! If it is spoilt, I can use powder and paint; and things. People really admire made-up complexions much more than real ones. I wonder if the Forrests would let me change my mind. I should like to mend my complexion by a little sea-air before I try paint." "We can telegraph," said Mrs. Lowther, dubiously. "I am afraid they would fill up your place on the yacht at once. And can you be ready to start to -morrow ? Cattle - show day at Redminster, too." "All the better. I shall have your protection and papa's from Monkchester to Redminster. It only means going by an early train to avoid the v.-.owd."

Than hour or two Mrs. Forrest's reply came: *Charmed to have Evelyn as her substitute has now failed us." It never occurred to Evelyn that Bedminster was on the line of rail which usually led from llionkehester to Ireland.

She went through the intervening hours with a word buzzing in her head: "Violette." Why on earth Violette ? She wouldn't have minded half so much had the creature spelt her name in the usual English way. Pride helped her to outward assumption of coolness, but it could not compel sleep; and she lay awake all night, wondering who was Violette ? What was her other name? How could Percy possibly have thought of marrying herself when he was engaged to another, if not married, as she fancied in her misery he might be? A cousin? Perhaps; but that made matters no better. It did not even justify the kiss, whose memory sent her blood tingling to agony; not in the case of a man really engaged to another girl— to herself—as he was! She repeated to herself: "The enemy's wiles! I am the enemy, and I have used wiles. Oh, was there ever in the world such a black traitor ? "

The platform at Monkchester was very full when they arrived. There was a crowd trying to escape from the cattle-show crowd. It was impossible to secure a compartment for any three people. They got into one of which the other places were occupied by bags, wraps, books, and newspapers. Something smelt of violets. Evelyn, shuddered and turned her absent eyes to the window, away from the crowded platform; till her father, looking up from his newly purchased paper to remove a rug nut of the way of somebody entering, uttered an exclamation of indignant surprise below his breath. There they were—Percy and his Violette struggling through the crowd towards that very carriage door. A lady was settling herself into the seat opposite, while a man at the door shouted to the loiterers to make haste.

Violette sprang in and turned round, filling tho doorway, to cry: "Good-bye good-bye! . You will write the minute you get there. Oh, dear, Frank, you need not hurry me so," as the other man jumped in and the train moved out. "Men are always in such an absurd hurry. There's Percy off like a shot, before I had half finished what I had to say. And we shan't be at an hotel for three mortal hours! I must write to him now and -post at the next place we stop at." She rummaged at once in her travelling bag for writing materials. A perfect atmosphere of violets rushed out of it. Mrs. Lowther sat in stony silence. Mr. Lowther had vanished behind his paper. Evelyn, very white, was apparently engrossed in the landscape on her right. "Haven't you said your say, Violette ? " laughed the lady beside her. "You have had him to yourself since six this morning, to say nothing of all yesterday evening." "The Postmaster-General is known to have reckoned up that the Government will pay half the expenses of this .war out of the postage stamps expended in your correspondence," remarked the man addressed as Frank.

Mr. Lowther looked interrogatively at his wife over his paper. She shook her head grimly. They must bear it for half-an-hour. It was an express train, and would not stop till they reached Redminster. The compfiny might fail to consider the situation such as would justify the pulling of the check-cord. , Meantime Violets covered sheet after sheet of pale purple paper with huge black writing, many deep notes of exclamation, and double, even treble underlinincrs. She wrote with a big, gold-cased pencil. Her now ungloved fingers were covered with so many rings that Mrs. Lowther, on her right, could not discover whether or not there was a wedding-ring among them. But she. saw the purple "Violette" embossed on the notepaper, and in big, black distinctness, "My dearest Percy," fairly jumped at her eyes. Violette finished her letter (Mrs. Lowther dared not glance at the signature, with all its numerous postscripts) and crammed it into an envelope, which she prudently left unclosed lest some fresh matter should occur to her for addition. Then she had time to glance at the view from the windows. "Nothing but flat fields," she commented in her shrill, sweet tones. "By the way, Dolly, you can't imagine what a stranded old ark of a place Longwood is, where Percy has been staying--" "Excuse me, madam," said the elderly gentleman before her, laying down his paper. "I am Mr. Lowther, of Longwood. I am sorry my house does not meet with your approval." Violette burst into melodious laughter. "Well, this is a warning!" she cried. "I have been scolded all my life for saying unfortunate things. I might have guessed, as you got in there, that you might at least be a friend of the Lowthers." She turned abruptly to look at Evelyn, who kept her face averted. Then she said: "I am Violette Barclay. I daresay you know my name as well as I know yours." Mrs. Lowther sat in stony silence, but her husband was a man and a gentleman. Violette was a pretty young woman, and, in spite of deep offence received, he felt bound to atone for his wife's irresponsiveness. "Oh, perfectly," he replied, pleasantly. "Percy told me lots about you," she said, carelessly; pulled herself up, and blushed very much. _

"You are a relative of his? " stiffly. She laughed. "Oh, yes; a relative, by all means. It is a funny sort of relationship." Then she turned to Evelyn. "You look rather ill. Do you mind sitting that way? Do change seats. I can sit any way." Mrs. Lowther felt compelled to interpose. "My daughter is perfectly yell, thank von. Evelyn, you want to see the Free Lance, don't you ?" Evelyn silently took the paper from her mother, and pretended to read it, while Mrs. Lowther, as superficially, but more demonstratively, became absorbed in the Monthly Review. Violette might be thoughtless, but she was not stupid; and she could not but perceive herself most insolently snubbed. But she would not for the world have shewn con- sciousness of rebuff. She merely diverted her chatter to her own friends, who were longing and endeavouring to make up for lost hours of slumber, until they reached Redminster. Nevertheless, after the first dizzying shock,

Evelyn begairi to take wi=tful interest in the girt whom Percy loved. "She is dreadfully vulgar; but she may be an American," she thought. She smothered a sigh, for she knew that one "vulgar " American woman is more dangerous as a rival than a whole rosebud garden of well-bred English girls. "She is not so very pretty," she decided, after another stolen glance. She thought of the kisses, and her soul was tortured. Every word spoken behind the garden vall rang in her head, words that surely could liave been spoken only between betrothed lovers. And she knew that American girls, for all their freedom, have their own standard of manners, and do not allow such liberties as kisses unless between engaged people. And how very rich Violette must be to wc w such clothes and rings ! "Nasty, stuck-up cats!" Violette was thinking, while she prattled to her friends of anything that came into her head. "What in the world could Percy see in her ? She is quite plain." Then they all got out at Bedminster. "Whom t d he say the violet letters were from ? " Evelyn whispered to her mother, as she changed trains.
"His maiden aunt, or his grandmother, or some- thing of the sort. You see what he is, how far you could have trusted him ! "

The Forrests' sailing yacht was bound for the Scottish isles—Hebrides, Orkneys, Shetlands. They had a small but charming party on board. The weather was fine and promising until the very hour after sailing; then a strong north-easterly wind came up and Mrs. Forrest, green and tearful, declared that if she were not at once set ashore, she would jump in and be done with it. Larne was the nearest port suggested by the fitful, fan (..y of the wind. Once landed, Mrs. Forrest refused to leave shore until they should pick her up on the way home. It was represented to her that she could not stop alone, and it would be selfish to detain her visitors at Larne, who were all well and full of courage, and had their hearts set on Orcades.

"Evelyn Lowther isn't well. She is dying for a colourable pretext to get out of the trip. She will stop behind with me, and we will send for one or two landlubbers, and do the Giant's Causeway." Evelyn declared she was well, but her pale face contradicted her, and she consented to stop on shore. Ireland was more interesting to her than Scotland. Curiosity excited desire to run against " Violette " somewhere on the island. She told herself there was no chance of meeting Percy, who was going to Trentmore.

Yet Percy was the first person she met on walking out of their hotel on the morning after the yacht's northward flight.. Suddenly, as an angel or a ghost, he appeared before her. "Evelyn!" he exclaimed, looking ready to open his arms and bid her fly to their shelter. But he refrained, as the place was public. "Come along the lough with me," he said, quietly. "With you I "—indignantly. "Something wants clearing up." Then she found herself walking beside him as if it were in a dream, so little will had she to control her action. "I know you love me still," he said, gravely. "I saw it in your eyes just now. Why, then, have you treated a poor fellow so, whose only desire
He stopped, choked by feeling. "Why ? " she echoed, bitterly.

"Yoi are under some strange mistake." She collected herself, and spoke quietly: "I did make a mistake, but I found it out." She paused. She could not bring herself to tell him she had listened behind a wall. Then she said, coldly: "We travelled, as I suppose you know, with Miss Barclay." "Mrs. Barclay," he corrected, though he looked innocently perplexed. "What difference can that•make ? A widow is only the more .alluring." "But I am not in the least allured by my grand- mother, who is not a widow, but a married woman."

"Your grandmother !"—indignantly. "I told you—didn't I tell you she was my grandmother? my step - grandmother, to be accurate, but it is all the same, practically. A girl my grandfather chose to marry a year or two ago—for her money, I fear, poor thing!" "You seemed very fond of each other, for grand- mother and grandson—l. mean, you had a great deal of correspondence." "Correspondence! Tons of it!" he laughed. "Violette drives inc nearly wild by her impulsiveness and unreasonableness." "Why do you call her Vielette, if she is your grandmother? She is much too young!" "j call her Violette because she is so young. I used to call her grannie for fun, but she got not to like it. She is six months younger than I am." "Can a man never marry his grandmother?" "Certainly not,. And Violette is about the last person *I should wish to marry if she were my granddaughter—l mean, if she were no relation whatever. She is generally on bad terms with my grandfather, poor little girl! quarrelling about money matters; and I have to make peace between them. She insisted, too, that I should see her money all settled upon herself, according to the, Married Woman's Property Act. She only came into it lately—after the marriage. What a time I have had of it with her!" he groaned. "And what a time I have had of it! [Tux END.)

div.head: STRUGGLE ON A BRIDGE. Warrington Policemen Savagely
div.p: STRUGGLE ON A BRIDGE. Warrington Policemen Savagely
Assaulted.

A fierce struggle took place on the iron bridge which spans the Mersey at Arpley, Warrington, on Monday afternoon, as the result of which Henry Billingo, of Prince-street, Latchford, appeared before Alderman Sutton and other magistrates at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, charged with having been drunk and disorderly and assaulting Constables Dennett, Gibbs, and Clarke, and David Henry Guest, cycle manufacturer. From the statement of the Chief Constable it appeared that at 25 minutes to two on Monday after- noon P.C. •Dennett, who is a member of the staff at the police buildings, was coming on duty and was crossing the Arpley Iron Bridge when he passed the prisoner. who was drunk. Not wishing to irritate the man he took no.notice of him, but the prisoner called after him and asked him to come back, It the same time making use of a foul expression. - The officer, seeing that the prisoner was determined to be awkward, remonstrated with him and told him to be quiet. The prisoner then buttoned his jacket and inde a terrific onslaught on the officer,striking him and kicking him. He also seized him by the leg and attempted to throw him over the bridge. The officer struggled with .. the man and both fell to the ground. At this time two gentlemen came up, namely, Mr. Guest and Mr. Downs, who was an assistant at the Royal Court Theatre, nnd went to the assistance of the officer, and they were also assaulted by tiTit3 prisoner who was wild drunk. Ho was more like a maniac than anything else. The officer blew his whistle and P.C.'s Gibbs and Clarke came upon the scene and had their share of prisoner's violence. Billinge bit Gibbs' finger and kicked Clarke and butted him in the face. He gave all the men a bad time of it on the bridge. The prisoner had to be carried to the station in the style known as the" frog's march," and immedi- ately he was released-at the station he continued his onslaught on the officers, butting P.C.Clarke in the face. A gentleman of considerable experience had suggested that the prisoner might have been conveyed to the station in a cab, but he could not have been put in one, owing to his violence. In all casMs where a Cab could be used to avoid a scene it, was used. By order ,of the Watch Committee he (the Chief Constable) used vehicles for the conveyance of prisoners, but in this case it would have been physically impossible. The suggestion was made by the gentleman in all good faith, and he thanked him for it.

Evidence was given in support of the statement, P.C. Denriett informing the Bench that he had been seven years in the force, but had never seen a more violent man than the prisoner. It would have been impossible to get Billinge into a cab, as he would have broken the windows.
The Chief Constable said, prisoner had a bad record baying served a term of penal servitude for house- hreaking. He had also been convicted of stealing a watch and drunkenness.
The Bench decided to send prisoner to gaol for three months. They expressed their thanks to Messrs. Guest and Downs for rendering such valuable assistance and awarded them ss. each.

Major-General T. Carlyle Bell has died at Craig's House,Dumfries,aged 73 years. He had a distinguished !career, and saw much active service. Serving in the Persian War 45 years ago; he was present at the storm- ing of Fort Bushire, and the surrender of that town,and I at the battle of Koosbab, for which he held the medal I and clasp, and was mentioned in despatches. He took part in the Afghan War,and wasasecond time mentioned in despatches. In 1881 he was in command of Hyderabad, end afterwards of the Sciende district. He retired from the service in .1886. Two sons and two daughters stir- vive him. I Owing to the formation of ice on Niagara River the ; water supply of the Canadian town of Niagara Falls was cut off last week. The Emergency,. however, was ! met by running a fire hose across the Niagara Bridge land connecting it with the mains in the American town of Niagara. 5, St

div.head: THING TO BE PROUD OF.
div.p: A THING TO BE PROUD OF.

Many hard things have been said against pride, some of them undeservedly. Pepe calls it 'the never failing vice of fools," without distinguishing what are and what are not legitimate objects of Pride. The man who lives a long life without making one enemy has achieved something of which he may be justly proud, while the man whose pride is founded on the glory achieved by his ancestors is a fitting object for ridicule. A man who was boasting of the wisdom of his ancestors, once met with the retort: "So all the ability of your family was possessed by the first generation." Similarly, the great Lord Chesterfield (whose family. name was Stanhope), inn fine spirit of satire, placed among the portraits of his ancesters two old heads which he labelled respectively Adam de Stanhope and Eve de Stanhope. Only a few things justify pride, and among those few, good . health must be numbered. To have . inherited sound health speaks well for your parents; to preserve sound health. or win it back when lost or impaired, speaks well for yourself. To no one could health be more important than t 6 Mrs Waller, of 14, :•_'kipton Street, London Road, Southwark. For the last three years Mrs. Wailer has scarcely known what it is to be free from pain; but thanks to Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup that is now past and over. "I used," stated Mrs. Waller on 27th November, 1902," to look forward to meal times with dread,because of the agony that I suffered after eating. Cutting pains, like the stab of a knife, used to seize me between the shoulders, and run down the left side. At times my. chest felt as tight as if it had been encased in iron bands. Frequently I would be violently sickafter taking food, and my heart palpitate painfully. Sometimes an awful feeling of faintness would seize me, when I would tremble like is leaf. My system was thoroughly run down. I could not sleep, and my nervousness became so intense that I was afraid to go out by myself and dreaded to be left alone. I was fast becoming weary of life when a friend advised me to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I did so, and felt a little better after taking one bottle. When however, I had taken a second bottle,l experienced a great change for the better. There was less pain after eating, less heart palpitation, and I felt stronger in every respect. With the completion of a third bottle my sufferings ceased, and once more I enjoy the privilege of good health."

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. Monthly Meeting.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. Monthly Meeting.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Bewsey Chambers on Wednes- day afternoon. Mr. Joshua Ball presided and there were also present :—Messrs. Halton, Mather, Backhouse, Brooks, Forshaw, Knowles, and Dr. Murray, with Dr. Sephton (medical officer of health), Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk),T. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), and H. H. Burnage (assistant surveyor).

div.head: MANCHESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: MANCHESTER PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The Local Government Board wrote stating that the Manchester Port Sanitary had applied to the Board for the issue of a provisional order for the inclusion of the Ellesmere Port and Whitby Urban District Council as an authority to contribute to the expenditure. The Board would direct that an inquiry should be made by one of their inspectors with regard to. the application.
It was deeidea that Mr. Brooks and the Clerk should attend the inquiry if it were thought advisable.
iIIJRTONWOOD ROADS. The Clerk to the Burtonwood Parish Council wrote complaining of the bad state of the roads in that parish. The matter was left in the hands of the Surveyor.

A TRAP ACCIDENT AT LONGFORD. Mr. T. C. SHAW, Church Farm Winwick, wrote stating that on December 2nd he had the misfortune to have his horse thrown down owing to the bad state of the road at Longford which was undergoing repair at that time. The animal caught its foot against the raised portion of the road and both its knees were broken. The shafts of the trap were also broken and Mrs. Shaw was thrown out of the vehicle and injured. He asked the Council to pay him £2 2s. which would be expended in replac- ing the shafts. The Surveyor reported that he had written to Mr. Shaw that the accident in question could not many way be attributed to negligence on the part of men or methods employed in the repair of the road, that he (Mr. Newcombe)- had happened to be on the ground the same afternoon before the accident and could vouch for the exact condition of the road. No greater care could possibly have heen taken in carrying out the work of repairs. In any case if there were liability it would rest with the county Council. -
No reply had been received from Mr. Shaw.
HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

Dr. Sepliton reported that during the month there had been 31 deaths and 22 births. The death-rate was equal to 30 per 1,000 against 23, the average for the past three months and 12 for the corresponding month last year. Twenty-five deaths occurred in Winv,ick Asylum and exclusive of these the rate was 5•9 per 1,000. The report was adopted.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL GRANTS
div.p: COUNTY COUNCIL GRANTS
The Surveyor reported the receipt of spe3ial grants from the County Council amounting to £2,111 which was equivalent to 74c1 in the pound for the whole dis- , - trict.
This wai all the business of public interest.

WARRING TON TRINITY V. TH EL NV ALL.—A large gathering of spectators witnessed this match at The' wall on Saturday. An interesting game resulted in a victory for the home team by 3 goals to 1. Woods (2) and Price were the scorers tor Thalwall and Bates registered the only goal for Trinity.

WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. (2ND DIVISION). WARRINGTON ALRIONS V. CABLE COMPANY.—This match was played last S Iturday at Liverpool-road before a large attendance andresulted in a win for the Albions by 1 goal to nil. Johnson being the scorer.

div.head: VAINT CEREMONY OF TRIAL AT BAR: SCENE IN COURT JUST PRIOR TO THE
div.p: THE VAINT CEREMONY OF TRIAL AT BAR: SCENE IN COURT JUST PRIOR TO THE
PASSING OF THE DEATH SENTENCE ON COLONEL LYNCH.
TRIAL AT BAR.

Among the many absurd formulm of English 'law, none is more open to ridicule than the cere- mony of trial at the bar. Details of proceaure almost barbaric and phrases that takn one back to days when superstition held sway almost wholly constitute the ceremony preceding sentence. That the latter should be the dread one of capital ;punishment would be disgusting to the most callous, but from the fact that commutation is practically inevitable. Therein lies the humour of the trial for those who can view the glaring defects of our judicial system lightly. To the sober-minded, however, the whole proceedings -cannot but awaken feelings of disgust that Such a state of things should exist in this England of ours at the beginning of the twentieth century. Mr. Justice Wills was unconsciously humorous throughout his f,rvid denuncia- tion of traitors. This unconscious humour is ob- vious to anyone who reads his remarks, though, perhaps, a pqrti- cularly spicy bit that attention may reasonably be drawn to was his assertion that "civilised com- munities exist for the purpose of mutual succour and support." Perhaps Mr. Jus- tice Wills could imagine France sue-
iYNCH, WHOSE CASE IS EXCITING 3ITICH
INTEREST
"mutually

couring and sup- porting " Germany, and Germany trying to keep a mutual eye on both France and Russia at the same time. The kind of succour the man in the street sees commonest between civilised com- munities is bought from Sir Hiram Maxim and the executors of the late Herr Krupp. Had Mr. Lynch lived 200 years ago, he would not only have ,been sentenced to be hanged; he would have been hanged, drawn, and quartered. Nowadays, justice is satisfied with mere death—or, perhaps, the merest sentence of it. Even in 1867' when Mr. 4. F. X. O'Brien was sentenced to be hanged, -drawn, and quartered, his punishment was some six years enforced retirement, after which he represented Cork in Parliament! There seems to be no case exactly on all fours with that of Col. Lynch. But many men accused of "treason felony " have become members of the House of 'Commons. Among them may be recalled: Mr. 'Michael Davitt, Sir Chas. Gavan Duffy, who -eventually became Prime Minister of Victoria, John Mitchel. the " rebel " of 1848, John Martin, his friend and the predecessor of Mr. Joseph Biggar, and Dr. O'Doherty, another 1848 man. The Lynch sentence has in several instances moved the London press to humorous comments. One of the best is that of an evening paper which, under the head, "Latest War Cables," says: .." Lynch Kopje has been taken (inlarge quantities, to the newspaper offices) after sharp (forensic) fighting, but Lynch's Nek is not believed to be in any immediate danger."

weighed considerable with the staff-officers who have had to select automobiles in which they themselves will have to travel many hundreds of miles on inspection p and at manceuvres. We give an illustration of this latest purchase, and it will be seen that it is quite on unconventional lines. It is a very low car with a wide wheel-base which practically precludes side-slipz, the bugbear of motorists, and the works are placed in the centre between the driving seat and the tonneau. The front and rear wheel are carried on separate frame, which are coupled to the car frame by patullel motion, which helps to retain all desirable rigidity over the roughest roads. The War Office Car is painted and upholstered in Kharki with gun-metal fittings, and over the tonneau, which is exception- ally roomy, a hood can be drawn in bad weather. The engine is a 10-h.p. balanced one, and tha car is capable of two or three times the legal HIEN. In future it will be quite a common sight to see our Generals and Army Corps officers careering wildly through town and country in kharki cars breaking the law in their enthusiasm for duty.

div.head: NEW CAPE COLONY JUDGE.
div.p: THE NEW CAPE COLONY JUDGE.

A. most popular appointment in South Africa is that of Judge Kotze, the ex-Chief Justice of the Transvaal, to the judgeship of the Eastern Districts of Cape Colony, which has been an- nounced by telegram from Cape Town. Judge Kotze has in his time played an important part in South African affairs, and has been much before the public eye. Of German extraction on his father's side, on his mother's he belongs to one of the original Dutch families, dating back to 1691, and was born in 1849 at his father's farm " Leeuwenhof," at the foot of Table Moun- tain. His father was twice mayor of Cape Town, and represented that city in the House o f Assembly,
und the son wiE; educated at the Sodth African
Colleire.
quently he came to England and _
graduated in law at the age of thirty at the University o f London, and a
year later was called to the Bar
•of the Inner
Temple. Upon his return to the ,Cape he became
an- advocate of
the Supreme Court, and prac- JUDGE KOTZE tied with great WHO HAS DEW; APPOINTED TO
success till he - THE JUDGESHIP OF THE EASTERN was appointed DISTRICTS OF CAPE COLONY. Chief Justice of the Transvaal.

In this capacity his life was a constant struggle with the corrupt Government of the South African Republic. which sought to make its High Court of Justice its slave for its own ends, but Judge Kotze was strong enough to foil the Hollander section for a time and to protect the independence of the Bench. In 1894 he was instrumental in getting thrown out by the Volksraad an amend- ment to the Constitution, which aimed to subject the Judiciary Courts to the Executive. Two years later, however, he was dismissed and expelled from the country owing to the machinations of President Kruger and Dr..Leyds—an event which greatly aggravated the crisis which ultimately led up to the late war. Judge Kotze threw all his in- fluence on the British side; and in due course he was appointed Attorney-General of Rhodesia, which 7post he now vacates for the above-mentioned ;position on the Bench of his native colony. div.head: NEW TURKISH AMBASSADOR.
div.p: THE NEW TURKISH AMBASSADOR.

Musurus Pasha, who is to succeed the late Anthopoulos Pasha as Ambassador of Turkey, was born in 1841, at the Turkish Legation in Athens, where his father was Minister. He accompanied his father to London in 1851, and for thirty years was practically a resident in this country. He was at first educated privately, and afterwards took his degrees in Paris as a student of law. In 1861 he entered the Turkish Diplomatic Service, and was appointed Second Secretary to the London embassy, He served successively as First Secretary and Councillor, and frequently acted as Charge d'Affaires in the absence of his father. In 1881 he was offered and rccepted the post of Turkish Am- bassador atßome. He remained in
Italy until his marriage in 1884,
when he was re:
called to Con-
etantinople, and
appointed a, mem- ber of the newly- organised Coin-
mission of Public
Works. Six years
later, owing to the necessity of effecting econo- mies, the Corn-

div.head: mission was
div.p: mission was
abolished, and Musurns Bey re- _ _
tired for a time
from active ser- MITSURYe PASHA, • vice. In 1896 TILE NNW TIYBKISH AMBASSADOR when 13erovich TO ENGLAND. Pasha was trans- ferred from

Samos to Crete, Musurus was offered the post of Prince of Samos. His occidental training, and his experience of con- stitutional forms of government, peculiarly fitted him for this important office, as Samos is a consti- tutional oasis in the Ottoman Empire, possessing a little Parliament of its own, and enjoying all the luxury of party government. The administration of the new Prince was exceedingly saccessful, notwithstanding that the outbreak of the Turco Greek war rendered his position somewhat difficult. He was very popular with all parties, and on his retirement in 1900 he was followed by the regrets of the whole island. The Samians have, indeed, since suggested his reappointment. On returning to Constantinople, Musurus Bey was appointed a member of the Civil section of the Council of State. He remained in this position until last month, when he was raised to the rank of Vizier, with the title of Pasha, ana appointed Ambassador to Great Britain. Musurus Pasha is an able diplomatist, of wide experience and liberal views. He is perfectly acquainted with English institutions, and he speaks our language with the ease and accent of a native. He is as amiable as he is intelligent, and, in short, lacks nothing to make him a success in the distinguished office to which his Sovereign has called him.

div.head: LORD ROSESERY $ DAUGHTER S ENGAGEMENT.
div.p: LORD ROSESERY $ DAUGHTER S ENGAGEMENT.

One of the features of the recent coming-of-age celebrations at Dalmeny,when the Earl of Rosebery's eldest son attained his majority, was the announce- ment of the engagement of the Lady Sybil Primrose to Mr. Charles Grant, a brother officer of Lord Dalmeny. This young lady, who made a very unusual debut into society, "coming out-c at a private presentation to the late Queen at Windsor, is one of the most distinguished and well-dowered partis in Great Britain, and ha: been linked by society journalists to many eligible bachelors, including the Earl of Beauchamp, who last year married Lady Lettice Grosvenor; but, despite many offers and the early marriage of her younger sister, Lady " Peggy " Primrose, now Countess of Crewe, Lady Sybil has preferred to wait and chose in her own good time. Mr. .Grant is a young soldier belonging tr Scotch family
LADY SYBIL PRIMROSE,
LORD ROSEDERY S DAUGHTER, WHo IS ENGAGED TO
MARRY MR. CHAS (RANT

and will in due course be a wealthy man, and Lady Sybil Primrose herself will be ultimately very well furnished with this wortd's goods, principally through her mother, who was a Rothschild. At her marriage, however, she will only receive a small portion of her _dowry. and it will mean that, after having been hostess of one of the leading London houses for some years, she will have to be content with a comparatively small establishment. At the recent coming of age festivities she made a graceful and pretty 1i tie speech ;ti response to the Oast of health and happine4s to Mr. Grant and herself. All the other members of the family, except the Countess of Crewe, who was unavoid- ably absent, spoke too, and, though Lord Dalmeny did not show much aptitude for public speaking, his younger brother, Mr. Nigel Primrose, made quite a hit and gives promise of following in his witty and distinguished father's footsteps. He is keenly interested in politics and goes to all the meetings at which Lord Rosebery speaks.

The administration of the Education Act is exciting much interest amongst Free Church. men. The Act contains vast possibilities in the direction of filching away the liberties of citizens and injuring the education of the children. Much harm will undoubtedly be done to national education, but many of the evil tendencies of the measure are permissory only, and Free Churchmen must be very active in order to prevent bad use being made of many of the weaknesses and ambiguities in which the Act abounds. The National Council has just issued a communication to the Councils all over the country urging immediate action on a number of points. To ascertain what Free Churchmen should do in these matters is the object of a very instructive interview with Mr. E. C. Rawlings, solicitor of the Supreme Court, in the February Free Church Chronicle. He regards the Act as "a Machiavellian master- piece" which it is almost impossible for a lay- man to understand.
The Examiner, Friday, January 30, 1903. THE FREE CHURCHES. THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE ACT.

This return match at Leigh attracted 8,000 spectators. At the interval Leigh led by a goal to nothing. After an exciting attack Leigh were penalised, and Mason equalised the scores by placing a goal. Brilliant passing by Leigh was neutralised by good tackling, and Wigan were very threatening in the later stages, but found the defence impenetrable. Result: Leigh 1 goal (2 points), Wigan 1 goal (2 points). OLDHAM v. HULL KINGSTON RtiVERS. The return meeting of these teams took place at Watersheddings. Half-time score—Oldham '2 tries (6 points), Hull Kingston Rovers nil. The last quarter was all in favour of Oldham, Cash registering two tries and A. Lees dropping a oal. The return match between these clubs, fraught with se much importance to both as regards the ownership of "the" wooden spoon," was played at St. Helens,before a good attendance. The play was fairly even for some time, but the home team gradually pressed, until Baker relieved with a run to the opposite end. div.head: TRUST DERDS.
div.p: TRUST DERDS.

Mr. Rawlings emphasises • that action is necessary with regards to trusts deeds, which should not be allowed to be altered in the C.irection of increased clerical control. The Act, it will be remembered, gives until the 18th of March for these deeds to be altered, and Free Churchmen need to exercise extreme vigilance; local Free Church Councils should first ascertain what are the trust deeds in connection with the schools in their area. In all cases where there is no trust deed, or one of a generally un- denominational character, steps should be taken to secure that the new deed, or any alteration in the existing one, shall be such as will strengthen the undenominational character of the schools. The National Council invites direct conununication in cases where there is no trust deed, in order that a suitable one may be framed.

div.head: GUIDE TO THE EDUCATION ACT.
div.p: GUIDE TO THE EDUCATION ACT.

Mr. Rawlings, it is interesting to note, is just publishing, through the National Free Church Council, "The Free Churchman's Guide to the Education Act, 1902." The contents include the full text of the Act, with explanatory and advisory notes and appendices, and a sketch of the History of Popular Education in England and Wales by Dr. Townsend, President of the National Council. All Free Churchmen con- cerned in the working of the Act should obtain a copy, which is published at 2s. 6d. net.

div.head: NATIONAL COUNCIL AT BRIGHTON.
div.p: NATIONAL COUNCIL AT BRIGHTON.

Considerable attention is being directed to the meetipgs of the National Free Church Council at Brighton on March 9to 12. These gather- ings, it is confidently anticipated, will be more interesting, representative, and important than any that have preceded them. Nearly eight hundred Councils are expected to be repre- sented. A complete session will be devoted to education, while many other questions of supreme importance will bo fully dealt with, including such subjects as "Modern Forms of Sabbath Desecration," "How Free Church Councils may Prevent De- nominational Overlapping," " How Free Church Councils may Promote Aggressive Re- ligious Work," "The Place of Women in the Free Church Councils," "The Free Churcieee and the Outside Masses," "Are We Losing our Young Men ?" "The Revival of. Family Worship," "The Need for the Revival of Per- 3onal Religion." These will be introduced by the following, among others: Rev. C. Silvester Horne, M.A., Rev. Alfred Rowland, 8.A., D.D., Dr. Rendel Harris, Ms. W. S. Caine, Rev. J. Brierley, B.A. (" J. B." of the Chrktion World), Rev. J. S. Banks (President of the Wesleyan Conference), and Rev. W. J. Dawson. One morning will be devoted to a Memorial Session to the late Dr. Parker, who was to have been the President for this year, and the Rev. Hugh-Price Hughes. At this meeting the Pre- idential Address, written by Dr. Parker for this occasion, will be read by the Rev. R. J. Campbell.

div.head: REV. F. B. MEYER'S MISSIONS.
div.p: REV. F. B. MEYER'S MISSIONS.

The Rev. F. B. Meyer, who has just returned :YAW a visit to the United States and Jamaica, holding a series of missions in connection with .?.ie National Free Church The meetings aro considerably varied in character, comprising devotional services at which Mr. Meyer's message is evidently addressed to Chris- tian believers, meetings for the discussion of that large group of questions comprised in the relation of the Christian Church to public life in the widest sense, and meetings of a more directly evangelical character. Mr. Meyer is about to hold a mission at Bradford, and will then visit Southport, Bacup, Halifax, and other places. Mr. Meyer, yielding to the persuasions of many friends in all the churches, has decided to coptinue his pastorate at Christ Church, Westminster-bridge-road, London.

div.head: " LIFE " OF REV. H. P. HUGHES.
div.p: " LIFE " OF REV. H. P. HUGHES.

It is announced that the " life " of the Rev. Hugh Price Hughes will be written by his eldest daughter, who is now collectiug material for that object. It is probable that a consider- able portion of the biography will be devoted to Mr. Hughes' connectidn with the National Free Church Council. Mis well known, Mr. Hughes took a very prominent part in the formation of the National Council, traversing the country, together with Dr. Berry and the Rev. Thomas Law, to advocate the formation of local councils. He had hoped to have spoken at the meetings at Brighton in March, definitely arranging this only a few hours before his; sudden death.

THE YOUNG PEOPLE OF NEW ENGLAND. The Rev. Alfrea Rowland, who not long since returned from Canada with the degree of "D.D.," contributes a very interesting article to this month's Free Churchman on "Religious Life a longst the Young People of New Eng- land." He noticed that the churches in the States use a great number of organisations for the employment of young Christians. At Hart- ford, for instance, he met with the "Daisy Chain," "Violet Circle," "King's Daughters," "Hyacinth Circle," "Flower Committee," and other societies, the work of which he interes- tingly describes.
TEMPAANCE CRUSADE.
The work of the Free Churches' Twentieth

Century Crusads has been brought to a close after a two years' energetic campaign. The number of pledges reported is over half a million, and hundreds of Temperance Societies bave been founded as a result of the work.

THE NORTHERN UNION. THE LEAGUE.--FIRST DIVISION.
RUNCORN v. W.A.RRINGTON.

The above match was played on the Irwell Lane en- closure on Saturday afternoon. Considerable interest centred in the contest, there being a crowd of about 4,000 lining the ground. A large number of visitors travelled with the Warrington contingent to support their favourites, while Widnes enthusiasts availed them- selves of the opportunity to cross the bridge to see the contest between the old time rivals. The ground was a trifle heavy for good football, and a slight wind blew from end to end, otherwise the climatic conditions were all that could be desired, the sun breaking through the clouds, as the rival captains led the way on the field. Both clubs Vlayed representative teams. Jolley took the place of Houghton at back, and Foster took the place of Jolley at half-back. The following were the teams ; . .

Runcorn : Jolley, back; Jones, Butterworth, Price and Moran, three-quarters ; Richardson and Foster, half backs; Walker, Farmer, Woods, Gayter, Moulton, Higgins, Williams and Houghton, forwards. Warrington: Hallam, back; Fish, Dickenson, Burgess and Bailey, three-quarters; Hunter and Hockenhall, half backs ; Boardman, Morrison, Forster, Edmondson, Harmer, Swift,Naylor,and Roberts, forwards. Runcorn won the toss, and aided by a slight wind, immediately commenced offensive tactics. For a moment play settled at centre, but Jones initiated a passing movement which, though nipped in the bud, enabled Butterworth to mark well within the visitors' 25. Offside play saw Runcorn ! contesting matters on the visitors' lines where Fish relieved, intercepting a pass to Richardson, and, by a tricky run, transferred the leather to midway, Price finely stopping his career. A penalty improved matters for the wirepullers, who made a hurried incursion into the home territory. Foster next came out conspicuously ! with a well-judged kick and run, grassing Hallam before Iho could part. From the subsequent scrum the home backs indulged in a neat passing movement, Jones miss- ing a rare chance by throwing forward. For some time the visitors were kept on the run,mainly by some choice kicks by Price. Over-eagerness Haw Runcorn penal- ized, Dickenson and Burgess getting well away, when Butterworth came to the rescue, by grassing Burgess. Richardson took the pass intende d for his partner. Bailey.and again pierced the Warring- ton ranks. Moran improved matters by a neat kick and run leaving the lineat the mercy of Walker, Hallam sav- ing at the right moment. Headed by. Walker,another serious attack was opened out by the forwards. From a close pack between the posts, Foster handed out smartly to Richardsou,who feigned to pass aids° eluded his man touching down the leather just over the line. Farmer added the necessary points from an awkward angle. So far the home contingent had forced the play, but the reverse had the effect of momentarily stirring up the wirepullers. Price who was playing a good game, was next applauded for a smart bit of work which for some time kept Warrington penned on their lines. Danger was averted, Jolley being called upon to save from a splendid dribble by Morrison. Knocking on by Jolley let the visitors in, Dickenson sprinting away only to be stopped by Woods. Fish next gained possession, taking the leather well into the home lines, Jolley again kicking badly and giving Warrington a good chance. Richardson relieved, Price, later,saving when a score seemed imminent. Play afterwards settled at centre where Fish finely fielded the ball from Foster but being well watched could not get away. Butterworth and Price essayed to break away but the defence was too strong to admit liberties. After a period of desultory play Jolley and RiChardson were called upon to stop a passing bout between the visiting backs, Forster, for Warrington, enabling his side to maintain offensive tactics. Jones nailed Dickenson who looked dangerous,but his kick found touch in the home line where the defence was taxed to the uttermost, Bailey being eventually collared by Moran. Exchanges between Hallam and Richardson left the home team in a poor position,but Richardson and Butterworth between them carried the leather to the other end. Foster handed to Richardson ; and he to Moran who dashed through his opponents and got in at the corner. Farmer again converted. Half- time : Runcorn, two goals, two tries; Warrington, nil. On the re-startHallam cleared his lines,Jolly mulling. Fish next gathered and rounded his opponents gallantly but gained little ground. From the scrum the visiting forwards dribbled down with a rush,Jolley and Moran saving grandly. Judicious play kept Warrington out, but they were now showing much better form. Hallam; contributed materially to the attack by judicious kicking a tricky run along touch giving the,homesters a warm five minutes. Forster cleared, but the visitors could not be repelled. Taking an intercepted pass Moran I broke away handing to Richardson who handed back,l Moran being held on the line. Runcorn were not, how- ever to be denied and from a scrum Price, receiving from Forster' got over at the corner. Farmer again kicked a goal. After a little exciting play Swift, who had been previously cautioned for rough play, was sent off the field for fouling Jolle:v. After this Warrington had several narrow escapes, Run- ' corn's over-eagerness making them lose the ball repeat- ' edly at the critical moment. A free kick enabled the I visitors to work the danger away, Hallam being collared ' however before he could part. Two brilliant sprints by Hockenhall and Dickenson saw the home lines in danger. Several scrums were formed but the visitors did not utilise the chances. Dickenson made a grand opening, but the opportunity was lost, Butgess next makjnff desperate effort to get in. Hallam still enabled his side • to keep on the offensive, and up to the close the visitors Iwere well in the home quarters until time, when 'Richardson kicked across to Moran, who followed up and scored at the corner, Farmer failing at goal. Final: i Runcorn, three goals, four tries (18 points) ;Warrington,

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON "A" V. RUNCORN "A."

The "A" team continued their successful career on Saturday and defeated the Runcorn "A "team by seven points to nil. Runcorn started the game before about 1,000 spectators. The opening exchanges favoured War- rington, several scrimmages being fought in front of the goal posts. Aided by a free kick, the visitors gained relief, but Harris retnrned with a good run. By good forward work the visitors gradually bore down on the Warrington line, but their efforts to score were frus- trated by Knight. Edmonds gathered the ball from a scrimmage and passed several opponents, but lacked support., Warrington still kept up the attack, and Runcorn being penalized, Knight had a shot for goal, but the ball went the wrong side of the upright. Another free kick to the Warringtonians saw Knight place the ball safely between the uprights. The homt team were now pressing hotly, and Harris was going strong.when the visitors' full back safely accounted for him. Edmonds was conspicuous with a clever run, and passing to Duckworth, the latter kicked over the line, a race for possession ending in favour of the visitors. Half-time arrived with Warrington leading by two points to nil. In the second half the visitors were the first to make headway. Knight, with a strong kick, sent the ball in touch near the centre, thus giving Warrington welcome relief. Following this the home forwards forced the pace, and for some time the forwards were penned in their own half. Harris made a dash for the line, but was checked at the critical moment. The home three- quarterspassed splendidly, Brooks spoiling a movement by failing to take a pass from Edmonds. The Runcorn backs now got going, but Edmonds intercepted, and kicking acroAs to Watkins, the latter safely planted the leather behind the posts for Knight to add the additional points. No further scoring took place, and an interest- ing match ended in favour of Warrington by seven points to nil.

div.head: ALLEGED FATAL FIGHT AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED FATAL FIGHT AT WIDNES.
Verdict of "Manslaughter."

Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at Widnes, on Saturday, on the body of James Cain, twenty-three years of age, of Catherine-street, who, it is alleged, met his death from injuries received in a fight with Lawrence Bowles, of 2, Edmund-street, on Sunday night. From tile evidence of the police, read by the coroner, it. appeared that Cain was drinking in the Ship Inn, when Bowles entered and demanded a drink. This was refused at first but he subsequently was supplied. A quarrel ensued and both went outside and fought. It is alleged that Cain received such injuries as caused his death.

Dr. Hutchinson, as the result of a post-mortem examination, would prove that death was due to meningitis caused by a fractured skull. Bridget Cain, mother of the deceased, said he left, home on Sunday at twelve o'clock. On Mondor morn- ing he was ill on the sofa. They had a conversation, and he went to sleep. When he awoke he vomited blood and his nose bled. At night he commenced moaning, and a doctor was sent for. He became worse, and died on Thursday.

Eliza Stafford, 40, Margaret-street, said she saw the men fighting in the street. She heard Bowles say, "Pull off your jacket and have it out." Both stripped to the skin for the fray, and Cain had some hard knocks on the ground, his head on one occasion coming in violent con- tact with the kerbstone. Witness saw Bowles kick deceased on the body.
Peter Carrol, 34, Margaret-street, also gave evidence. but it was quite different from the evidence he had given the police, which caused the coronor to give him a severe admonition.

The Coroner, in summing up, pointed out that there were circumstances in the case sufficiently extenuating for him to advise the jury to return a verdict of man- Slaughter. The jury returned a verdict of "Manslaughter," and the prisoner was committed for trial on the coroner's warrant. _ _ _
•On Monday prisoner appeared before the local Bench and was remanded.
