THE British trade-

MORE ABOUT THE unionists wh) made MOSELEY COMMISSION, a tout: through the United States on the invitation of Mr. MOSELEY have still to issue their report. But it has already come out that they were not at all discouraged by the signs of enter- prise which they saw in the factories, and they think our defects lie rather in our machinery than in the character of our men. It is something to get that concession, for we know that if the workers had not looked so askance at the intro- duction of machinery in past years much of our trade that has gone across the Atlantic would have been preserved. In the new number of the " World's Work" there is an article from a gentle - man who accompanied the Commission. It is in - teresting because he can say things with a greater freedem and less responsibility than apper- tains to the delegates. \Vtiat struck Mr. CUNNIF, and, indeed, has long been realised by Mr. MOSELEY, is that the friction between employers and employed in America always indi- cates vitality. Often it does a lot of harm to one or the other side; the conflict of interests, when it occurs, is generally sharper; the trade-unioniits hit out with a freedom that is impossible in the old country; and the capitalist allows no kind of sentiment to stand in his way in suclia straggle But in tights of this kind there is somathing to think about. Tempests of this sort cannot be kept up fur ever; and these labour troubles are followed by an increasing dispsition to settle the controversies by an appeal to reason. In Great Britain our trade-unionists are inclined to be moody, suspicious, distrustful. Tney are, it i trio, curbed and fetterep4 by the law in a way that is unknown in America, and it is at to make them look at everything .with pre- judice. The non-unionist is even worse. Each individual, fighting for himself, regards every new movement as boding mischief, and his one concern frequently is to maintain the old

'order and rely upon reputation. All these con- Zitions are unsatisfactory, but the point to be brought home to the British workmen is that the Americans are at least " awalie." The fault, of course, is not alone with the work-people. If this Commission serves for anything, it will tend, Mr. CIINNIV thinks, to bring into relief the short-com- ings of employers in Great Britain. Mr. MOSELEY does not hesitate tc say—and he knows a good deal about our English factories—that a man who •offers a suggestion towards improving methods of work is likely to be sacked. "British industrial life is so crystallised that a foremaii resents a 'suggestion as a hint of his incompetence likely to bring his discharge." In the States it is quite .different. That pious theory, that within the Re- public all men are equal, serves at least to 'enable people of all grades to be on easy 'terms of conversation. A master welcomes a word from any of his men; and .if the master does, the overseers must be equally receptive. Some of the alleged triumphs of the Americans;however, are not so magnificent as they 'seem. They are susceptible of explanation, which your English trade-unionist secretary gives bluntly •enough. The assertion that the American lays 1,500 bricks while the Britisher lays only four or five hundred is absurd. The American -record •at Westingnouse fat:tory, near Manchester, was done on straight foundation work, and as the 'edifice rose the pace declined until it got nearly down to the ordinary British Tate. The reason that greater speed is got in America is declared to be simply that the erection is flimsier. Our archi- tects require' the overlaying of bricks in every layer—that is, locking every course instead of every fifth course, which used to be the case; and that adds a third to the labour cost of bricklaying. There is one aspect of American industry at which our own people look with a natural feeling of horror. This is the sub- division of labour to such an extreme as to make the working life hardly bearable. *Prosperity may be bought at too high a price if it destroys the intelligence of the people, and reduces them to skilled automata, marvellous in one line but good for nothing else. At a packing house in Chicago six girls about a talaie divide the simple motions that go to filling phials with beef extra it ; and day after day they/do exactly the same work, the one consideration being speed. Mr. ROBERT BARR: who is, by the way, an American resident in England by choice, has affirmed, half in jest and half in earnest, that the American race will decline rapidly in the course of a few generations; and a hundred years hence some prairie farmers will occasionally be seen coming to look at the ruins of New York. He bolds that the town workers are consuming their vitality. One of the points as to which the MOSELEY Commission had to inquire, was whether the average life of the American work- man is shorter than that of the English workman; and whether, if this is so, the overstrain is due to climate or conditions of labour. The answer can- not be quite conclusive; it can only be appreciated a generation later.

The most noteworthy feature of the annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Conamerce Was the presidential address of Mr. C. E. Parker. Very briefly and concisely, the President contras- t? d American methods of securing the co-opera- tio nof the inventive genius of their workpeople, With British methods. He pointed to the signifi• earit fact that a very large portion of the labour- saving appliances and machinery in use in this ace'untry are of American origin and manufacture, In ascribing a reason for our reliance upon the thgentlity of the American people, he expressed e ?Pinion that the conditions and prejudices associated with the British industrial system do nt call forth and encourage the skill and ingenuity of those engaged in mechanical pursuits. He drew a rosy picture of what the trade of this •country would he if it were possible to get the brains of the British workmen to assist in the cheapening of the cost of production and in im- proving the style and utility of the finished article. The question will naturally arise ? How is this very desirable end to be secured? To answer the -question it is necessary to cast our eyes across the Atlantic and see how the American manufacturer has solved the problem. A concrete case was given by Mr. Parker which aptly applies to the point. It aPPears that by means of "suggestion boxes" placed in the various departments of a large American works, the operatives Were indticed, with the incentive of substantial prize money,to make 4,000 suggestions in a single :Year for the improvement of any process, machine, Oi method. Of these suggestions it was found P.ractical to adopt 2,000. It will be seen from this a,ingle instance that a spirit of co-operation nrcathes through the American industrial system, „and both employer and employed are profiting ',torn a mutual desire to turn out the best manu- factured article with the best results.

When we wrote, a few weeks ago, the obituary notice of the notorious Green Dragon, we did not anticipate that a new and more active Green Dragon, would rise, Phcenix-like, from its ashes. 'Thanks to the pusillanimity of the Warrington magisterial bench, however, the abhorred Green Dragon is alive once more and has at last secured a habitation at the Brooklands, Lovely-lane, in the centre of a hostile community. They neither require nor want any dragons in the shape of Public-houses in this locality, and to at last have one foisted upon them by a body of justices—save the mark—who have obviously truckled to the brewery influence, has naturally roused keen resentment. Lovely-lane is one of the few districts—if not the only one—which are comparativly immune from the public-house 'element, and that .the magistrat m should counten- ance the intrusion is not only to be regretted, but it .reflects seriously upon their judgment and eapaclty. Our readers will probably recollect that the Green Dragon application , has been refused twice, but the brewers evidently believe in the potency of "third times " fer they tried again and inecessfully,on Monday. The only newS evidence of any importance consisted of an offer by Messrs. 'Greenall, Whitley and Co., to surrender two 1869 beerhouses—" profitable businesses.' we are told— in return for the transfer of the Green Dragon trom its doomed lair in Bridge-street, to Lovely- Jane. The bait" took," we are sorry to say, and in the face of conscientious opposition from reqi- dents, and the firm opinion of the Chief Constable himself that a licence was not required in this dis- trict, the magistrates by a majority of nearly two to one granted the application. Thus has the 'baneful power of the "bung,"which we had thought and hoped was waning in Warrington, shown its domination once more. Warrington has long suffer- ed from this cause,and the day of its emancipation 'seems as far off as ever—unless the next generation of magistrates happily prove themselves to be made of sterner stuff than those of to-day.

It is questionable whether the Town Council will welcome the action taken by managers of the 'Warrington Church schools with reference to the -working of the new Education Act. The resolu tioo which was Passed at the meeting last Thurs-- ,day is certainly delicatsly framed, and simply asks •the Town Council if they are willing to receive nominations from a representative body of Church Day School managers in regard to the constitution of the Education Committee. But even such a resolution cannot fail to eacite suspicion. an the event of the Town Council reply- ing in the affirmative the Roman Catholics and Nonconformists will be entitled to ask for a similar privilege. The acceptance of nominations or recommendations from outside bodies will have the effect of introducing the religious question

div.head: ALARMING FIRE AT EARLESTOWN. Shops Gutted. An Inefficient Fire Brigade.
div.p: ALARMING FIRE AT EARLESTOWN. Shops Gutted. An Inefficient Fire Brigade.
Prompt Action of the Warrington Brlgade.

At an early hour on Wednesday morning, an outhrelk of fire was discovered in the shop known as the City Supply Stores, Market-street, Earlestown. At the out- set it wa,s Of an insignificant character, and as the policeman on daystated, he could LINO extinguished it had he been able to Obtain water. .Owing to it being shut off from the town during the day, this he was uhable to do. Consequently all he could do was to rouse the inmates of the adjoining shop, a confectioner's, in the occupation of Mr, J. Derbyshire. The City Supply Stores was fortunately unoccupied, the manager, Mr. J. Littler, residing elsewhere. The premises had been left apparently safe the previous night,and it is difficult to ex- plain the cause of the outbreak,but it is supposed ,some Christmas decorations on a gas bracket being of a highly inflammable character,and the gas being left alight,took fire and rapidly spread. The alarm was figiven, and the , town fire brigade summoned, but it was found that the DOW steam fire engine was Useless owing to it having been . supplied incomplete, but oven had it been turned out, it would ' have been of no use, as the water could not be .obtained. A telephone message was sent to Warrington for assist- ance, and in 25 minutes after receiving the call, the steam fire engine and the brigade, fully equipped arrived on the scone In the meantime, Mr. R. Cummings of the Viaduct Works fire brigade had been summoned, and the brigade turned out. When it was found the town's water supply was minus, the London and North-Western Company's valve was opened, and immediately,the fire- men were in a position to cope with the flames, which by this time had got a firm hold of both buildings, hav- ing had free play for nearly two hours. The town's water was then turned on, and the firemen had an adequate supply, but it was too late to be of any benefit in saving the premises, both places being completely gutted, and the furniture and stock destroyed. When the Wurrington brigade arrived,the local firemeq had got ' the upper hand, and their services of course were not required, but the Warrington men deserve the greatest praise for the promptitude with which they responded to the call, and it was certainly no fault of theirs that they were too late to take. part in the work of fighting tho flames. Had a strong wind been blowing from the east, they would have had more than enough to do, as owing to the absence of the water, nothinr, could have saved the adjoining drapers .shop of Mr. E.T. Evans,and in all probability the whole of the block of shops on that side of Market-street would have been swept away. The damage dode is considerable, but the buildings are covered by insur- ance.. Much indignation is felt in the town at the farcical failure of the Town's fire brigade and the useless- ness of an engine which was purchased less than 6 months ago at a large expenditure of money, and there are threats of an indignation meeting of long-suffering ratepayers.
e DARING ROBBERY AT EARLESTOWN.

On Saturday morning the inmates of the Ram's Head Hotel were astonished to find that the patent check till and its contents had been removed, somewhere between closing and opening time. The house was locked up and left secure soon after :El o'clock on Friday night, hut about £l2 in gold and silver was left in the till which was attached to the counter, the remainder of the day's takings being removed to the safe. The thief or thieves had forced the till from its fastenings and carried it away, but how they had effected an entrance to the house could not beascertained. it is supposed,however, that the entry has been made by way of the cellar trap- door in the backyard, as none of the fastenings to the house doors were disturbed. Up to the present the police have no shadow of a clue. ST. JOHN'S SUNDAY SCHOOL, EART.ESTOWN. .

The annual distribution of prizes in connection with the above Sunday school took place in the Mission Hall on Monday evening. The Rev. I'. R. Matthews was in the chair and in his opening re-,,arks referred' to the work of the school during the past year. In consequence of the attendance having fallen below: the average, the number of prizes gained were not as great as last year. A new department had been opened at the Manor school which was superintended by Mr. T. Allen. During the evening, songs were rendered by Miss Winstonly, Mrs. Jackson, and Mr. Joseph Brown. Gramophone selec- tions by Mr. Greening and a pianoforte solo by Miss Ada Woods, whilst a dialogue entitled "A Sprig of Holy," brought the programme to a conclusion. The prizes were distributed by the Rev. T. R. Matthews. LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER the CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt

In appointing such a committee, the Town Council will not require much outside assistance.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDEES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDEES.
CHARITY BALL AT P. VNCORN.

On Wednesday the annual Catho 1 o charity ball in con- nection with St. Edward's Church was held in Runcorn Public Hall, which was tastefully decorated. The function was a great success, and the funds for the erection of new day schools would materially benefit. Music was provided by Mr. T. Knight's quadrille band. The duties of M.C's. were fulfilled by Messrs. H. and G. Prescott, and Mr. J. Donellan was the hon. secretary. The refreshment department was in charge of Mr. and Mrs Conway, Mrs. Nixon, Mrs Prescott and Mr. Wylde.

div.head: A.SSAULT ON A. GIRL AT RUNCORN
div.p: A.SSAULT ON A. GIRL AT RUNCORN

Michael Feeney, farm labourer' of Whitley, near Northwich, was charged before the Runcorn magistrates on Thursday, with assaulting Mary Cunnington, aged fifteen years, on Tuesday. The girl said she was servant at Mrs. Woodfme's lodging-house in Fryer-street. There were thirty lodgers in the house. She was showing an old man to his room, when the prisoner assaulted her, •and Police-constable Gregory apprehended him. Prisoner who stoutly denied the charge, was sentenced to a month's hard labour. THE SMALL-PDX AT THE 'WORKHOUSE.

There htt:Ce been Two-fresh cases of small-pox notified during the week end at Dutton Workhouse. The first was notified on Saturday and the second on Monday morning. illoth patients are men who have been in the hause some time, and is is supposed they came in con• tact with the man Walker who contracted the disease a fortnight ago. They have been removed to the Moore Hospital. When the first case occurred,the Workhouse was placed in quarantine for 18 days. The period-has been extended for a similar time. The meetings of the Board of Guardians and Rural District Council have been held at Daresbury. PRIMITIVE METHODIST_ SALE OF WORK.

On Thursday, the "Sale of Work" was re-opened by Mrs. Brockbank, Mrs. Eyre presiding in the unavoidable absence of Mr. F. Beck. Miss Ball presented to Mrs. Brockbank a handsome basket of flowers and Miss Lizzie Eyre gave (on behalf of Mrs. Ball) a lovely spray of flowers to the President and a pretty buttonhole to Rev. W. A. Eyre. The proceedings throughout were of a most interesting character. Proceeds of Sale, for both days including (in addition to those already announced) donations, A. R. Norman, Esq., £2; J. Pritchard, Esq.. £2; Mrs. Brockbank, £3; Mr. F. Beck, £1 is.; Mr. James Stubbs, £1; Mr. Dutton 135.; £B5 ss. To this must be added £3 10s. collected by the choir, ChristmaS singing, for the same object.and.£`4s ss. raised by" Sewing Meeting" teas for reduction of .debt. Total £ll4. in last weeks issue the names of Mrs. Fleet (refreshments), and Miss B. Fleet (New Year's Tree) were inadvertently omitted from the list of stallholders.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

It is with feelings of deepest sympathy with the Master and matron,that Runcornians view the spread of the small-pox epidemic at the Workhouse. Everything that can be done is being done to check the disease,and it is to be hoped that the efforts will prove sitccessful. Sine the last meeting there have been two fresh cases and one suspect which may prove later on to be a small- pox case. The house has been put in quarantine for a still further period and there is every likelihood that the next half dozen meetings will be held at Daresbury. Owing to the Daresbury Sessions the next meeting will beheld at Frodsham and the Council might well con- sider the advisability of holding the further meetings at that place it being much more central and "get-at- able "than Daresbury.

Should inupers have a vote •? This question was dis- cussed at the Guardians meeting and a proposal in the negative was carried. Mr. A. R. Norman was decidedly of opinion that out relief should not disenfranchise the recipient and there is much more to. be said for,than against this view of the question. As Mr. Norman pertinently argued,there are a great many persons who have become reduced in circumstances through no fault of their own and it is manifestly unjust to deprive them of their vote. It would be far better,he contended,to let all have a vote than allow any to suffer unjustly. Mr. Norman lost his motion but there is no doubt that he ought to have carried it.

Father Chambers, though about to leave the town, does not intend to retire Rom his position as member of the Board. The rev, gentleman is quite right in acting thus, as he is the only representative of the Catholic interest in the town. However, a week or two longer on the local education authority does not make much odds, as he will be compelled to retire with the others in a few short weeks under the Education Bill.

Judging from Mr. Handley's remark the juvenile life of the town is much infested with sickness at the pre- sent time. In the infant schools there has been a great falling off in attendance With, the exception of the National School. There may be other causes at work which may account for the absentees, but unquestion- ably sickness is the prime factor,

The drunks are still a minus quantity at the Runcorn Police Court. Really if the townsfolk continue in the process of moral evolution our gentlemen in blue will have to be given marching orders for fields and pastures new.

With respect to the recent case at the Court where a teacher ws fined for excessively punishing a boy, two letters appear in our correspondence columns to which we direct our readers attention. One good result of the prosecution is that the Cottage Hospital Fund is likely to be the richer by upwards of .123.

St. Paul's home missions this year have been among the most successful ever held. On Sunday and Monday the Church was crowded to its utmost apacity at all the services. On Monday many could not obtain a seat. The Rev. Owen Watkins was the preacher and special interest centred with the fact that he had been shut up with Sir G. White in Ladysmith. The thrilling incidents of the siege were listened to by a spell-bound congregation for over an hour and a half. The col- lection realized about ,£5O compared with £l5 last year.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Warrington were the visitors at Trwell-lane on Satur- day, and for once received at the hands of the Linnets a regular drubbing. The losing side were decidedly off form, while Runcorn combined in a splendid fashion throughout. The only wonder is that the score was not much heavier. The game was fought keenly, and with the exception of one or two regrettable little incidents there was nothing to mar the good feeling which pre- vailed. The home backs were far superior to their vis-a-rig, Foster, for Runcorn, playing on the whole a very fair game. Jolley did not shape so well as was anticipated at his new position. But for Hallam, who played a capital defensive game, Warrington wouldhave had to mourn over a considerably heavier defeat.
APPOINTMENT OF A CURATE FOR ST. JOHN'S CHURCH
EARLESTOWN. The Rev. Mr. Ainley, curate of Maryport, Cumber- land, has been appointed Curate of St. John's Church, Earlestown. He will, it is expected, take up his duties about Easter.

Mr. Nfaclntyre said that the Parliamentary Committee had resolved not to support the resolution. Mr. Norman said that he could not agree with the recommendation of the Parliamentary Committee. He knew many deserving people who had appealed to the Board through sheer necessity, and he did not think that such ought to be disfranchised. He thought it quite possible to discriminate between the deserving and the undeserving case. He moved as an amendment that the Board support the resolution. Mr. Collier seconded.

Mr. Woodward said he could not support the amend- ment, as they could not discriminate between the deserving and the undeserving. After a further discussion the amendment was lost. THE MAINTENANCE OF PAUPER LUNATICS.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

Mr. .Tames Pritchard presided over the monthly meeting of this Board on Tuesday evening. There were also present Messrs. F. J. Norman, W. Handley, S. 'Taylor, E. Imison. J. W. Lightburn, (clerk), A. Light- burn,(deputy clerk). The School Management Committee recommended that accounts amounting to £219 His. Bd. be passed for payment. At the committee the Clerk presented a report on the accommodation of the Victoria-roadßoard and Granville-street schools, which was approved. The report was to the effect that in the annual report of the Board of Education a passage occurred drawing attention to insufficient accommodation for the average attend- ance at the Victoria-road schools. This should be at once remedied or the grant next year would be endangered. Mr. Keep, one of H.M. Inspectors, made the following entry in the log book on... October 28th, 1901 :—This school is overcrowded, especially the class rooms occu- pied by Standards 11., 111., and IV. Standards 11. and IV. are insufficiently staffed. It is almost impossible for the teachers to properly manage Standard IV., as many children have to be accommodated in the adjoin- ing rooms when any writing has to be done." The Clerk's report went on to say that in the presence of these two official reports it was incumbent upon the Board to takl action in the matter either by increasing the accommodation or revising the average attendance. The latter process, if not impossible, would be extremely difficult: The School Management Committee reported that an inspection on the enlargement of these schools by which the increased accommodation of 134 would be secured,would take place. The report was adopted and plans were submitted to, and affirmed by the Board at the monthly -meeting held on December 23rd last, the Clerk being directed to forward the plans when corn- pleted,to the Board of Education for its sanction. The completed plans were received on the 6th inst., and for- warded the same day to the Board of Education. The receipt thereof was duly acknowledged, but no infor- mation had yet beenreceived by the Board. To obtain immediate increase of accommodation it was thought wise to utilise the room in Granville-street, occupied by the Pupil Teachers' Central Class, which was certified to accommodate 70 children. It was - proposed to reserve the room for the next stan- dard, namely Standard 11., which had hitherto been taught by the Board in the school when thus occupied, and thus certified accommodation for 285 children would be utilised. Messrs. Pritchard, Imison, and Handley subsequently were unanimous in considering that the unused room originally intended for the cloak room on the first floor, 133- the Granville- street school, could be well and cheaply adapted for the occupants of the Pupil Teachers' Central Class. Thel necessary alterations consisted chiefly of the erection of wood partitions,and this room had the advantage of being a part of their ; own premises. The offices and private room were available as before. Twenty two children belonging to Standard 11,were transferred, one teacher being re-transferred from the Victoria-road School, thus increasing the staff. The average number of children in excess of accommodation referred to by. the Board of Education when Mr. Keep made his re- port was 84.—The Clerk reported that Mr. R. A. Naylor of Warrington, had, through Mr Posnett, presented the Board with a set of parallel bars and fittings, and that he had on behalf of the Board thanked Mr. Naylor for the gift. Mr. Handley proposed that the minutes be passed. The Clerk's report was so 'exhaustive that no ad- ditional informationwas required from him. It showed that at any rate they-were trying to cope with the over- crowding referred to. He had noticed from the report that although they- had opened in Granville-street a school for the teaching of Standard IL they had some- thing like 200 more scholars on the books at Victoria-road than they had certified accommodation for. This showed that although they had met the case,they were ' still at fault,which would not be remedied until new accommodation was provided,for which plans were being considered by the Department. They had sufficient teach- ing power for all the scholaraattending all the schools. With regard to the school attendance work the report showed that there must be a fair amount of sickness in the town amongst the young children. For the first time he knew that all the infants' schools were thus affected. At Mill Brow there were 36 away. ,That meant accommo- dation in exeess of the average attendance of 36. In Granville-street there was room for 115. In the National schools there were places for 45; Newtown, 17; Trinity,l64; and St, Edward's, 40: Thus there were 335 places in excess of the average accommodation which pointed to a large amount of sickness. He hoped that before long the children would be in such a state of health as would cause a diminution of sickness in the town, and a correspondingly better attendance. Mr. Imison seconded, and Said he did not quite grasp what Mr. Handley said about the attendance at the schools. He did not think the National , schools were affected in any way. So far as the figures showed there was an increase in the attendance compared with the same time last year. Mr, Handley said it must be remembered that the accommodation at the National schools had been very largely increased. Mr. Imison: I am not carping,bnt I want to know whether it can be shown that sickness is the cause of the falling off in the attendance. The extra acco{nmo- dation provided would not affect it at all. Mr. Handley said he inferentially took it that sick- ness would be the cause of the falling off in attendance. He knew there was a great deal of sickness in the town, and this would affect the schools. Mr. Taylor said that applied equally to other schools as the National. There might be other causes why the children were absent. It was not always wise to spread a report about the town that they had a large number absent from their schools on account of sickneas. Mr. Handley Not for children from sto 14.

The Clerk said Mr. Handley was quite right. The Parish schools were not affected though the other schools were. It was a remarkable thing that some schools were affected,such as Granville-street and Mill- brow, and others might not be affected at all. Thirty- two boys were absent from the Victoria-road school in consequence of sicltnesS,while the National schools escaped. The minutes were passed. 'FATHER CHAMBERS THANKS THE BOARD.

The Rev. Father Chambers wrote to the Chairman to the effect that he would probably know that he was leaving Runcorn, and he wished to express his deep gratitude to the members of the board for their kindness to him. He regretted leaving the town at a time when, naturally, it would be interesting to watch the working out of the new Act. It was impracticable in the present stage of the education question to speak of resigning as a member .1 the Board. He hoped that the committee that would be formed under the new Bill would justly consider the interests of the Catholics of Runcorn. and that they would have adequate representation. The chairman said Father Chambers had always proved himself an agreeable member ever since he had been associated with the Board. He might be under the impression tha he could no longer serve as a member as he was taking up his residence in another place, but he need not resign. That was not exactly a resignation. Mr. Norman: No, not at all. It was resolved that the Clerk write to Father Chambers. pointing out that he could still be a member of the Board, although he was leaving the town and that if he desired he could continue his services.

The fortnightly meeting of the above authority was held on Tuesday at the Daresbury Sessional House, under the presidency of Mr. J. Stokes.—Present : Messrs. A. R. Norman,S.Taylor,T. Woods, T. Mr. Riley, relieving officer, reported that he had re- lieved 52 vagrant cases at a cost of 17s. against 3 the previous fortnight. MORE SMALL-PDX CASES AT THE WORKHOUSE. The Clerk reported the removal of Thomas Worrall. aged 56, and John Antrobus, aged 74; • from the Work- house to Moore Small-Pox Hospital. Mr. Woods asked whether there were any suspeet3 in the house. _ _
_ The Clerk replied that there had been one suspect reported that morning.
A LEIGH .PATIENT -THROUGH THE CASUAL WARD.

The Local Government Board notified. the Gnardians of a case of Small-pox at Leigh Workhouse on January 15th, the patient being a vagrant who had spent January 2nd and 3rd in Runcorn Casual Ward. The communication was handed to Dr. Selby, who, in reply, stated that the man named had never been in Runcorn Casual Ward. _ _ _ _
The Master stated that he had ihad the cells and rugs thoroughly fumigated. .

div.head: LETTER OF INQUIRY.
div.p: A LETTER OF INQUIRY.

A letter was read from Miss M. W. Kett, secretary of the Northern Workhouse Nursing Association who stated that Nurse IVlary Hampson would on February Ist have completed'her term of three years service of the Association and before granting her her service certificate and silver medal, the Association Committee would be glad to know whether her work and conduct have been quite satisfactciry during the three years she had worked under the Runcorn Board, and whether Nurse Rae had also given satisfaction. in reply, Mr Cunnah the Workhouse Master, said Nurse Hampson and Nurse Rae had performed their duties in a satisfactory manner.

div.head: LABOUR COLONIES.
div.p: LABOUR COLONIES.

Mr. John R. Rigby, assistant clerk to the Ashbourne Union,forwarded copy of the following resolution passed by his Board,and asked for the support of the Runcorn. Board :—That this Board r6quests the Local Govern- ment Board to obtain the sanction of Parliament to a scheme enabling Poor Law Unions throughout England and Wales to combine for the Purposes of the provision and maintenance of Labour Colonies and for the deten- tion and employment therein of vagrants, and that this Board, generally speaking, supports the suggestions made by the Richmond Union in June last on the sub- ject, and further, that the Local Government Board be strongly urged to deal with the whole question of vagrancy with the least possible delay. Mr. Mclntyre said that the provision of labour colonies was a very intricate one and they might, if introduced, have a very beneficial effect upon the vagrancy question. He contended that they ought to have more power in dealing with the vagrancy question. The Chairmen .was of opinion that the vagrancy question was an important oneand demanded immediate attention. The Leigh authorities said that a man had broken out with saiall-pox in the area who had been traced to Dutton. There should be some means of re- gistration so that they could tell the, deserving work- man from the tramp. Mr. Norman pointed out that the Leigh authorities did not attribute the blame to the man having passed th rough Dutton casual ward. The manhad been in other infected areas and it was impossible to say where he had contracted the disease.

The Clerk said that the Leigh authorities had stated that the probable source of the infection was Oldham. Mr. Woods remarked that there were already organised labour colonies in Germany where vagrants found begging,were given work to do. It was ultimately resolved that the Board support the resolution.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. By " Ovalist." Bravo, Runcorn! allegiance is transferred from the " wirepullers " to the "linnets "—until the fortner begin to win matches. . I have got tired of pinning my faith to an incapable and unlucky, team like Warrington,and Runcorn so took my eye on Satur_ _ _ _ _ _ _ . _
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. By " Ovalist." Bravo, Runcorn! allegiance is transferred from the " wirepullers " to the "linnets "—until the fortner begin to win matches. . I have got tired of pinning my faith to an incapable and unlucky, team like Warrington,and Runcorn so took my eye on Satur- _ _ _ _ _ _ _ . _

_ .day that I fe-el that I must henceforth, until the afore- mentioned miracle happens, shout for the Runcornians. They are a gallant crew and the workmanlike way in which they "mopped up" the -aspiring Warrington men was a treat to behold. Probably the bulk of the visiting spectators think differently,t Lei r parti-coloured spectacles do not permit them to see any treat under such circumstances, and in such case they are unfor- tunate. After the first chill realization: of the fact that Warrington were going to be beaten, it was possible to forget it and admire the play of the winners. • And there was plenty to admire ! Runcorn played better football on Saturday than I have seen any team play this season—and I have witnessed a few good games. The Linnets were very chirpy and put up what stands, I believe, as a record beating for Warrington in the annals Of the contests between the two clubs. Eighteen points to nil is the worst jar Warrington have had this season and the least ex- pected.

From appearances in the morning, • when torrents of rain fell, it seemed as if the match was going to be entirely spoiled. But the elements improved, and there was sunshine during most of the afternoon, while the ground itself was in surprisingly good order. About 200 WarringtonianS accompanied the team, while many Widnes folk crossed the bridge as the " Chemicals " were away from home. There would be a good 4,000 on the ground when operations started, and this is considerably above Runcorn's average of public support. Warrington's chances were considered fair until it was learned that the Cap- tain, Isherwood, was unfit for play. This made a big difference to the side, and Runcorn were not slow to take advantage of it. Bailey was the substitute for Isherwood, and played on the wing next to Burgess.

Winning the toss was a great advantage to Run-: corn who went about their work from the kick-off in a style which showed their determination to get a lead before .the change of ends. They attacked per- sistently and numerous efforts were made to get Davie Jones in on the right but Fish and Dickenson were always more than a match for the Runcornians on this wing. In fact the attack was reversed by Fish who robbed Jones and ran beautifully half the length of the ground before he was grassed. The Linnets then changed their tactics and getting within striking distance .once more, they worked , the other wing. Richardson broke Away and with a sham pass bluffed Burgesa and Bailey, crossing the line just as Hallam brought him down. It was a clever try, but Farmer's goal. was even better.. Before long Warrington were again in extremis and fine combination by the home backs proved too good, and Moran crossed at the cor- ner, Farmer kicking another remarkable goal and putting Warrington ten points in arrears. Before the interval the visitors made a couple of good ~fforts but were repulsed. The re-start soon saw Warrington on the: offensive. Thy pegged away in the home quarter, and Dicken- son had hard luck in not getting through. There was not the same cleverness manifested by Warrington, however, and they were easier to keep at bay than Runcorn. }or all that,they appeared likely to score until a fine break-away by the home backs changed the venue, and the next minute Prince scored the third try and Fanner kicked the third goal. Back came Warrington again, Burgess going to the base of the scrum and livening things up considerably. Hunter and Hockenhall both fell back, and the unique spec- tacle of one half and five three-quarters was witnessed. Burgess prOved quite equal to the occasion though the men behind could not score, Fish once missing a lovely opening from a pass which went in touch. Then Swift got marching orders for a •small offence, and Runcorn making another spurt scored again through Moran,and thus completed the tale of Warrington's misfortunes. They only got well into the Warrington half twice after the interval,but the two visits yielded them eight points. ----- There was no question which was the better team. Runcorn were umneasurably superior to Warrington ill the finer points of the game. Their combination was equal to anything in the history of the club, while Warrington's was correspondingly ragged. It was here that the difference was most marked. Warring- ton worked quite as hard as their opponents and held their own forward, but they were thoroughly beaten at half and threequarter. Richardson was the best man on the field and had a hand in all Runcorn's tries. His work at half-back was distinctly classy. I liked, too, .the way the Runcorn threequarters Tined out, well behind the pack and at a good distance from one another. The passing was always clean, quick, and long--giving the defence little chance to stop the men when once on the. move. Price and Butterworth were also excellent at centre, while Walker and Farmer led the forwards • gallantly. Hallam was better than .Tolley at fullback and did glod work. Burgess and Dickenson also distinguished themselves. Fish .was toe well marked to do much, and the other backs were outclassed. Bailey shaped well at times but wati no match for the men in front of him. Morrison and Forster w6re the best of the forwards.
Widnes and Huddersfield were also beaten on Saturday, so that Warrington escaped any further de- scent in the league table. Broughton's draw with Swinton again opens out the championship.
The League table up to date is as follows : For Agst.

On Tuesday evening Swift's case came, before, the League Committee, and be was suspended up to February 7th. . Warrington's postpone match with St. Helens was ordered to be played on February .2 Ith (Shrove Tuesday).

Warrington spectators could not Wish for a more interesting engagement than that down for decision at Wilderspool to-day. Batley are the visitors, and as the rivalry between the tWo teams hasheen of the keenest character since the Northern Union was formed there is sure to be a big crowd. The teams have already met once this season at Batley, when Warrington got the better of a hard struggle by a goal to nil. Dickenson, on that occasion, played a superb game, and had most to do with keeping the home team on the defensive. Fish and Wattie Davies were also very prominent but each was too well watched to do any scT%ring, though Fish kicked the winning goal for Warrington. Batley are sure to make a big effort to win, and as they have been doing as well lately as Warrington have been doing badly, they will doubtless not lack confidence. It is just ttlis latter qnality Warrington need, and if they can defeat the "gallant youths " to-day there is every probability of the team coming ,back to form again. Batley have *on their last eight engagements in succession while Warrington have only won once in the _last ten matches. If form counted for very much, the visitors should have an easy journey, but I they will certainly not have that.

Isherwood is still unfit—and by the way his in- jury was received on the occasion of Warrington's last victory, at Widnes--and Dickensoi . will again partner Fish. Harris comes in again vice Bailey and will have Hockenhall as centre, while Burgess and Duckworth are :to operate behind the pack. The changes should prove beneficial, and with the follow- ing team Warrington have a good chance of stopping the progressive career of the Batleyites : Hallam, full back; Fish, Dickenson, Ifockenhall and Harris, three-quarters; Burgess and Duckworth, half-kicks ; Boardman, Morrison, Roberts, Harmer, Forster, Naylor, Edmondson, and Ashton, forwards.

The " A" team is just as successful as the premier team is otherwise. They beat _Runcorn "A" on Saturday by 7 points to nil, this making the twelfth successive victory. Edmunds 'and Watkins both played finely, and it was mainly through their efforts that the smart Runcorn juniors were sent back point- less. Werneth away is:the fixture for Warrington " A" to-day.

div.head: E. Pierpoint
div.p: E. Pierpoint
WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COMMERCE. Annual Meeting. interzsting Address by the President.
At the Town Hall, on Monday, the annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce was held. The President (Mr. C..E. Parker) presided.
THE YEAR' " WORK'.

1 Councillor A. Bennett (secretary), submitted his annual report on the year's work. He mentioned that Messrs. Fletcher, Russell, and Co., Ltd., communicated ; an interesting statement of the anomalies of the exist- ing law upon the registration of designs to the Council, ! and were instituting further inquiries with a view to ; the submission of a resolution at the autumnal meeting of the Associated Chambers. With respect to the I growth of cotton within the empire, Messrs. Armitage I and Rigby were appointed as the representatives of the Chamber on the committee formed in Manchester to further this important question. Admiralty leather patterns were once again displayed at the offices of the I Chamber, and forms of tender sent to all the local tanners who are members. Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., Ltd., submitted a copy of a circular which they Are issuing to all their workmen announcing that they had arranged to give their staff a week's holiday in August instead of during Whit-week, and asking for the opinion of the Council as to the expediency of such a change. It was pointed out that the question didnot greatly affect Warrington, and that it was not, there- fore, necessary to take any action in the matter. Mr. E. L. Fleming (Messrs. W. A. Bishop and Co., Ltd.), submitted an interesting statement as to his arrest for shipping certain goods to Americawhich, although com- plying with the conditions of the American tariff, were seized and retained by the American Customs autho- rities, in spite of the fact that Mr. Fleming's action was successfully vindicated in the American courts. At his request, the Chamber wrote to the local member (Mr. Robert Pierpoint) requesting him to use his influence with the Foreign Office. Mr. Pierpoint had a personal interview with the Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs upon the subject ; but unfortunately, up to now, has not been able to secure the desired redress. Attention was called to the inadequate train service between Warrington and London, and, in reply to a letter from the Secretary, the London and North-Western Railway Company have promised to consider the matter in the spring.—Mr. Andrew Rath- bone (the Firth Co., Ltd.), submitted an interesting statement of the hardships inflicted by the operation of the " Owner's risk " clause, which was corroborated by other leading local firms. It was peinted out that the Mansion House Association on railway and canal traffic were dealing with the matter, and after some discussion, it was decided to leave the matter, for the present, in their hands. The unfairness of the terms imposed by the South African Shipping Ring on manu- facturers who occasionally send their goods by other lines was strongly criticised, and the President and Mr. Holman Kingdon (Messrs. Crosfield and Sons, Ltd.), were appointed to attend the coming conference in Liverpool upon the subject.—Mr. Kingdon pointed out how detrimentally the prohibitive tariff on raw alcohol affected several leading industries, and urged the desirability of taking steps to get the same reduced. Certificates of origin have again been issued at a small fee,to any local firm that trades with foreign countries which require them. Mr. Kingdon has been good enough to regularly send a copy of Mr. Henry Sell's invaluable weekly "Commercial Intelli- gence," to the Chamber, which, amongst much other interesting matter, contains a series of articles by his special commissioner, Mr. Edward Porritt (a gifted Warringtonian), on "South Africa after the \Var, the Outlook for British Trade."

THE MAYOR AND BANE QUAY STATION. The MAYOR said he was glad to notice in the report, allusion to the train service between London and War- rington. The chamber might also take into considera- tion the question of what he described as the inadequate state of the station at Bank Quay. The platforms were too low and also too narrow, and when there were a lot of people about, and luggage waggons being moved along,it was very inconvenient and difficult to get to the trains. It was a matter which the chamber might take up. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: BALANCE SHEET.
div.p: THE BALANCE SHEET.

The SECRETARY read the treasurer's statement. At the commencement of the year they had in hand £l5 ss. Bd.; the subscriptions amounted to £l3 Gs., making a totai of £63 115.9 d., and after paying expenses there was still a balance on the year's working of £6 Gs. 10d. (Applause.) • MR. FLEMING AND THE BORAX *TRUST.

Mr. FLEMING read the following letter from Mr. R. Pierpoint, dated November 25th :—"I duly received your letter of the 21st. I do not think that it would be of use that I should further argue the matter in hand, one way or the other, seeing I have no power to make the Foreign Office act as you want. Apparently you have cause for complaint against the Customs authori- ties. of New York, but as faros I can see you have not any way of proceeding against them other than that suggested in Messrs. Woolf and Company's letter of September 24th. I have, as you know, seen the Under Secretary more than once. I have written to him also. I regret t have not succeeded." 'Mr. FLENtiNG also read the following from the Secre- tary of the Democratic Congressional Committee, Washington :—" I have your favour of the 9th inst., enclosing me the history of your brother's case, inwhich the Borax Trust showed their hand, and not only per- secuted him but debaurched.this Government. It will have our attention and also that of the public as soon as pos- sible,"—Mr. Fleming went on to say that the Democrats took the matter up in America and issued millions of pamphlets about it, and he thought they were instru- mental in winning eleven seats. He thought he could not do any more in the matter, and wished to express his thanks to - the Chamber for the action they took in approaching the Member. The PRESIDENT said their regret was that the Cham- ber had not been able to help Mr. Fleming more defi- nitely. They seemed to have helped one of the parties in America, hut not to have done much good for Mr. Fleming. - Mr. FLEMING It is only that this Trust is debauch- ing the Government there and as a Britisher I object. (Hear, hear.) The PRESIDENT moved the adoption of the report and statement of account's. Mr. LONG in seconding the proposition, congratulated the secretary on the state of things generally. He himself had not been, able, during the year, to take the same personal interest in the chamber as he had done iii former years, but it was not through any diminution of interest on his part,or anv feeling that the associa- tion was not one that ought to be liberally and well supported by the people of Warrington. He felt that very strongly. He thought it was not sufficiently realized in \\Torrington the inittifinae importance of such chambers—not only to the commercial interests of the country, but even to the Government of the country. Perhaps there was one present who attended more meetings of the Associated Chambers of Commerce than himself. He had been struck by the fact that. whenever any question of great importance came for- ward before the Associated Chambers—brought by say individual chamber, or any matter affecting commercial interests generally—there was almost certain to be pre- sent perhaps a member of the Cabinet or some official member of the Government to hear what they had to say, and he thought that the result of Legislative action upon their recommendations was sufficient to show that the suggestions they made had been carried out,or some reason given why theyeould not be. (Hear, bear.) .
The proposition was carried unanimously. THE PRESIDENT AND THE INVENTIVE GENIUS OF BRITISH WORKMEN. HOW IT CAN BE UTILIZED. '

The PRESIDENT stated that last year he set the pre- cedent of delivering a presidential address and he . intended to repeat the experiment on that occasion. I (Hear, bear.) The position of commerce—of which the Chamber was in some sense local guardian—was not such as warranted us in adopting optimistic views much as we should prefer to do so. In all the principal in- dustries,there had been during the past year a steady falling off of profits finishing with the year at the worst. Profits at present were cut to the 'bone and there was a general curtailment of produc- tion in many industries, consequent on vanishing margins. This lessening of the spending power of the populace reacted on industries which remained healthy until the spending power of the great body of the people was curtailed. The conditions of which trade and active I commerce were the outcome,were too complicated to be I dealt with as a. whole. Permit him to isolate one phase of the many problems bearing on that subject and for a. few moments to recommend it to their thought. It was a significant fact that a very large portion of the labour saving appliances and machinery in use in this country were of American origin and manufacture. There were few of our industries that were not .in- debted to American ingenuity and skill, for their best machines. The import of tools and machinery from the States had doubled during the last five years and now reached the large value of two and a quarter millions sterling. We did not care to admit (at any 'rate until we could not help it) that the brain of an Englishman was inferior in inventive genius to that of an American. I.f we were to avoid this conclusion we must find some other explanation. Was he far wrong .when he put forward the suggestion that the main reason we had to rely so much upon the ingenuity of the American people,was because the conditions and prejudices associated with the British Industrial system Nn-Ogteilnduitnyotofetahl(l)sercen;ltghagnetdldinelillceocihiratecaltphiewssukitils ? A skill and far as the workers themselves were concerned there was no motive to call forth a full expenditure of thought and energy. The members of the Chamber would agree with him when he said that British employers made little intelligent effort to secure the co-operation of the inventive brains of their workpeople, while. the work- people themselves in very many cases still hugged the idea that the invention of any labour-saving appliances was against, the interest of their class, and whether it be on or not, it was none of their business, that to alter, svent, suggest improvements was the work of the boss nd for his benefit only, and concerned them only when

they saw in it something that they feared Would touch the continuity of their particular work: And yet what. an unworked mine of skill, energy,ingenuity and enter- prise there was dormant amongst the British workers! And the most vital problem of the industrial question of to-day,was how, to call 'these forth and secun. the co-operation of the English workers in retain- ing and developing British manufacture for the benefit alike of mastet and workmen, and for the com- monwealth and commonweal of the Community. If it were possible to get the brains of those engaged in industrial pursuits to assist in the cheapening of the cost of production, and in improving the style and utility of the finished article, the trade and commerce of this country would advance with the proverbial leaps and bounds. Work would be plentiful and wages would advance. We should then he no longer depend- ent on a foreign country for our machinery and labour saving appliances, our exports of manufactured goods would increase from the stationary point they had reached. How then was the desirable end to be gained? First,the policy that treated a man practically as & machine with a given capacity which ought not to be reduced, and which could not be increased, ought to be abandoned by master and workmen. It might appear to be a mere truism to say that the capacity of a human being to accomplish any task, however mechani- cal its nature, was largely dependent upon the amount of thought and zeal he put into it. And any system, or any empioyer who allowed the eagerness, the zeal, and. the thought of .the workers associated with him to be dormant, neglected one of the most potent elements in production. If however, we were to secure the best thought and work from the workers, there must be some adequate motive to call these forth. The only motive in the great majority of cases was a wage based gener- ally on so much an hour. Now in organised trades, all workers, whatever their capacity pr ability, got tha same with the same class of work. The inevitable tendency was to lower the individual output to the capacity of the slowest, for why should a smart man I put in his best, when his neighbour working at his side ' got just as much although he might do a good deal less? The general wage system alone was not one that would produce the best results. But he frankly confessed he did notsee how the union of the workers could be effec- tive unless they adopted the principle of a universal rate per hour for the same class of work. It was clear, therefore that there must be some motive over and above .what everyone got, if we were to secure the best thought and work of the best workers. And here they came to the crux of the whole question. He realized how much easier it was to diagnose an evil than to curer it. But on the correct diagnosis of any trouble must the cure depend. He was not going to air any of his own ideas, although he had with varied success attempted a good deal in that direction, but he would mention a method employed in some very large works that had proved successful. For particulars he would once more ask them to turn their eyes westwards to find in the operation of the American Automatic Cash Com- pany, the particulars of the method to which he referred. What were called "suggestion boxes" were placed in each department, and the operatives, numbering 3,000, were invited to put suggestions for the improvement of any process,machine,ormethod unto them. As an incentive and eneouragement,prize money lamounting to .C2BO a year was distributed amongst the one hundred employs who made the best suggestions. The amount of the prize money was allocated as far as possible in proportion to the value of the suggestion. In one year 4,000 sugges- tions were made, and it was found practical to adopt 2,000 of these. One improvement made by an employs was a device to do away with the necessity of the work he himself was doing. Now he did not hold. this out as a patent method for revolutionising the British manufacture. No doubt such a plan was more applicable to seine industries than to others, but he greatly feared that objections to it would at once be raised by some masters, by a good many foremen, and many of the workmen themselves would treat it with. indifference and neglect, if not with actual hostility. He mentioned this, not so much for the sake of giving importance to the method, but that he might direct their attention to the spirit whiqh gave the method birth, that feeling of co-operation of thought and invention, existing in many American works between em- ployer and employs, and which to-day was doing so much for the development of their trade, in many cases to the detriment of our own; He trusted that in that excursion into the fields:of indus- trial economics he had not travelled out of the sphere and interest represented by that Chamber. He felt strongly that above all laws, tariffs, rates and such like, which so often engaged their attention in dealing with the commerce of our town and country, the human factor was the most important, and most influenced the prosperity or otherwise of the country of which they formed a part. (Applause) Mr. LONG suggested that the address should be printed. Mr. KING-DON said Messrs Crcisfleld's would be pleased to print it free of charge. The offer was gratefully accepted.
ELECTION or A NEW PRESIDENT.

The PnEsIDENT invited his worship the Mayor to honour the chamber by accepting the position of presi- dent for the coming year. He knew very well that the calls made upon the Mayor's time were very great, and they, in that chamber, could not Tightly expect that he should give a great deal of his valuable time to the work. He felt it would be an honour to the chamber to have his worship's name' linked as president of the ' association, and he moved that he be asked to accept the position. The MAYOR said his time was very much occupied, and he felt that his qualifications wore far below what were requisite for the position. He had listened to the President's address with the greatest interest and he felt that to place any other gentleman in the position would be a disadvantage to the Chamber of Commerce; ' At the same time he would be very happy, if the, cham- ber so wished, to accept an honorary position. (Hear, hear.) Mr. LONG seconded. .
Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH supported the :motion..
The PRESIDENT said they W'ould be pleased to make the position as nominal as Mr. Parr _wished.
The motion was unanimously carried.
The MAYOR acknowledged the compliment and said he would be very pleased to give any service he could to the commerce or the town of Warrington.

div.head: ELECTION OF OTHER OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OTHER OFFICERS.
On the proposition of WI-. LONG, seconded by Mr. JOHN Ruucr.ouou. Mr. Parker was elected to the vice- chair. Mr. Skinner was appointed hon. treasurer and. Mr. Tunstall auditor. VOTES OF THANKS.
Mr. JOHN' FAMCLOUG tr moved that a vote of thanks be given to the officers of the chamber for their services.
Mr. T. E. GARNETT seconded, and it was carried unanimously.

The PREgEDENT, in replying, said he was sure the officers were much obliged for the kind expression of thanks. They were under a constant obligation to Mr. Bennett for the amount of enthusiasm. which he, put into the work of secretary. He trusted he would long be spared to the chamber to conduct its affairs iu the same excellent manner he had done in the past. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair- man, and remarked that he had been extremely interested in the able address he had given. Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH seconded, and bore testimony to the -admirable manner in which Mr. Parker had con- ducted the affairs of the chamber during the past year. The motion was carried and Mr. PARKER. acknow- ledged the compliment.'

div.head: LOCAL OBITUARY. ?iir. E. -.lilirkconnel.
div.p: LOCAL OBITUARY. ?iir. E. -.lilirkconnel.

Death has removed a well-known and. highly-re- spected citi:.4en of Warrington in the person of Mr. E. Kirkconnel, senior partner in the firm of Messrs, Robert Davies and Company, solicitors, Market-place. Less than a year ago this firm of solicitors, winch is the oldest in the town, suffered the loss of Mr. Robert Davies head of the firm, and the partners now left are : V. B. Davies, Mr. J. Burgess and Mr. H. Hatton. Mr. Kirkconnel had been ailing since before Christmas; and with the hope of recruiting his health he visited the South of England and afterwards South- port. it was while staying at this seaside resort that he gradually grew worse,and he peacefully passed away early on Thursday evening. He was nt his GI st year.

---- - Mr. Kirkconnel was a North of England man and served his articles at Prescott. He was admitted a solicitor in 1864 and came to Warrington in 1871 and took over the management of the conveyancing department at Messrs. Davies' Office. In this particu- la r branch of business he displayed conspicuous ability and greatly enhanced the reputation of the firm. In 1879, he became a partner in the firm and took an active part in the conduct of the business until within a few weeks ago. On the death of Mr, Davies he became deputy-steward of the Crow-a manors of Halton and Widnes. Mr. Kirkconnel had a large experience of building societies and was actively connected with the Warrington Permanent Benefit Building Society and the Earlestown Building Society. He was of a retiring disposition and never sought public honours. His wife pre-deceased him some years ago. He leaves onean d son, (laughter. , at present at essrs. Davies's office The funeral will take place at noon to-day (Saturday) in the Warrington Cemetery, where his M wife and a son are buried.

div.head: INFLUENZA INCREASING.
div.p: INFLUENZA INCREASING.

The Influenza Epidemic is again spreading over the ; Country. The visitation is of a very prostrating nature, and the disease is certainly on the increase. The origin of the disease or rather the circumstances which bring it about is as much a mystery as ever. You cannot trifle with Influenza. It undermines the Nervous System to a greater extent than almost any other disease, and it is Pneumonia that kills, and Pneumonia strikes the man who imagines he has only amild form of Influenza, and can go about the street just as usual. It can hardly be doubted that the prevalence of Chest and Lung ' Complaints must be ascribed to the baneful influence of Influenza, whose after-effects so frequently take this form. It was a bad day for this Country when this malignant scourge first visited our shores. Year after year it has never since failed to revive at its due time, and to extort its tribute of human life. Having observed its ravages, and its dreadful effects upon the constitution on the occasion of its former visits, we cannot but regard its recurrence with much fear, as a great many have not yet, if they ever will,regain their former health. div.head: JUNIOR CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION.
div.p: JUNIOR CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION.
SPEECH BY MR. E, MARSHALL HALL, K.C., M.P.

Parr Hall was on Friday the scene of a Unionist demonstration, held under the auspices of the Warring- ton Junior Conservative Association. The chair was occupied by the President (Mr. Roger C. Parr, J.P., C.C.), and amongst those also on the platform were: Mr. E. Marshall Hall, K.C. (Member of Parliament for Southport), Sir Gilbert Greenall Bart., Mr. W. Joynson Hicks (candidate for North Manchester), his Worship the Mayor (Mr. J. C. Parr), Sir A. Croft, Alderman J. Smethurst, Councillor A. Bennett, Messrs. A. Lister Kaye, E. Draper, William Owen, Segar Owen, E. J. J H. Smethurst,W. L. Williams, and C. S. Burgess. Before the meeting dbmmenced, selections were played on the organ by Mr. Percy Randall and patriotic songs were sung. The hall was filled in every part and the proceedings were of an enthusiastic character. There was a profuse display of Union Jacks. OPENING SPEECH BY THE CHAIRMAN.

The CHAIRMAN, who on rising to open the meeting was loudly applauded, said it was very encouraging to those who took an interest in the welfare of the Junior Conservative Association to see such a splendid gather- ing. He was only sorry that Mr. Pierpoint was not present to take his part. (Hear, hear.) He promised to be there but unfortunately his health broke down and he had to give up all idea of coming. He was now, he (the Chairman) believed, abroad, and all they could do was to hope that he might soon return fully restored to health. (Applause.) Letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from Colonel Pilkington, Sir Peter Walker, Admiral Jones-Parry, Mr. White, and many other good friends. CONGRATULATIONS TO MR. AND MRS.

div.head: PIERPOINT.
div.p: PIERPOINT.

On the proposition of Sir Gilbert GREENILL, seconded by Mr. James Henry SMETHURST, the following resolu- tion was passed unanimously :—" That this gathering of Conservatives and Unionists in the County Borough of Warrington heartily congratulates Mr. and Mrs. Pierpoint on their recent marriage." SPEECH BY MR. MARSHALL HALL.

Mr. E. MAItsHALL HALL, K.C., M.P., who had a cordial reception on rising to propose a resolution of complete confidence in His Majesty's ministers and the policy they are pursuing at home and abroad, said they' were there as representing a great. party which supported a great imperialism. A great claim of their imperialism was that it was a democratic imperialism. He proceeded to contrast the English constitution with that of Ger- many and referred to the speech of •Count von Balmy in the Reichstag when he had to apologise or at any rate to justify the speeches of the German Emperor. In this country the public utterances of our King needed no justification or apology. Prince Bis- marck had said that they must not mistake the Reichstag for the English House of Commons, but he (Mr, Hall) hoped the time was far distant when the English King should be confounded for a German Emperor. (Hear, hear.) Proceeding to sneak of army reform. he thought that there was not, sufficient roomto mancenvre in England andhe was of opinion that some great manceuvring ground should be found in South Africa where the science of war could be thoroughly learned. He had read the speech of Mr. Winston Churchill at Oldham a 'few days ago and he must admit that although he could not attempt to emulate the brilliant indictment which he.chose to hurl at the heads of the War Office, he, for one, found the scheme put forward was an impracticable rcheme,.and the time had come when those who were responsible for the maintenance of the army should put their heads together and evolve some thoroughly practical and radical reform. (Ap- plause.) He proceeded to speak of the mission of Mr. Chamberlain in South Africa and said that his scheme whereby he obtained £30,000,000 from the mine owners was a master stroke. (Applause.) Mr. Chamberlain was the ablest man of the Constitutional p arty. He put him first, but he did not wish to forget Mr. Balfour who was the type of an English Statesman and the type of an English gentleman. Than there was Mr. George Wyndham whose beneficent rule of Ireland promised to bring to a solution the Irish land question. Mr. Hall roceeded to speak of other leaders, viz. : Mr. Waiter Long, Lord Lansdowne. Mr. Austin Chamberlain and Lord Curzon. These were the leaders of the Conserva- tive party and what was on the other side? He could only think of a triple-headed Cerberns— (laughter)—Lord Rosebery, Sir Henry Campbell- Bannerman and Mr. Lloyd George. He thought Mr. Lloyd George was the ablest of the trio and could not be left out of any minintry which the Radicals could form. Defiling with the Education Act Mr. Hall said he believed it to he the best legislation that the Governnient conld bring forward under the circum- stancas. The hyster:cal and violent opposition to the Bill was not a legitimate oppoaition. It was an op- position of political wire pullers endeavouring to play upon the religious feelings—which they knew to be the s:rongest feelings in our natures—for political ends —to try and get back a political supremacy by the aid of a Nonconformist vote. (Applause). He thought Mr. Balfour WAS right when he said the position of the NonconformistA when the Bill had become an Act ,is better than it was before the Bill was introduced. The hysterical and violent opposition was already dyn down, and Englishmen with the great commonsense th characterised them had settled down not to try and ma the Bill—as Dr. Clifford and his satelites would hay them make it—a dead letter,but to make it what it ()ugh to be Made—a workable measure fo the benefit 03 th people and the benefit of the youngsters in whom they all took so much interest. (Applause.) Mr. Marshal Hall also referred to the LicensingrAct whibh he des cribed as a good workinr, Bill which was be inning to do good already. As 'far as he knew the great rock ahead was the religious queption. He quite agreed that as the State Church was governed by the law it was the absolute duty of those who drew the revenues of the Church as their emoluments to obey the laws of the Church. (Applause.) Every man, however, was entitled to his own religious opinion and they wanted absolute freedom of opinion for all. Toleration and tolerance were the only safeguards against fanaticism. (Applause.) Mr. W. JOYNSON HICKS seconded, and said 'the Educa- tion Act was an act of justice all round. Other speeches followed and the usual vote of thanks 'concluded the meeting.

While walking across the Atlantis City Railway at Jackson-street, Philadelphia, Walter' Pedrick got his foot caught in the rails. The desperate efforts of three friends to release him were of no avail. A moment later an express train came past and dashed Pedrick to pieces before their eyes.

div.head: WARRINGTON WIRE IN SOUTH AFRICA.
div.p: WARRINGTON WIRE IN SOUTH AFRICA.

series of articles on "South Africa after the War," have been contributed to the well-known trade paper "Commercial Intelligence," by our townsman, Mr. Edward Porritt who has been on a visit to South Africa, as a special commissioner for the journal mentioned. Writing from Port Elizabeth on August 111th, Mr. Porritt refers to the position which War- rington wire holds in South Africa. The story he tells,deals with its wide use there and also with a contest between two Warrington firms for supremacy. He says :

"Another fact which came to light in my Port Elizabeth enquiries is that, in spite of American and German competition, the bulk of the enor- mous trade in fencing wire is still in the hands of Lancashire manufacturers. German wire, to sell, has to be offered much cheaper than Lanca: shire wire. A particular brand of British wire is almost in possession of the market here. The story of its entry into this field affords an illustra- tion of the methods of British manufacturers, although in this case it was'a competition between a new and an old established British fins, and not between a British and a German or American firm. The older firm had long been in this mar- ket. Its goods came out here before the days of jetties, when they had to be landed from surf boats on the heads of the natives. The newer one came into the field, and by dint of advertising and lower prices, began to cut into the trade. An importer, who had acted as the selling agent of the older firm, called its attention to the inroad of the new-norner, and urged a vigorous competi- tion. The answer was that the plant of the new concern was insignificant as compared with its own, and its brand had been on the market for a generation, while the new brand was com- paratively speaking an affair of yesterday. There was no attempt to vary the policy of the older firm, and its younger rival quickly pushed into the field. In telling me the story of the contest between these two brands, the importer impressed upon me his conviction that the older firm per- mitted its position to slip from tuider it,solely on
a point of pride. It will be noticed that no names are mentioned but we have authority for our statement that the two firms alluded to are both located in Warrington.

div.head: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS. Services and Meetings at Bewsey-road and Ellesmerestreat Chapels.
div.p: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS. Services and Meetings at Bewsey-road and Ellesmerestreat Chapels.

There were good congregations at Bewsey-road Wes- leyan Chapel on Sunday, when the Foreign Missionary Anniversary was celebrated. Sermons were preached in the morning by Councillor Upson and in the evening by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees. In the afternoon a young peoples's missionary meeting was held, Dr. Ferguson presiding. The Rev, R, Wilkins Rees delivered an ad- dress and exhibited some interesting curios from heathen lands. A quartet was effectively rendered by Messrs. A. Parkinson, George Gough, H. Sinclair, and J. Hannan, while the anthem "Sing, 0 Heavens," was creditably interpreted by the choir at the evening ser- vice, the soloist. being -rAfr. Hannan. The collections for the day amounted to £ll 135., the amount realized last year being £9 18s 4d. On Tuesday evening the annual missionary meeting was held, the chair 'being occupied by Mr. John E. Richardson. There was a good attendance. The Rev. R. W. Hams read the annual report, from which it appeared that the total income of the society for the past year was £130,528—an increase of over a thousand pounds on the previous year. The expenditure, including a debt of nearly £l,OOO, was over £7,000 more than the income, which was caused largely by the state of affairs in the Transvaal. Now that hostilities had ceased it was hoped that matters would soon be restored to a more satisfactory basis. An increase of 1,300 mem- bers on the mission field was reported. Last year the Warrington circuit contributed towards the general in- come of the society the sum of £241 12s. lid., towards which £43 10s. id. was subscribed by Bewsey-road. This year they hoped to do better by means of mission- ary boxes, which would be given out in the Sunday school and might also be obtained by anyone desirous of helping the work. He proposed giving one-third of the amount raised to foreign missions, one-third to general home missions, and the remainder to home mission work in Warrington. Anyone knowing the neighbourhood, especially Si! ver-street, would recognise the necessity there was for local mission work. (Applause). The CRA ERMAN said he had several personal friends engaged in foreign missionary work and during a visit to South Africa he came into contact with missionaries andreceived the kindliest treatment from them. The chairman spoke of the self-sacrifice of the missionaries and asked that the prayers of his hearers might go out to the missionaries and that they might be strengthened and sustained in their admirable work. He was sorry their missionary enterprise was not very sitisfactory. The funds for the last 25 years had remained almost stationary, and he thought they had been well advised in determinating to make a .step forward during the ensuing year. Civilized nations had opened vast dis- tricts in various parts of the world, and their was a great opportunity for missionary enterprise. He hoped they would be successful in raising a large sum that evening to aid the work. (Applause.) The Rev. GEORGE MORRIS, who had been a most successful missionary in China, then gave an address on "Life and work amongst a curious people." The rev. gentleman is an able and entertaining speaker and his remarks were listened to with the greatest interest. A collection was taken on behalf of the Missionary funds.

div.head: ELLESMERE STREET MISSION.
div.p: ELLESMERE STREET MISSION.

The annual Foreign Missionary raeating in connection with this Mission was held on Monday evening when the Rev. G. H. Carnson (superintendent minister) delivered an interesting address. The audience were conducted in imagination round the world, calling at the many mission stations in Chinl, Rome, South Africa, Western Africa, West Indies, America, and many other places. Some thriliing incidents were related of a missionary's life and work. The rev, gentleman pleaded very earnestly for continued and increased help both in prayer and 'gifts towards the work of evangelizing the heathen world. Mr. G. H. Bean presided over the meeting and expressed his pleasure at being amongst the Ellesmere-street brethren for the first time, assur- ing them that it should not be his last visit. The amount of collection e‘cded that of last year's.

div.head: Warrington Entertainers at Croft.
div.p: Warrington Entertainers at Croft.

The Warrington entertaining Society gave a suc- cessful concert in the B )ard Schools, Croft, on Mon- day evening, the proceeds being to liquidlte a small debt in connection with the erection of the public clock. An excellent programme was submitted and was taken part in by Messrs. W. H. Kendrick, F. Warburton, G. B. Kendrick, W. H. Ireland,', E. A. Sanders, W. H. Whittaker,F. Fieldhouse, G. F. Free- man. and F. R. Bickford—at the close Mr. Cawthorne thanked all the subscribers to the concert, and re- marked that the proceeds would wipe off all the debt. He also thanked the War ringt ln Entertaining Society for their services which had been very much appre- ciated, and he hoped to again secure their services. Mr. G. F, Freeman (the secretaty of the society! re- turned thanks. Messrs. Gibson and Burnage acted as stage managers.
