div.head: Examiner, Frida7„Tantlary, 30, 1903 FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: The Examiner, Frida7„Tantlary, 30, 1903 FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
SKIPPER SP,,VID.
' Narrow Escape of Lowestoft Crew.
The thrilling escape of Captain Powley and his lrew from a sinking ship

one of those aories hich excite little more ,han local attention. Yet, !eading between the lin& of the brave skipper's 'ailorlike words (tersely -eported in the " Lowestoft Neekly Press") one re- ;ognises a story of heroism and pathos. "I was caught in the gale, said he with seamanly brevity, "between Dover and Ramsgate. The ship sprang a leak, and I stood at the tiller for six hours, ,he expecting to go down. A

lost yacht'. steamer hove round, but went on without speaking to us. We had lost the dinghey, and made up our minds that we should have to sink with the yacht, when a Dutch galley saw our plight, and took us on board. Our yacht sank ten minutes after. I had been standing all those hours in the cold and wet, without food or drink, and the exposure made me ill. This was two years ago. I suffered greatly since, in my home at Carlton Colville, near Lowestoft, and until I began to take Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale peopl• could obtain no relief. "I had splitting headaches, my eyesight grew dim, anp I had severe pain in the pit of my stomach and in my limbs. One day I read of Dr. Williams' pink pills' and I bought a box at a Lowestoft Chemist's. In less than twenty-four hours I noticed an improvement. By the time t had taken a box of the pills my eyesight cleared, and the pains in my limbs and stomach ceased. Now if I feel out of sorts a little at any time, I fly to the pills, and soon am all right again. And lam not a youth: I am seventy." "And are you all right now?" asked the reporter. "As right to-day as ever I was in my life." The gallant Captain, who is now living at 4, Colville- villas, Carlton Colville, Suffolk, also gave the reporter particulars of the case of a young woman. the daughter- in-law of one of his friends, who had been greatly bene- fited by the same pills upon his recommendation. A similar case will be found reported on another page of this paper. And indeed, considering their great tonic power, and the numerous cases of rheumatism, kidney disease and consumption they have cured, it is no wonder that they did so. "I make them known to everybody," said he, "and there are not many places between here and Cowes where I am not known."

he for one would not at all object to laymen the being co-opted on to the Education Committee of only Council. This plan, he believed, would help the Coun- cil over a difficulty, and at the same time would avoid the scandal that might be caused by discussions respect- ing religious differences arising in the Council Chamber. At any rate the plan was worth a trial, and he thought they ought to approach the Town Council upon the sub- ject as soon as possible, because until it was settled, they could hardly decide whom they ought to recom- mend for co-option. If the Council agreed to the pro- posal, then it would be very easy to select the names of a number of laymen. If on the other hand they declined to accept the proposal they (the managers) would wish to suggest two at least of the parochial clergy for co-option. Mr. C. S. BURGESS asked when the Association of Warrington parishes was founded,who ere the members, and what was its constitution. He had not heard of the Association before that meeting was called,and other people whom he had spoken to about it, had also been unaware of its existence.. It also struck him as very remarkable that the Rector was not the Chairman of the Association' although be did not wish to cast any reflection upon Mr. Carleton for whom they all had the highest and deepest respect. (Hear, hear.) It seemed to him that an Association of Warrington parishes with- out the Rector of the oldest church in the town was somewhat incongruous. The CHAIRMAN said the association was formed by agreement among the Warrington incumbents. The Rector had not joined but he (the speaker) thought he ultimately would do so. Mr. Carleton detailed the objects of the Association which affected various rights of incumbents. The Rev.JAmts DAVIES pointed out that they were not present as an association but simply as school managers. The Rev. F. A. SCREETON asked the Chairman if h ad any reason to think_ that if the meeting passed resolution with regard to the constitution of the Cons mittee the Council would take any notice of it.

The CHAIRMAN said the resolution would certainly have its influence in the town and the Council would probably give an explanation. The Rev. F. A. SCREETON thought they should have more time to consider the matter before they com- mitted themselves. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH moved a resolution to the effect that the Town Council be asked if they are will- ing to receive nominations from a representative body of Church day school managers in regard to the constitu- tion of the Education Committee.

The Rev. F. A. SCREETON secoßded. In reply to Mr. W. P. PROUD the chairman said he thought the schools were represented. Mr. BURGESS said he'did not think the resolution ought to go o the Council without it being fairly understood that the Parish Church schools were in no way represented at the meeting. Mr. R. T. FAIRCLOUGH said he was a representative of the schools.

Mr. BURGESS: I understood you represented Christ Church, Latchford. Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH Said the Corporation had certain duties to perform and he thought they would resent any intrusion on the part of anyone to tell them what they had to do. If they wanted assistance they would ask for it, and unless the Corporation were pre- pared to receive suggestions,he thought it would be a great mistake to • take action and would make the managers look ridiculous. .
After discussion the motion was carried with two dissentients.

The Rev. J.DAVIES suggested an additional resolution to the effect that the school managers be represented on the Committee in proportion to the amount of accom- modation provided by each denomination. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY, who voted against the previous resolution,asked if it were reasonable to suppose that co-opted members should be selected on theological grounds. The Town Council had been entrusted with great powers for the purpose of improving education all round. The question of religious instruction was left in the hands of the managers of the schools except in relation to any new Schools which wolild be erected. He did not see why the religious question should enter at all into the constitution of the Committee. He felt strongly that the Council ought to take absolutely the power of appointing the Committee, and not accept`eny nominations or recommendations from outside bodies. If members were going to be co-opted in proportion to the amount of accommodation, the Committee would be a very large one and might be unworkable. The best- interests of education would be served by a small Coin. mittee carefully selected on purely educational grounds The CHAIRMAN said he did Not believe that religion entered into the work of the Education Committee He was simply thinking of the new schools which would be erected out of the rates. The children attending those schools should be entitled to religious education. It might meet the difficulty if the Council agreed to hand over the drawing up pf the syllabus to ministers o religion. Mr. A. J. JOLIEY said no educational scheme had yet been agreed upon by the Council but he understood that they were trying to formulate one to bring forward at the February meeting. The proceedings then terminated.

There is little doing at this season of the yeat In the weirW of dress, for we are all enduring the so called "silly season" with as good a grace as possible, and therefore this is, perhaps, the best time of all to devote our attention to those things which are not seen but are none the less important, namely, lingerie and under- clothing generally. These details are of great importance to a refined woman, and it is a sure sign of want of curcivation when such matters are viewed with indifference.

Indeed, it is most surprising how some women devote all their attention to their dress and yet hardly give their under garments a moment's serious consideration. And yet how much of the success of a gown and the smoothness of its fit depends upon the quality and cut of the under- clothing. To a French woman the correct adjust- ment of her chemise and the curves of her corset (which must be so arranged as to conceal defects and enhance her good points) are matters of profound attention paramount even to the care and thought she bestows upon her gown and hat.

div.head: EDUCATION ACT.
div.p: THE EDUCATION ACT.
The Constitution of the Local Authority. Warrington Church School Managers and the.
Town Council.

A meeting of managers of Warrington Church schools convened by the Association of Warrington Parishes was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on. Thur- sday last week "to consider how best to promote the successful and equitable working of the new Education Actin the district." The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton pre: sided over a fair attendance.

Thc CHAIRMAN, in the course of his speech, pointed out that the Rector to whom he had written upon the subject with a view to having his help and presence, was very anxious that they should not take any action until they had a communication from the Organization Committee which had been formed in Liverpool to aid in bringing the various schools under the Act. This organization committee sent out a circular a few weeks ago to the various school managers asking them to delay any action until they received the circular which the committee hoped to issue in a few days. A few weeks had now elapsed but nothing had been heard from the committee. He (the speaker) thought the circular had reference only to action that might be taken by each separate body of managers with regard to the trust deeds of their own particular school, in applying to the Board of Education for an order. Mr. Carleton went on to point out that there were matters in which the Organization Committee could not help them and which they must settle for themselves. They, in Warrington, knew the local circumstances best, and they would do their best to give effective applica- tion to the new Act to Warrington: At the same time, while he thought action ought not to be delayed,they must be careful on the other hand to avoid the opposite extreme,of acting with undue haste and it might be advisable that afternoon to content , themselves with deliberation without committing themselves to any resolutions of a grave character. It would be advisable to have further meetings to discuss various matters in the. Act which would require their attention. That afternoon they were concerned with the general question of manauement, a question that they regarded with paramount interest owing to the new position which the Town Council Would be called upon to occupy in connection with their schools. He had no doubt whatever but that the Town Council would welcome any efforts made by those interested in the matter to ensure the successful working of the Act. There was really no body of men in the town more de- serving of consideration or more likely to help than the managers of the voluntary schools who had been quietly interesting themselves in the work of education for years, without fee or reward and without bringing themselves before the public. Under the new Act there would not be any change to which they could not accommodate themselves as regarded the manage- ment of the existing schools. There was, however, anothiv class of school that would be called into exist- ence under the new Act. The erection of new schools to meet the requirements of the growing population instead of being done as heretofore by voluntary effort would be in the future met out of the rates.: It was the management of these new schools that would require thought and consideration under the Act. The schools, of course, would contain the children of parents of all classes of the community, and the feelings of the parents in the various districts on the matter of religious teach- ing would have to be considered and dealt with. It was found that even in Board schools religious. teaching was demanded and there were few of those schools without a syllabus of religious in- struction. It was this subject that made the composi- • tion of the management committees of the new schools a question of considerable importance. They would all agree that the committees ought to be fairly representa- tive, having due consideration to the views and wishes of the parents in the locality. If the committee were elective and the parents had an opportunity of express- ng their opinions at the polling booth, it would not be a matter that required so much • consideration from that Meeting, but the parents had not the power of electing members of theie committees and would be dependent 1 on the fairness and sense of justice in the members of the Town Council, which he was sure would not fail them under such circumstances, and he felt certain that any suggestions that meeting might make in the interests of fairness and justice, would receive due consideration from the Council. The Town Council was required to act in this matter through a committee specially appointed for the purpose, and as that committee would have absolute power to appoint the several committees of management for the new schools, they (the Church school managers) naturally felt anxiety as to how the Town Council Committee itself was to be appointed. Sometimes Town Council Committees were appointed in rather a haphazard kind of way without method or principle—so it seemed to hiin—and it was their duty to impress upon the Town Council that every care and precaution should be taken to see that the Education Com- mittee was formed with a due regard to the various interests that were involved, The Act required that the committee should be constituted of a given number of members of the Council to which there would be added by co-option a certain number of persons not in the Council, but who were known to be interested in education. The number of Council members was required to exceed the number of co-opted members. As regarded the Council members they had no particular right, he supposed, to interfere. That part of the committee rested with the Council itself, the members of which were responsible, to the ratepayers. As regarded the co-opted memben,he thought they had a right to express their opinion—and indeed the Act called for and provided for such an expression of opinion by bodies of management such as that —and he was sure the Council might be aided by any suggestions they might make on that head. He thought if the meeting could agree as to what should be the qualification of those who were to be co-opted, it would be advisable to embody what they thought in a resolu- tion. They might for example agree that the co-opted members should be selected ,from the managers of schools of five or eight or ten years standing. A quell- 'fication of that kind was an obvious one and would be a guarantee that a man knew something of the work he would be called upon to undertake. With regard to the clerical and lay members of the committee, there was this difficulty, he thought, about co-opting clerical members. If clergy of the Church of England were put on, it would be felt that the Roman clergy ought to be represented and the ministers of the Nonconformist bodies, in which case there would not be much room for lay members. He doubted whether the com- mittee would desire this. He would like to ' suggest a way out of the difficulty for their consideration. The ministers of. religion desired to have a say ill the management of the schools, simply that they might look after the religious interests of the people committed to their care in the matter of education. With regard to secular education, although , they were quite as interested in it as were the other members of the community, still he for one would be quite willing to leave it in the hands of the laity, if the laity were only equally willing that the ministers' responsibility for the religious training was recognised by them. (the laity) If the Town Council would only see their way to hand over to the various minieters of religion the agreeing upon and drawing up of a religious syllabus for the new schools, such as already was in use in most of the Board schools, then

div.head: Runcorn Petty Sessions.
div.p: Runcorn Petty Sessions.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—At the Runcorn Petty Ses- sions on Monday beforit Messrs. A. R. Norman (in the chair) and W. Timmins the following persons were fined for neglecting to send their children to school : Mary Ellen Morris, Os. ; Patrick Kilkenny, 2s. 6d. ; J. Booth, ss. TRANSFERS.—George Herbert Andrews of the Bird in Hand was granted a transfer to the Elephant and Castle, George A. Jones being granted a transfer to the Bird in Hand.—Mr. Walker of the Castle Hotel was granted an extension of one hour for ,Monday the 26th, it being the occasion of the Co-operative party.— Au application to transfer the license of the Royal Hotel, High-street, from George Curzon to William Faulkner was adjourned until the following Monday the bench being of opinion that. some irregularity had occurred. It appeared that the house belonged to Messrs Greenall and Whitley who had leased it to a man named George Haining who had, since the last transfer day,gone to the Royal Oakat Weston.—Haining had put in Curzon and then Faulkner as managers, temporary authority having been granted to both in succession. Curzon, who had been dismissed by Haining,opposed the transfer on the ground that he had been treated shabbily by him. Mr. Pearson, who represented the brewery company, said that Messrs. Greenall and Whitley had no knowledge that Haining had put in managers to look after the premises and that such conduct would not be to lerated by his firm in the future.

in the House of Keys on Wednesday the Bill,abolish- ing tied houses was passed a second time, having pre- viously been rejected by the Council. Mr. Laughton repudiated the charge. made in the upper branch that the advocacy of the Bill was an" organised hypocrisy." The Gainsborough Bench on Wednesday fined John Garbutt, of Kirtote Lindsey, £2 and costs for ill-treating a disabled thoroughbred horse by leaving it in a yard for several hours lying in a thawing snow. The animal could be heard groaning 30 yards away, andafter efforts had been vainly made to get it on to its feet, it was killed ask lay.

div.head: FASHIONABLE CORSET.
div.p: A FASHIONABLE CORSET.

Even a poor Parisienne will pay • for her corsets what an English woman would consider an extravagant amount, but is in reality a saving, as a really good corset wears well and when carefully made will wonderfully improve the lines of a defective figure. Cheap rubbishy corsets stiffened with cane instead of whalebone are a thankless investment. The accompanying sketch depicts tle lines on which a corset should be " built " t'o give the correct effect demanded by fashion at present. It will be noted that the upper part of the corset is cut rather low at the bust, thereby allowing the figure to fall into natural curves, while, at the same time, the requisite amount of support is given. The corset is straight fronted and comes well down over the lower part of the figure at the sides and front but is cut shorter at the back. Suspenders attached to the front of the corsets not only keep the stockings well in place but also help to keep the corset in place, especially when the wearer is at all inclined to enbonnoint.

There are some very comfortable corsets which were much in demand in warm weather. These consisted of a deep band of a strong make of ribbon shaped like a Swiss belt and well bound at the sides, back and front. They allow com- plbte liberty to the figure while giving a certair

div.head: NOVELTY.
div.p: A NOVELTY.

amount of support, and are the ideal corset for wear when going in for any kind of sport which demands a considerable amount of physical exercise such as sculling, golfing, riding or cycling. Another point regarding the manner of ad- justing the undergarments affected by the French is that nothing is allowed to encroach on the waist line, and thereby increase its dimensions, all underskirts being kept lower down by a hook attached to the front of the corsets. _ _

Tho garment illustrated shows one plan by which the difficulties attendant on the correct 'adjustment of an underskirt are overcome. The garment is, indeed, a chemise of fine lawn and lace, which is made considerably longer in the skirts than usual, and forms a petticoat as well. The lower edge is finished by frills of lace, finished at the top by lines of insertion. To lessen the expense the frills could be made of Cash's frilling, or of the lawn itself finished by a narrow edging of Valenciennes lace. There is (pile a revolution of late years in the style and make of our undergarments. Twenty years ago calico was what was considered correct for a middle-class woman, trimmed with Swiss embroidery, the latter, in many cases, worked by the wearer in leisure hours. There is no doubt that much better and longer wear was got out of underclothing at

this style than the flimsy lawn or cambric- trimmed garments affected by the twentieth century damsel. but though this point is un- doubtedly of vast importance in the eyes of every sensible woman; it is about the only good quality these unsightly and clumsy garments possessed. One of the prettiest and yet simplest nightdresses I have seen for some time was picked up at half its original cost at one of the recent sales. The decrease in price was owing to it being slightly soiled. Its fascinations are depicted in my last sketch. The yoke of lace insertion, interspersed with very narrow lines of embroidery, is transparent, and fastens at the side, where bows of ribbon are arranged. The sleeves are full, and come only a little way below the elbow, where they terminate in deep lace-edged frills. There is also a narrow edging of the same `lace round the upper edge of the yoke, which is cut slightly square. The same nightdress, made in pink or cream flannel or flannelette would look very well, and be very cosy for winter wear, while to make it warmer the lace yoke could have a lining of washing silk.

The fashion for coloured silk underwear is still in evidence, and ene sees wonderful ar- rangements of delicately-coloured silks, trimmed with a profusion of black or white lace; but it Is not a fashion which meets with general ipproval, as there is something much daintier and more delicately feminine about pure white lawn or cambric. Silk underskirts, however, still hold their own, and are to be seen in all styles, from the plainer modes for out of doom io the elaborate affairs of chiffon silk and embroidery for evening wear.

div.p: STATE OF CRIME IN WARRINGTON,
r-The ',Chief Constable's Annual Report.

The Chief Constable (Mr. Luke Talbot) presented his annual report upon the state of crime in the Borough for the year ended December 31st, 1902 to the members of the Watch Committee on Thursday last week. For facility of reference, the principal tabulated forms of the return are here summarised side by side with the corresponding figures for the previous year : INDICTABLE OFFENCES COMMITTED, APPREHENSIONS
PROSECUTIONS

POLICE ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT.

The Police Force consists of 1 Chief Constable, 1 detective superintendent, 1 chief inspector (who is also chief clerk, drill instructor and storekeeper), 2 patrol inspectors, 6 patrol sergeants, 1 court sergeant (who is also warrant officer and process server), 1 bridewell sergeant, and 53 uniform constables. There are 3 de- tective constables, one of whom acts also as assistant hackney carriage inspector and coroner's officer. One of the patrol inspectors is inspector of hackney carriages and is curator of the sessions house and bridewell. The total authorized strength of the force is 69, and is in a proportion of one constable to every 931 of the popula- tion (64,242) and to every 45.71 acres of the Borough. The average strength of police forces in the northern district of England is one constable to every 68192 of the population. In addition to the authorized strength there are 1 sergeant and 2 constables appointed and maintained at private cost for duty upon the premises of their em ployers. They are under the control of the Borough Police Authority, and make a total of 72 men so con- trolled. Sixty-five members of the Force hold the certificates of St. John Ambulance Association, and have rendered first aid to 45 injured persons during the year, On July 10th the entire staff removed from the old Bridewell in Irlam-street to the more commodious premises in Arpley and Wilson-Patten streets. The old police premises have been demolished.
HORSE AMBULANCE CARRIAGE

The horse ambulance carriage has been used on 14 oc- casions. No charge is made for it use inside the. borough, and it is available for the movement of sick persons (under medical direction) where the eases are of a non-infectious character. It has proved a valuable adjunct to the police equipment.
DISCIPLINE AND VARIATIONS IN THE POLICE FORCE.

One constable resigned, through continued ill-health, and three constables were called upon to resign after having been reported for misconduct. Generally speak- ing, the conduct of the men has been excellent.
The Examiner, Friday, January 30, 1903.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS INFORMATION.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS INFORMATION.

During the year the police have specially supervised 441 houses whose tenants were temporarily away from home, and there was no robbery or similar interference with such premises. Once again I respectfully ask per- sons who may be leaving their houses unoccupied for a period to acquaint me with their intended absence, with a view to the special watching of their residences. There are now in the Borough 87 licensed victuallers, 39 beerhouse keepers, and 73 Shops licensed for thesale of intoxicants not to be consumed on the premises. There are, in addition, 12 places licensed for the sale of wine. Forty-five places are licensed for music and dancing, and 12 for the performance of stage plays. The licence for the Y.M.C.A. on Friars-green has lapsed, the premises being now used as an autioneer's establishment. 'Thirteen alehouses, 4 beerhouse licences and off-beer licences have been transferred during the ye. • _

The sum of k7O 4s. has been collected from parents and guardians by the police under magisterial orders, towards the partial maintenance of children detained in Reformatory and Industrial Schools. This sum was forwarded to H.M. Inspector of Reformatories. There are 7 proprietors of cabs in the Borough, and 94 drivers licenstd to ply for hire. Electric trams are now running between Sankey Bridges, Latchford, and Wilderspool, and Longford Bridge and the Cemetery. The duties of the police during the construction of the lines and since their inauguration have been enormously increased through the difficulties of regulating traffic. The necessity of keeping a number of men continuously at fixed points has greatly strained the numerical resources of the Establishment.

During the year the police have executed 213 war- rants for apprehension or commitment, and have served 1,020 summonses. Town Council and Corporation Committee Notices to the number of 5,640 have also been delivered by them. During the same period, l'i persons wanted for offences committed in other locali- ties have been apprehended by the Warrington Borough Police, and handed over to the proper authorities. Four hundred and ninety-seven persons have been conveyed from Warrington to H.M. Prisons during the year. 'Three convicts on ticket-of-leave, and one person under Police Supervision have reported themselves to the Warrington Police during the year. Three have left for other districts and one is still reporting. Seven runaway 'horses have been stopped by the police at personal risk. One Constable for conspicuous bravery in one of these cases, was awarded the badge of merit. During the year lost property to the value of £9B has been found or recovered by the police, and in most cases restored to the owners. Ninety-two cases of sudden, premature, or violent death have been investigated-1)y the police and reported to the Coroner. In 43 cases there were no inquests. In 49 cases inquests were held, and verdicts returned as follows, viz.: 33 "Accidental death," 4 "Death from natural causes." 4 "Suicide whilst temporarily insane," and 8 "Open verdicts." Lost children, to the number of 106, have been re- stored by the police to their parents or guardians. Twenty-seven horses, cattle and sheep were found straying, taken to the pinfold, and subsequently handed over to their respective owners. _

The police upon night duty have found -161 shops, warehouses, and private houses insecure through doors, windows, etc.., being left open or unfastened. The occu- piers of the premises in such cases were notified and cautioned.
- The gross cost of the pay and clothing of the police establishment for the year 1902 was £6,317 13s. 6d., halt of which is fepayable by the Government. During 1901 the cost was £3,265

The Police Superannuation Fund amounts to £12,956 7s. ld., the total income during the year being £979 155., the charges upon the fund amounting to £305 18s. Bd. There are upon the pension list 2 ex-Chief Inspectors, 1 ex-Sergeant, and 1 ex-Constable. I deeply regret to report the death of two old and faithful public servants, viz., ex-Chief Constable Samuel Hunt, who died on December 12th, and ex-Inspector George Cox, who died on December 15th. The remains of the former were interred in the Warrington Cemetery on December 15th, full police honours being accorded. The latter having died in Monmouth (where he had resided since his re- tirement from the force), was buried there on December 18th, the force being officially represented .by Chief Inspector Phillips. Lieutenant-Colonel Eden (H.M. Inspector of Con- stabulary), inspected the force on the 21th of April, and pronounced i t efficient as to physique. numbers. discip- line, and equipment. He also expressed his high ap- proval of the method and accuracy with which the police books and records were kept. In concluding his report, the Chief Constable tenders his thanks to the Chairman and members of the Watch Committee, the Town Clerk and other kind heads of Corporation departments and also to Mr. G. F. F. White, clerk to the Borough of Justices, for the assist- ance they have given him.

div.head: NEW STANDARD DICTIONARY
div.p: NEW STANDARD DICTIONARY

Messrs. Funk and Wagnall are now advertising their new standard dictionary. Having one in our possession we can with confidence say that the dictionary is all that its compilers claim for it. Its first and not unim- portant quality is that it is a marvel of cheapness. But its second and primary quality is the encyclopmdie knowledge cgi e may obtain from 'a perusal of its pages. The work is so excellently compiled as to he invaluable to busy men, who are enabled to quicky find the inform- ation required,and thus lighten in a surprising degree the labour so often associated with dictionary consulta- tions. It is sufficient to say that no one should be with- out this new, first-class dictionary, upon which so much time, money, and labour has been expended.

MANCHESTER. Astronomy.

"Some problems on Astronomy" was the subject of a lecture delivered at a meeting of the Warrington Field Club by Mr. J. Watson, F.R.A.S. The chair was occupied by Mr. F. Womersley, and there was a large attendance. Prefacing his discourse with a few explanatory remarks on gravitation and on Kepler's laws, the lecturer proceeded to describe the move- ments and orbits of the major planets, explained how the velocity of light was first ascertained, and then passed .to the consideration of parallax, of the distances of the sun and of some of the stars. He illustrated his subject with a number of lantern slides, some cf which were diagrammatic and other actual ph6to- graphs of the surfaces of the sun and moon, of star clusters and nebulte. A vote of thanks was heartily accorded to the lecturer on the motion of Mr. Charles White, seconded by Mr. May, and supported by several others.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the above authority was held on Tuesday at the Daresbury Petty Sessional House, Mr. J. Knowles in the chair. There were present Messrs S. Woodward, T. Wright, C. Roylance, J. Mclntyre, .T. Stokes, J. Whitlow, T. Darlington' T. Baxter, C. E. Linaker, T. Lewis, H. Mawdslev, J. T. Collier, G. Pilling, P. Gleave. E. Bretherton. J. pruce, T. Reynolds, R. Billington. J. Mountield, and J. B. Chadwick, G. F. Ashton, Hulse, Dr. Adams, J. Farrington, J. Diggle and Swinton.

div.head: £6,000 LOAN.
div.p: A £6,000 LOAN.

Mr. J. T. Collier moved "That application be made to the Local Government Board for a loan of .26,000. sufficient for the purchase of the undertaking of the Helsby and District Water Company, and for the erec- tion of the machinery necessary for a new pumping station inconnection therewith". The resolution was approved. THE POLLUTION OP HALTON AND KINGSLEY BROOKS.

The Cheshire County Council inquired through their clerk, Mr. Reginald Potts, what further progress had been made by the District Council to prevent the pollu- tion of the Kingsley Brook and other streams without the rural district. _ _ -

The Clerk said he had replied that steps had been taken to prevent the pollution, and that negotiations were then in progress to further cleanse the streams. Mr. Linaker said that if the Council went on in the way they were doing, the small villages would belanded in for costly sewage schemes. It was most unfair. Mr. Woodward said it was perfectly ridiculous to suppose that Kingsley Brook was seriously polluted, or that all the pollution could be taken out of a stream. Mr. Linaker said that samples of water should be taken from Kingsley Brook and sent to the County Council. _ _
The Nuisance Inspector replie4 that the County Council ignored all the samples that had hitherto been sent.
On the motion of Mr. Woodward it was resolved that samples be taken from Kingsley Brook at its lowest point and that they be submitted for analysis by the County Council.

div.head: NORTH-WESTERN ELECTRIC POWER 11LL.
div.p: THE NORTH-WESTERN ELECTRIC POWER 11LL.

The Clerk said that the Parliamentary Committee had met that morning to consider the above bill and had referred its farther consideration to a sub-committee. consisting of Messrs. Chadwick, Woodward, Pilling and Monateld, who would report in due course.

div.head: SMALL-PDX OUTBREAK.
div.p: THE SMALL-PDX OUTBREAK.

The Medical Officer said that since the last meeting there had been three cases of small-pox at the Union Workhouse. The house had again been disinfected and all the contacts vaccinated. The road to the hospital wanted repairing as the patients were considerably jolted in being taken to the isolation hospital. The Board had not yet appointed a medical officer to the small-pox hospital. It was resolved that thermic? be repaired and Dr. Adams be appointed the medical officer to the hospital.

div.head: SUSPECTED CASE.
div.p: A SUSPECTED CASE.

Dr. Adams, in reply to the chairman, said he had visited the Workhouse yesterday in company with Dr. Selby and had found a suspected case in the woman's ward. The person had been isolated and he hoped that the rash would not prove to be that of small-pox as it might prove serious to the other inmates.

div.head: WEASTE LANE SEWER THEL WALL.
div.p: WEASTE LANE SEWER THEL WALL.

The Medical Officer recommended the putting down of a syphon catch pit to ventilate the shaft at the top end of Weaste-lane sewer, Thelwall, opposite Mr. Hewitt 's farm, at a costof Approved on the motion of Messrs Roylance and Gleave.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

' The newly formed Pers7evet7auce Angling Society, whose headquarters are the Cattle Market Inn, have chosen their officers as follows :—President,Mr. James Bancroft ; Vice-President, Mr. L. Spencer. Com- mittee, Messis. J. Millington, C. Crozier, and 'Robert Hayes; ,Treasurer, Mr. Fred Bonnell and Secretary, Mr. W. Bradbury. The meetings will be held on the first Tuesday in each month. Another new. club has been formed at the Shakespeare Inn, Pinner's-brow, which will be known nas the "Jolly Anglers." Their officials are : President, Mr. A. Lomax ; Vice-Presi- dentf Mr. T. Powers ; Committee, Messrs. R. Lf,max. P. Rooke, E. Lawton and J, Buckley ; Treasurer, Mr, Alfred Shaw; Secretary, Mr. Arthur Forster.

The secretary of the Provincial Angling Association has, issued his report and balance sheet. The balance sheet shows £l7O Os. Bd. to the credit of the Society, a balance which ,s the greatest that the Provincial Angling Association have ever had. In connection with the Xational, Electrical and General Trades Exhibition which will be held at the Tiinglvy Birmingham, March 30th to June fith, there will be a "Provincial Association Fish Section." The sum of £l2 is offered in cash prizes for the best specimen fish in cases. The entrance is free and open to all the members of societies connected with the Provincial Angling Association.
