div.head: Examiner, Friday, January 30, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Friday, January 30, 1903.

a petition signed by 320 people who werehouseholders, and the Bench had intimated that they dipl not want to hear witnesses. This was the reason he had not called them. The Green Man was only 142 yards away from a fully-licensed house, whereas "The Brooklands" was over 700 yards.

Mr. Harrison called Elias Griffiths, who said he was an owner of property in the neighbourhood near the Brooklands. He had taken the opinion of his tenants, and he had found that they did not want the public-house. Five or six of them had said that if the licence were granted they would leave.

Mr. Swift: You have neverhad anything to do with a licensed house ?—No, sir. Did you ever build one?—No, sir. Did you once build a house which you proposed to ask for a licence for?—No, I did not. Further questioned, witness said he !kept a grocer's shop but he did not think of gettily, a licence for it. He could not have got one if he haddesired. Didn't you abandon the idea because you thought you would not get the licence?—lt MIS no use if I had thought of getting it. (Laughter). Witness added that he did not buy the shop for that purpose. You would have asked for the licence if you had had the remotest idea that you would get it ?—I tell you it was no use asking. (Laughter.) Mr. Swift : Is not that conduct n bit of dog-in-the- manger style? You could not get.what you wanted and no one else shall.

Witness replied that he had never applied for licence. Further questioned: His house was in Percy-street about 30 yards from Mr. Throssell's. Ernest 'Wilkes, professor of music, said he lived opposite the Brooklands. In his opinion a licence was not necessary in the neighbourhood. Mr. Swift: Are you a teetotaler? Witness: I consider that rather personal. Mr. Swift: It is very personal. Witness : lam a teetotaler, but I don't thrust my opinions upon anyone. You object to licensed houses anywhere would not like to go so far as that. You won't object so long as the house is not near you ?--.1 think the house would injure my profession. Mr. Swift: Is not that selfish? (Laughter.) Occasionally people think music is a. nuisance don't they? (More laughter.) ' Witness : I don't think so. Mr. Swift: You did not consult the neighbourhood before you put a music shop there? Witness: I did not think it necessary. Mr. Taylor, solicitor, said he appeared on behalf of Mr. T. J. Lee, of Bridge-street, draper, whose firm had carried on the business for upwards of 80 years. In the widening of Bridge-street the distance between Rylands- street, and Market-gate would be diminished. If the present, application were not granted, and the Green Dragon was brought to the front of the street, that distance would be still further dim- inished for the shops in the main street. The result would be that 'certain shopkeepers would be crowded out. If the Green Dragon were re-built the result might be thatthis old standing business would be driven out of the street. It had been intimated by the Corporation that such land as they had left for the pur- pose of rebuilding shops would be offered in the first instance to the shop-keepers who already had interests in the site. Therefore it depended upon the application as to how far the Corporation would be in a position to carry out their pledge. He appeared to support the application on behalf of Mr. Lee. Mr. Harrison : This is entirely beside the question. Mr. Taylor: They (the shopkeepers) are all in the same position, but Mr. Lee is the one who has taken .the initiative in the matter, _

The Chairman asked the Chief Constable if he thought the licence was required. The Chief Constable : Certainly I don't think it is required, andl told the magistrates on the last occasion that in my opinion a licence was not required. ' I have had no reason to alter my opinion. After twenty minutes' consultation in private,the Chairman intimated that the magistrates had decided to grant the t pplication.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
" Does the Church Fail to Reach the People ?"

This was the subject of a paper read at the weekly meeting of the Latchford Baptist Improvement Society on Monday evening by Mr. Druett. A very interesting discussion followed. The Rev. J. F. Matthews conten- ded that the pew rents should be abolished, which would be a great advantage to the majority of would-be churchgoers. The parson should look after the people, irrespective of class or purse. Other speakers were Messrs. Hamlett, Cliff, J. Albinson, Bamber, and H. Ford. The opinion was expressed that the Church does fail to reach the people, and the meeting urged various reforms and more activity. A vote of thanks to the ssayist concluded the meeting.

div.head: Baptist Church, Golborne-straet.
div.p: Baptist Church, Golborne-straet.

The Pastor (Rev. H. Dunnico) preached to a very large congregation on Sunday evening on the question "What is Christianity?" The preacher emphasized the exclusiveness of Christianity. It was a dogmatic religion, but its dogmatism was sweet and rational. In the first place it was distinctly a gospel of redemp- tion, and in the second place it was a message of con- ciliation to a sad and suffering world. Mr. DUnnico will continue his series of sermons on the subject throughout the Sunday evenings of February. In the afternoon the annual prize distribution took place,when the scholars and friends assembled in large numbers. Mr. T. Longshaw reported a successful year in the school, and Mr. S. Fearnley stated that the adult bible class numbered 90 members and 85 had qualified them- selves for a prize. The pastor then distributed the awards to the scholars and to the members of the adult class, and expressed his pleasure at so large and so successful a gathering of young people. It augured well for the future of their church.

div.head: Buckley-street Methodist Free Church.
div.p: Buckley-street Methodist Free Church.

The members of Legll-streA Primitive Methodist Choir, under the conductorship of Mr. A. Sprace, gave an excellent musical service in the above church in con- nection with the P.S.A. Society on Sunday afternoon. The chair was taken by Mr. T. H. -Ashcroft, who gave it brief address. The choir then gave selections from "The Messiah." Miss Alice Bridge sang with effect "There were shepherds," "Come unto Me' and "Tknow that my Redeemer liyeth," and Miss E.Miller "Heshall feed his flock." Mr. J. Corrin was heard to advantage in "Comfort 3e," and "Every valley."-and Mr. A. Spruce was equally pleasing in "Why do the nations?" The choruses "And the Glory," " Glory to God," "Behold the Lamb of God," and "Hallelujah" were rendered with excellent taste and greatly appreciated. Mr. F• Podmore, M.T.U.M., was the organist. Mr. W. Shaw,on behalf of the P.S.A. Society, thanked the Chairman and choir for their services. The collection was in aid of the church renovation fund.

div.head: Wycliffe P. 5.11. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P. 5.11. Society.

A well-attended meeting of this society was held on Sunday afternoon. Mr. J. Hawthorn presided, and in alluding to the religious census which had been taken at Liverpool, London and New York he stated that the result showed that the majority of the people in these cities were outside the churches. He referred to the work which the P.S.A. movement had accomplished in bringing many men into the churche3,and pointed out the need for more energetic work on the part of the churches to bring those outside, within the pale of religious influence.—Mr. Thomson, of Liverpool, delivered an inspirating address on the "Religious Scarecrow." He contended that the Christian com- munity was not to beheld responsible for the few black shed]) who used religion for all kinds of hyprocrisy and deceit. He referred to the way in which many Christians acted as scarecrows by their long faces and un-Chi-istian- like conduct. He showed that Christianity was a religion of love and was intended to make men happy.— Mr. A. Griffiths gave an excellent interpretation of "The good Shepherd." The service was also taken part in by Mr. Farrar and Mi. Cotton.

div.head: St. James' Church, Latchford.
div.p: St. James' Church, Latchford.

Success attended the annual tea and entertainment in coruaection with this Church, which took place in the schools on Monday evening. About 350 people sat down to a capital tea, the following ladies presiding at the tables :—Mesdamek Frost, Gibson, H. N. Houghton, • Hutchinson, F. R. Pierpoint, G. Venn, Dickson, Chester, 'Hallwood, Kenyon, Millwood, Tonge,. Acton, Davy, Davies, and Morris, and the Misses Parry.—After tea there was an interesting entertainment, which included pianoforte solos by Miss Gibson, songs by the Vicar (Rev. F. R. Pearson), Miss 141ckersley, Miss Jessie Howard, Mr. Hill and Mr.- F. A. 'Morris, a duet " Excelsior "by Miss Eckersley and Mr. Hill, and humorous readings by Mr. H. M. Ashton. Each item was submitted in a highly creditable manner, and the artistes were warmly applauded. Mr. E. Davies discharged the duties of accompanist.— During the interval, the Vicar delivered a short speech • and said he was very grateful to the parishioners 1 for the very kind way in which they h,-..a received hirans their vicar, and for the sympathy they had shown to him , in his sore trial (the serious illness of his wife.) He ! referred to the circumstances leading up to the exchange of livings;with theßev. F. E. Powell,their late vicar,and • said he felt thankful that in Mr. Powell's case it 'had ; 1 resulted verysatisfactorily. He was sorry to say that I Iso far as be was concerned that was not the case. How- I ever, the danger was now over, and he wished to assure ; , his friends that the question of his remaining at St.! James' rested entirely with themselves. He was willing !to do his best if they wished him to stay. (Applause). He asked for their sympathy and help, especially from the Church Council. He wanted to see St. James' Church take the position he honestly thought it ought to take. (Applause). in conclus ion,he t hanked all who had helped to organize that party,and who had given him, , a comparative stranger, such loyal help and support. I (Applause.)—The room was• afterwards cleared, for dancing, which was kept up With spirit until 11-30 to • music supplied by Mr. Lomas.—On Tuesday the. children's tea was held, and an entertainment was given I by St. Hilda's Minstrels.

div.head: GREEN DRAGON RE DIVIVUS,
div.p: THE GREEN DRAGON RE DIVIVUS,
THIRD APPLICATION SUCCESSFUL. Licence to be Transferred to Lovely-lane. OLD LICENCES SURRENDERED.

A third and successful application was made to the I Warrington magistrates on Monday for the transfer of the licence of the Green Dragon Inn, Bridge-street, of which Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company are the owners' to a house known as "The Brook- lands" in Lovely-lane which is at present occupied as a residence. Mr. Rigby Swift, barrister (in- structed by Messrs. - Browne and Crompton) made the application on behalf of James Spencer Earle, licencee of the Green Dragon, and Mr. Reginald Harrison, barrister (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel) opposed the transfer on behalf of the Temperance Federa- tion and a number of residents in the neighbourhood of "The Brooklands." The magistrates On the BenchL were: Mr. John Fairclongh (in the chair), Aldermen' James Fairclough, T. H. Sutton, R. W. Francomb, T. Hutchinson, J; Smethurst, and R. Heaton; Councillors John Roberts and W.Pierpoint, Dr. Fox' and Messrs. S. Wright, John Geddes, E. J. Guest, Charles White,J.W. Hayward, R. T. Fairclough and H. Thornton. In his opening statement, Mr. Swift said that a similar application had been before the Bench on two previous occasions, and the applicant would not have come before the Court again to make an application for the third time, if he had not had fresh facts to bring forward; in fact to make the application under new circum- stances and considerations which he (Mr. Swift) hoped, and he ventured to say expected,would influence the minds of the magistrates so that they would give a different decision from those which their worships had felt bound to give on previous occasions. Mr.Earlehad kept the Green Dragon for three years and the Corpora- tion were now about to pull down the house for the purpose of widening Bridge-street. It was absolutely necessary for the purpose of the Corporation scheme that the Green Dragon licence should be dealt with, and he submitted that the most expedient way of dealing with it. both from the point of view of the Corporation and of the community at large,was that the licence should be transferred to Lovely-lane which was a growing neighbourhood. Within a radius of 400 yards in 1890 there were 429 houses with a population of 2,218. Since thnt!year 367 new houses had been built, making a total at the present time of 796 houses with a population of 4,171. The neighbourhood was likely to increase still further: Within that radius of 400 yards there was not one solitary fully licensed public-house. There was one off beer licence, but the nearest fully-licensedhouse was the Railway Hotel, Priestley-street, which was 743 yards away. The Chief Constable told the Bench on the last occasion that he (Mr. Swift) was correct in stating that the conditions were such as did not exist in any otherpart of the borough. As to the suitability of "The Brooklands "for a licensed house therehad never been any dispute. As he had constantly pointed out, his clients had acted in the matter originally at the instigation of the Corporation, and they were supported in that application by the Town Clerk. : Mr. Harrison asked if Mr. Swift was going to call the Town Clerk. _

Mr. Swift said his friend must not interrupt him as he would have an opportunity of commenting upon his (Mr. Swift's) case at a later stage. Mr. Harrison asked if Mr. Swift could give an asmr- ance that he would call the Town Clerk.
Mr. Swift would not give the assurance, and Mr. Harrison asked for the ruling of the Court on the matter.
Mr. Swift : This interruption is most improper. The Bench decided that Mr. Swift should proceed with his observations.

Mr. Swift said his instructions were,that the applica- tion was supported by the Town Clerk, who was that day in London, but was represented by his deputy (Mr. Stanley Wilson). The application on previous occa- sions had been made by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Company, at the instigation of the Corporation, but it had only been an application to transfer the Green Dragon licence to Brooklands, the company not having offered to surrender any other licences if the transfer were granted. For some years it had been the custom throughoat the country for magistrates when con- sidering the granting of a new licence, or a transfer like the present, to consider not only the particular case before them, but, having regard to the whole interests of the community, whether other licences ought not to be given up. The policy obviously had the approval of the legisla- ture,which had provided,that magistrates might consider transfers of licences from one part of a district to another. Messrs. Greenall were now prepared, if the transfer were granted, not only to give up the Green Dragon, but to close two 1869 beerhouses in Warrington: The 1869 beerhouses were the bete noire of a verylarge proportion ofllicensing benches, because they possessed a privilege which no other houses had got. They had a right to exist until they forfeited that right by being badly con- ducted. These 1869 beerhouses laughed at demolition areas, and knew nothing of the qualms which struck fully-licensed houses when a licensing Bench took upon itself to inquire into the wants of the neighbourhood. These licences were one of the most valuable properties a brewery had, because there was, at any rate, a vested interest and a right which could not be taken away. Therefore the Bench would agree that it was no small thing that Messrs. Greenall were offering. The houses the company proposed to give up,were the Ropemakers' Arms, in Crossley-street, and the Sceptre in Winwick- road. Both were profitable businesses and yaluable licences, and if the proposed redistribution of licenses took place there would be four licences less in the borough. The Eagle and Child Hotel had been closed, in consequence of the widening of Bridge-street, two beer-houses would disappear, and the Green Dragon licence would be moved out of the centre of the town to a part that was growing, and which was not at present sufficiently provided with conveniences of this sort. At present the widening of Bridge-street was at a stand- still because nothing could be done until the question before the Bench had been disposed of. The property owners and occupiers were. clamouring to have their premises put in order, but whilst the application was pending,nobody knew whether the Green Dragon was to be rebuilt or whether the transfer would be granted. Mr. Swift contended that the transfer would be for the benefit of the communityat large and pointed out that when .the two licences were surrendered it would facilitate police supervision as there would be only one house to look after instead or three. In answer to Councillor Pierpoint The Chief Constable said the nearest fully-licensed house to the Brooklands was the Railway Inn,74:3yards. The Bowling Green Inn was 747 yards away and the Green Man was 605 yards. The nearest off-licence was Throssell's, at the end of Percy-street 320 yards. There was another off-licensed house kept by Mrs. Potter close to, but the distance had not been measured on the Ordnance map. It was, however, about 150 yards or thereabouts further away. Replying to Dr. Fox, the Chief Constable said there was an off-licence in Mill-lane about 600 i yards away and two others in Aikin-street and Leicester- street about 700 yards distant. -

No evidence was called in support of the application. Mr. Harrison said he objected to the transfer of the licence to Lovely-lane on behalf of residents thereand on behalf of the Temperance Federation, and others. It was an extraordinary circumstance that those who objected to the transfer of the licence should have to appear three times consecutively before the Bench, in view of the magistrates previous decisions. Probably the other side thought they would ultimately succeed , by wearing downithe opposition,or they had not given the Bench credit for Inving the courage of their opinions. He repeated that in view of the two previous applications, it was extraordinary they should be compelled to appear here again. He contended that the question the Bench had to decide wasa very short one. The pulling down of the Green Dragon, surrendering licences, and the making of a bargain were entirely outside the question. All these were side issues. The only question the Bench had to decide was "Is this licence necessary for the wants of the neighbour- hood?" He contended that the Bench had given their opinion by refusing to grant an off-licence in Monks- street and a full licence to the Green Man. What the opponents of the transfer said,was that the inhabitants felt that Mr. Benjamin Kenyon had supplied their wants reasqnably and that if anybody was to have a full licence it should be Mr. Kenyon. No doubt with a lively recollection of the answer given to him by the Chief Constable on the last occasion with regard to the needs of the neighbourhood, Mr. Swift had not called any evidence to sulfstantiate anything that he had said. it was all very well to talk , in a specious manner about the value of 1869 beerhouses, ! but the Bench did not know what the value of the houses was, and even if they did they must not let that policy of bribe affect them in any way. Mr. Swift had , not called any evidence to show that since the last application any change had occurred to necessitate the granting of a licence for the Lovely-lane district. The district in question was a residential one, and he sup- posed the property was high class, and the inhabitants said the introduction of a public-house in their mids would deteriorate the value of property because it would introduce an undesirable element. Lovely-lane had been free from serious crime, and the hotel would bring at class of people into the district who were not wanted The residents were already adequately supplied by Mr. Kenyon.

Mr. Swift: I thought my friend represented the Tem- perance Federation. Are they supplied by Mr. Kenyon? Mr. Harrison said the opposition was not a fanatical opposition and his clients looked upon the matter with a broad mind. Temperance did not necessarily mean teetotalism. They would,lnot say that no licences ought to exist but they did not want a public house in Lovely- lane. Mr. Harrison pointed out that within a radius of about half a mile there were two fully licensed houses, one beer houserand five off-licensed houses,and therefore the district was adequately supplied. He hoped the Bench would confirm their previous decisions, and con- tended that the policy of co-ercion should not be entertained. - - -
Mr. Swift said that on the last occasion he presented

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE SHIP CANAL COMPANY.
WARRINGTON TRADERS' COMPLAINT.

In the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, on Saturday, Mr. Justice Byrne resumed the hearing of the action brought by Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons and other Warrington traders against the Manchester Ship Canal Company for various reliefs in connection with the alleged failure to dregs the river Mersey at Warrington to the depth required by the company's acts. This was the tenth day of the trial. Mr. Bousfield, K.C., Mr. Hughes, K.C., Mr. Norton, K.C., and Mr. Thompson appeared for the plaintiffs; Mr. Moulton, K.C., Mr. Cripps, K.C., Mr. Pickford,K.C., and Mr. O'Leigh Clare were counsel for the Manchester Ship .Canal Company. ALDERMAN MONKS GIVES EVIDENCE. Mr. Frederick William MoNtcs,manar,ing director of Monks, Hall, and Co., Limited, said that in July, 1901,a notice was given by Mr. Longdin that certain sections of the river were out of order. He did not remember how long the channel remained undredged. Witness was asked what the present position of the channel at . low water was.

Mr. MouvroN objected that, the condition since the date of the writ was not in question in the action. Mr. Justice Byrne said the material point was the condition of the channel at the date of the writ and previously; but if he were satisfied that the canal com- pany had since the writ made things satisfactory, that would have a material effect on the nature of the relief he should give.

_ Witness went on to say that the channel was now in an unsatisfactory condition, and his company's boats I were unable to navigate it. n consequence of this,they had suffered pecuniary loss through not being able to send all the material by water they would otherwise have sent. The cost of sending by AV tter wls less than by rail. In consequence of the reduced level of the water they had had to lower the opening of their intake pipe, which was laid in 1874, probably five feet. In cross-examination by Mr. Moulton, witness said that more water was taken out of the river than before the canal was construoted ; but what he complainsd of was the want of dredging. Mr. Justice Byrne said it did not matter whether water had been taken illegally or not if the effect of what the Canal Company had done was to reduce the depth of the channel contrary to statute. Witness was then cross-examined with a view of show- ing that iron scalings from his company's works had been thrown into the river, and that that had seriously increased the difficulty of dredging the river's bed. He admitted that complaints had been made of this, and that it necessitated a little more dredging. Mr. Frank Edward Priest, a me mber of the Institute of Civil Engineers, said that he was in partnership with the late Mr. Beloe' and was jointly responsible for the report which had been put in. The soundings were taken under his directions. He produced sections pre- pared from the soundings showing that in certain places the channel was of an insufficient width and depth. In order to maintain a channel eight feet deep it was necessary to allow a margin for the silting which would take place. The further hearing was again adjourned till Tuesday.

div.head: TUESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: TUESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

On Tuesday the evidence for the plaintiffs was closed. Mr. Hughes, K.C., on behalf of the plaintiffs, sub- mitted that on the evidence,it was idle to contend that the Ship Canal Compiny had anything like fulfilled its Parliamentary obligations. There was not a single day on which they could prove there was a channel of the size stipulated for, assuming the plaintiffs were right as to the defendants being bound to maintain a depth of Bft. According to the evidence there had never been more than one dredger working at a time, and the ettannel had never been made and completed to the reasonable satisfaction of the borough of Warrington. THE CASE FOR THE CANAL COMPANY.

Mr. Moulton, K.C., opened the defence shortly after I two o'clock. He said he differed seriously from Mr. Hughes as to what the rights of the plaintiffs were. His lordship had in section 86 of the 1895 Act of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company a difficult enactment to construe, and one which was unique in its form. It was a clause passed for the protection of the Corpora- tion of Warrington, and the traders ,and others carrying on business at or near that place ; but its provisions only held good if and so long as they were not varied by agreement between the Corporation of Warrington and the Ship Canal Company. He thought it would be necessary for his lordship, formally, to come to a con- clusion as to the proper legal inference to be drawn from that state of things, because he should show that all the I matters which were vital in this case were matters I which depended solely on the agreement. pie true I legal, consequence of this clause was that the protection of the traders at or near Warrington was placed in the hands of the Corporation. That was the reason why the clause was left to be altered from time to time, I with or without the consent of the traders or any of I them, by simple agreement between the Corporation I and the Ship. Canal Company. If it stood unaltered he I should submit that the present plaintiffs other than the I Corporation would not be entitled to ask the Court for , the relief they now sought. He did not think it neces- sary to discuss that somewhat abstract point of law, because what the plaintiffs now relied on, consisted entirely of matters defined by the agreement between the Corporation of Warrington and the Canal Company. One of the works contemplated under the Company's first Act was a dock at Warrington, Which was to ,be constructed before the Canal was actually opened. It was common.knowledge that the construction of the Canal proved a much more difficult engineering under- taking than had been expected, and there was a pros- poet of considerable delay in opening it. if the Warring- ton dock had to be constructed before the formal open- I ing of the canal took place. The Canal was intended to I be and had been a very great benefit to Warrington. I I The consequence was that the Corporation of Warring- I ' ton,,When approached by the authorities of the Ship • Canal, consented to vary the terms of the Ship Canal Act and entered into an agreement of 1893 in order to permit the canal to be opened on the Ist January, 1894, as in fact it was. In that agreement they varied very considerably, the position of themselves and of the traders of Warrington under the 88th clause. Counsel fof the plaintiffs seemed to think it gave to the traders of Warrington the rights he was attempting to set up for them. But it did -nothing of the sort. By the agree- ment. the Canal Company undertook that they , would allow four traders to use the Runcorn and Latchford route by a certain number of boats, the names of which werespecifically set down. There MN no arrangement for using the .Walton Lock, for the t,' very good reason that i was not constructed at that time. Under that agreement no trader could possibly sue, although it was quite possible for the Corporation of Warrington to take steps to compel the Canal Com- pany to perform ,their covenants. It had never been I suggested that the Canal Company did not give to the I traders the benefits which the Corporation contracted 1 they should have under the agreement. After June.lB9l, ' (the date at which the dredging should have been done), there was a dispute between the Canal Company andthe ,Corporation as to whether or not the former had com- pleted the dredging. it was not only a &sprite as to facts, but as to the law. The Canal Conipany were bound to dredge the river -IVlersev and maintain it, ' dredged. The Court would have 'll, difficulty in interpret- ing what that meant, because it could not mean there should be over the bed and banks of the Mersey a depth I of Bft. THE EXTENT OF THE COMPANY'S -OBLIGATIONS. He believed the Corporation, tried t;) contend that the Ship Canal Company ought to dredge the whole breadth of the river to a depth of Bft. The Ship Canal said that was preposterous and Was not the meaning of the agree- ment. Daring this quarrel,the Corporationappealed to Mr. Beloe to make a survey of the river and to find what the dredging actually done was. That survey of Messrs. Beloo and Priest was most important and he should submit it. showed -conclusiVely that the Canal Company had fulfilled it obligations. In the agreement of 1896 there was no recital that the Canal Company had not done their duty; and he was going to show that they had done it. The obligation of the Canal Company was to dredge the bed and banks of the Mersey and for ever after to maintain the same dredged, so that at all times there should boa certain depth. The Incas quo to which that obligation relatadavas a river exposed to tidal action and liable to have silt brought into it in large quantities by the rising tide. The obligation was not to reconstruct the river but to remove such silt and restore. the channel first made. He submitted that it was no breach of the obligation that there was an obstruction. The fact that - the Canal Company had to maintain it, dredged, showed thatnit was contemplated that there would be a need for dredging. He should show-that in 1895 there was sub- , stantial agreement that the Canal Company had dis- charged its obligations and dredged the river to a proper depth, The dredging, however, had been handed over to a contractor, who was of opinion that one dredger was sufficient, and that it would be difficult to use two dredgers in the river with any advantage. Counsel characterised the contention for the plaintiffs as one by which they were seeking to put upon the Canal Company a Sisyphus-like obligation. Nothing could prevent the channel being obstrncted at times by silt. But the obligation on the Canal Company W 33 not the impossible one of preventing silting ; it was the equitable one of removing the silt. The Canal Company had entered into an agreement with the Corporation to make and main- tain the channel, but that was quite compatible with the channel not being passable for a time because of the forces of nature. The .Canal Company was bound to do its best to remove the obstruction in the channel, and -that it had done. Tri any case there was no ground for saying the Canal Company were liable in damages in respect of any failure to do their duty.
Counsel hail not concluded his speech when the Court rose for the day. WEDNESDAY'S. PROCEEDINGS.,

Mr. Moulton, KC., resuming his opening of the de- fence. on Wednesday, said that when the Court rose on Tuesday he was on the point thet the whole of the claims of the plaintiffs in this case were under the agreement of 1896. Mr. Hughes, K.C., had told the Court that before 1896 the plaintiffs had a right to a free passage through Walton Lock. He was quite
ttmuromery uveuwe, wai4L.
COQI7IITTA

wrong. Walton Lock was opened in October, 1891, and from the first the Canal Company claimed tolls of 4d. and Bd. forgoing through it. When the agreement of 1896 was made the Canal Company insisted on the pay- ment of tolls,but reduced them to 3d. and 6d., which was one of the benefits the traders secured by the agreement of 1896. It was agreed that that ,should apply also to back tolls, and the tolls Were paid on that basis. What the traders of Warrington had a right to was a fre3 passage along the Runcorn and Latchford Canal route. and that.right ceased when the agreement of 1896 was made. Under the agreement,most valuable privileges were obtained for the traders. Besides paying 3d. and (Id. instead of 4.d. and Bd., tney were allowed to carry larger cargoes, and they had the right if the Canal Com- pany was in persistent default to go for nothing or have free lighterage through the Walton Lock. These were all privileges which the traders had enjoyed, and they could not go back to the original state of things. By clause 10 of the agreement, if any difference arose between the Canal Company and the Corporation they were to settle it between themselvef. This was 'vital, and Messrs. Crosfield could not raise questions under an agreement to which they were not "parties. He sub- mitted that they could not sue the Canal Company and that the Canal Company could not sue them. The Corporation of Warrington . were immeasurably more capable of taking care of the rights of the traders than the individual traders themselves. It was a pity the Corporation had not availed themselves of the remedy provided by referring the dispute to an engineer. The action turned to a great extent on the supposed right of the traders to go through Walton Lock without paying tell. Before they could say there was any right to do that,the Corporation had to give certain notices and to show that the Ship Canal had been irresponsive to them. Certain notices were given, and the Canal Company set to work, and for a long time no further complaint was made. In February, 1899, Mr. Longdin had a special man appointed to watch the river and until August no notice was given, which showed there was practically no obstruction. The man appointed had nothing to do but to make Complaints, and from August a range of complaints was made. But Mr. Longdin never gave the Ship Canal Company notice that they were not proceeding to his satisfaction. Evidence would be given to the effect that the difficulties of dredging were enormously increased by lime being thrown into the river. •

Mr. Justice Byrne: That will be good as against the persons throwing the lime in, but not against the Corporation. Mr. Moulton: lam gibing to put it much higher than that. I say the Corporation of Warrington had a statutory duty to prevent this pollution. I propose to give evidence as to the amount of lime thrown in, and after that,l shall take th evidenca of Mr. Hunter, the engineer of the Ship CAnal, and the other evidence with regard to the facts of the case.
EVIDENCE OF POLLUTION BY THE PLAINTIFFS.

Lieutenant Simpson, water bailiff under the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, said he had made complaints to Messrs. Crostield about clay and lime being allowed to get into the river from their works. Mr. Bousfield, fC.C., said he would admit that up to a certain time considerable quantities of lime went into the river—over 100 tons a week up to 1898. . Mr. Clare said his clients could not tell the quantity. All they could tell was that lime was being constantly poured into the river, notwithstanding the assertions crf Messrs. Crosfteld and the Town Clerk of Warrington that no lime was coming from their works at all. This lime was serious as regarded dredging. His suggestion was,that the quantity of lime thrown into the river was as much as 250 tons per week. . The witness went on to say that the lime seriously increased the difficulty of dredging the river, and he made reports on the subject from time to time to Sir George Nares. Sir George Nares, acting conservator of the river Mersey, said he first heard of lime being put into the river in January, 1897, from Mr. Simpson. He wrote to Messrs. Crosfleld warning them that unless the pollution was discontinued he would have to institute proceedings against them. It was his duty to take proceedings as acting conservator of the river Mersey. Tn 1899 the Conservancy took action against Messrs. Crosfleld, with the result that a nominal tine was inflicted.

Lieutenant Simpson, recalled, was examined as to the letters he had written to the plaintiff on the subject of refuse discharged into the river. One of these letters said there was no doubt that lime was being discharged into the river from Messrs Crosfield's works though not in such large quantities as before. their ccinviction. He produced samples of lime taken from the river. Some of them contained a large mixture of iron sgalings. in cross-examination by Mr. Bousfield, the witness said that with the exception of Messrs. Crosfleld he could not mention any manufacturers of Warrington who sent lime down the town sewer. His wish was that the Corporation of Warrington should be prosecuted. Longdin said they had no means of finding out where the lime Came from. He assumed the lime was sent down by Messrs. Crosfield, because it was near their works and quite hot. Lime had been dredged out of the river many times. _ _ _ _

Mr. Joseph Monk's, shipowner, of Liverpool and War- rington, said he was river inspector of the Mersey some years before 1900. it was part of his duty to see that people did not discharge deleterious matter into the river. His attentionwas first called to the fact that lime refuse, iron scalings, &c., were being poured into the river in January, 1897. Dnring the last ten or twelve years the river-side traffic of Warrington hadlincreased very much. He made a number of reports about the state of the river, some verbal and some in writing. Thehearing was 'adjourned. On Thursday Mr. Joseph Marks, in the employ of the Mersey Conservancy; and river inspector from 1892 until 1900, gave further evidence as to the putting into the river of solid matter, contrary to the Act of Parliament. In cross-examination witness said he did not know why Messrs. Crosfield only were prosecuted. In one of ! his reports he stated that after the prosecution he found a great change for the better, and that, indeed, the dis- charge of lima had practically ceased. Since the prose- cution no sample of time had, bean taken with anything like the substance of previous samples. Mr. William. Lawton Booth, special pollution inspec- tor of the river Mersey under the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, said it was part of his duty to watch the river from Runcorn to Woolaston Weir. In 1898 ! , he had special instructions to watch the sewers at War- rington for material corning in. He was the principal witness for the prosecution at Daresbury, where he pro- duced certain photographs, which he exhibited and ex- plained to the court. The dredger was at work on the 23rd January, 1899; and a quantity of fresh lime was dredged up. The lime must have come froin Crosfield's or through the Corporation sewer from the works of some other manufacturer. Two days after, the prose- cution, which was on the 28th March, 1899, he found that one of the pipes which had been discharging lime into the river had beend! smashed. This • ten-inch pipe was so corroded up with lime that • it had an aperture of four inches only. In the early months of A,899 Messrs. Cros- field's pumped lime into the river. He himself saw intermittent flows of water and lime. On the 2nd January, 1900, and subsequent dates he went to War- rington to view the river, and saw lime flowing into the river from other pipes connected with Messrs. Crosfield's works, but belonging to the Corporation of Warrington. Limewas difficult to dredge up, especially when it had been deposited for a long time. There was no truth in the suggestion that the lime dredged up was an old deposit coining from a depth below that which it was the duty of the Canal Company to dredge. Cross-examined: He could not produce a sample of lime and water taken direct from the pipes of Messrs. Crosfleld. Lime was more difficult to dredge than sand, being of the consistency of dough. He denied that the samples he took were taken front the channel. He explained the absence of any reference in the dredger log book to litue,by saying that, the. man who kept that book was not a chemist, and entered lime mid other materials simply as "silt." John Dunbavand, captain of the dredger, gave evid- ence as to the dredging of the channel. In re-oxamuinat.iOfl, witness said he remembered the prosecution of Crosfield's in 1899. 'Before that time there were large banks of lime in the river and on its banks. In one of his reports he said that .fine, heavy sand was the worst material with which they had to deal in dredging, but what he thought was fine, heavy sand contained a large percentage of lime. Jchn Ruddam, also gave evidence as to the dredging operations. Speaking of a large quantity of lime refuse taken from just before Crosfield's works, he said that on the previous day he had found an inch or two of lime. On other occasions he had found from 18 inches to 2 feet of lime. Mr.Longdin had told him that Crosfield's had a communication with one of the !ewers from which lime came. Sand mingled with lime was the worst stuff to dredge, because it was so adhesive it would not go out of the bucket or slip down the shoot, and they had to dig it out of the waggons. It took about six ti,nes as long to fill a barge with the lime mixture as it did with sand. \
, In cross-examination, witness admitted having taken a sample from the outfall which he threw away, because there was no lime in it.
Hubert Congrove, assistant engineer, also gave evi- dence as the difficulty of dredging up a mixture of lime and sand:
The further hearing was then adjourned.

An extremely dense fog has been exPerieneed in Chicago. In one factory devoted to the manufacture Of chewing-gum, eight exployes were completely pros- trated, and twenty others weregrendered dizzy and unfit for work. Physicians attribute the symptoms to fog poisoning. - - -

Judge o'Con.nor Morris, addressing the Grand Jury at Sligo Quarter Sessions,on Wednesday said the state of the country had very much improved from what it was .a few months ago, hut there was still a certain amount ' of disturbance. He was happy to say, however, the- quarrel between Lord Do Freyne and his tenants had been lettled, mainly through the influence of the Most Rev. Dr. Clancy. Bishop of Elphin. .He regretted to say that there was still much boycotting in the country butas he had to try two cases arising out of boycotting he would make no Observations on the crime at present. div.head: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RE'CHABITES. -- Warrington Juvenile District No. 4.
div.p: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RE'CHABITES. -- Warrington Juvenile District No. 4.

The annual meeting of the above District was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Sankey Bridges, on Saturday. The Council was opened by Bro. Wright, D.S.J.T., at 3.30 p.m., there being a good attendance of district officers, representatives, and also a number of visitors. present. Bro. T. Massey, D.S., presented his report,. which showed that there were 14 juvenile Branches ha the District with a membership of 589 and total funds amminting to £212 108. 6d., this giving an increase of 78 members during the year, besides transferring 15 members to the Adult Branches, one. Juvenile Branch having been opened at Haydock. Bro. Wright, D.S. J.T., gave his report on the 'work. that had been accomplished during e• the past year, and considering the material they had to work from, con- sidered that fairly goad work had been done although. only one new branch had been opened duritr, the year, but judging from the present surroundings the prospects. of the juvenile District were Of a most hopeful charac- ter. He also viewed and welcomed with pleasure some. of the Clauses of the New Licensing Act which ,came. in operation this year,especially the clause making any person drunk while in charge of a Child under 7 years of age, liable to be arrested and fined 40s. or a months, imprisonment, also the Registration of Political. Clubs and so-called Workmen's Clubs which were nothing less. than bogus drinking places, a step in the rightdirection. He also referred to the Juvenile Motto Card for 1903. "Cast thy bread upon the waters, for thou shalt find it after many days" and hoped, it would act as an incen- tive to increased effort on behalf of the different branches. Adjournment was made at 5.30, a splendid' tea having been provided by the officers of the Hope of Sankey tent which was done full justice to. A vote of . . thanks for the entertaining of the juvenile District was moved by Bro.B. Warburton and seconded by Bro. T. Winstanley. Bro. Lawton responded, on behalf Of the tent.

After tea a very interesting event took place. The officers of the adult and juvenile tents whose meetings are held in this place resolved to show their appreciation of the services rendered by their Secretary to the cause of Rechabitism and decided to take the opportunity at the district meeting of presenting to Bro. Robert Cragg,, a framed Emblem of the Order for special services rendered to the tents in the capacity as secretary from • the opening of the Branches at Sankey Bridges. Bro. Wright on behalf of the tents presented the emblem. Bro. Cragg in accepting the presentation said he was taken completely by surprise by this exhibition ' of the kindness and good-feeling of the -members of his tent, and hoped that it would be an inspiration to increased effort in behalf of the districts and Order. The election of officers took place and resulted as follows, W. Wright D.5.J.T.,.W. Blacker, A.D.S.J.T., G. Hough P.D.S.J.T, E. Cartwright,Levite,Guardian, Bro. Garlick, treasurer W. Baxendale, D.S. T. Massey, auditors J. Hill and B. Warburton. An invitation to hold the next quarterly meeting was given by the repre- sentatives of Jomfdeii tent, Brick-street Mission school- room, which was accepted. I ,

div.head: St. Paul's Home Mission, Runcorn.
div.p: St. Paul's Home Mission, Runcorn.

in connection with the home mission at St. Paul's. Church, services were held on Sunday- and Monthly. On Sunday the pulpit was occupied both morning and even- ing by the Rev..oiven Spencer Watkin, a minister who was with Sir G. White in Ladysmith, and has served elsewhere with the troops on active service.—On Mon- daya crowded meeting was held, under the presidency' of Mr. F. J. Norman, J.P.—The general annual report was presented by the Rev. Terry Coppin, who remarked' that the home missionarylmovement was most inspiring. —The local financial statement was presented by the. Rev. A. Wells,the total for the circuit being £5B lis 2d, only eight places in the connection beating Runcorn. Mr. Watkins then delivered a most interesting, lecture on the siege of Ladysmith. The usual vote of thanks closed the meeting. Daring the service a largely aug- mented choir gave . several selections from Handel's Messiah."

A telegram from Inuiston, Alabama, states that boiler explosion occurred on Wednesday in the foundry of the Southern Car and Foundry Company. Six per- sons were killed and twenty injured. Mrs. Mary Ann Snow, Maida Vale, who died on October 6, and whose estate has been valued at £87,511, has bequeathed to the cancer research fund of the Middlesex Hospital £7OO, to the cancer wards of the Middlesex Hospital £5OO, to the research fund of the Cancer Hospital at Brompton £5OO, to the London Mission, for their Home for the Dyinr, £5OO, to the Kingsdown Orphanage £500,t0 the Society for the Pre- vention of Cruelty to Children £5OO. . Thirty-five thousand pounds damage was caused by fire. on Wednesday night at the Prince's Dock, Glasgow, in the sheds allotted to Messrs. John Bruce and Com- panY. No vessels were moored there at the time, and nobody was injured.

On WednesAy afternoon Ellen Sharpies, aged thir- teen, was drowned in the Ribble at Walton-le-Dale. She was a half-timer, employed as doffer, and should have gone to work at Calvert's mill at noon. She acci- dentally fell into the water whilst playing, and the swollen river swiftly bore her along. The body was removed two hours later by a policeman.

div.head: LETTERS '2 THE, EDITOR
div.p: LETTERS '2 THE, EDITOR
-NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS,

Authors of letters intended for publication must mall eases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday-. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has a much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot under ordinary circumstances undertake to return the manuscripts which are not used.
The Recent Charge of Excessive Punishment at Runcorn,

div.head: Proposed Charity Organization Society.
div.p: The Proposed Charity Organization Society.

Sir,—How to deal with the poor has always been a great difficulty, and the national attempt to deal with it is about as great a failure as can well be imagined. Are we certain that an organised system of Charity Investi- gation Societies will be any more successful? What we want is to get at the really deserving poor, and give them such assistance as they need in time of stress and difficulty. If the existiq,g agencies in Warrington have failed, let it be pointed out how and where they fail, and let us have instances of overlapping where the fraudulent poorjare able to take advantage of any loose methods of distribution which a more highly organised system will prevent. We all know that there is a great deal of so-called poverty relieved out of sheer laziness when it is easier to get rid of an impecunious beggar by giving a copper than a persistent refusal—but no Charity Investigation Society will e'er reach this class of begging. We have in Warrington a society managed by Mrs. Joseph Harrison and an efficient staff, that, for economy and efficiency, will I* hard to beat, and its usefulness is only limited by the financial support it receives. It has carried on its work quietly and unostentatiously, hut none the less effectively on that account, for years. In Mrs. Lewis, Mrs. Harrison has an able assistant in the administration, one who combines sound common sense with tact and discernment and a motherly spirit of kindliness go valuable in dealing with the deserving poor. The district nurses can speak of the value of this society in manycases where immediate relief in food is needed of the right kind—cases of sickness where it is a matter of life or death, not investigation into the cir- cumstances and causes of poverty. I say nothing of the timely assistance given by the various ministers of religion out of funds provided by the wealthier mem- bers of their congregations,or by the medical profession who give sympathetic service worth more than money, and which no organization will ever reach. Mrs. Harrison took up the work years ago out of pure sympathy with the poor, and has managed to do an amount of good out of all proportion to the means at her disposal. If she has not been able of late to give the time and attention as formerly, we all know the reason, and I am sure she has the sympathy of all who know her; but the work has been going on steadily and effectively, as the last balance sheet proves conclusively. I hope Mrs. Harrison will not feel discouraged or in- clined to give up her useful work in Sank-street. As a aubscriber,l am quite content to leave the management entirely iu her hands, feeling sure that the best use will be made of any funds that may be entrusted to her care. She gives a clearstatement of receipts and expenditure to all who subscribe, and if they are satisfied no one else need complain.—Yours, ecc.,
F. MONKS.
Walton Old Hall, 2Gth January, 1903: How I Became a Non-Trader.

Sir,—After the much-vaunted boast of Mr. Doddsand his friends, viz-, that if any correspondent assailed the position he has taken up, and would only sign his name at the bottom of such letter, that he (Mr. Dodds), would justify his position, and in no unmeasured fashion. It was, with the greatest misgivines, that I took up my pen, to subscribe in defence of some of the members of our Council, and it was with great fear and trembling, that I picked up my last Saturday's "Examiner," to look for the result of my temerity. But, lo and behold! the great James was not there. He had refused to come out of his shell; presumably-, reserving his superabundance of invective, for the pro- test meeting in the Parr Hall. I 'mist, at the outset,sir, confess that I have great regard for the man, who, hav- ing once madea statement, and knowing it to be correct will stand by that statement; but I have no sympathy for the man, who having • found out he was wrong, does not take the first opportunity of correctinghimself,and I therefore take this opportunity of explaining, why I, Bre Many others, accepted the statements of the non. -traders as being true, and which also accounts, in a very large measure, for a great number of their follow- ing. It is a very well known fact, that the Non-traders had great difficulty, in securing candidates to stand in their interest at the last November election. With the object of filling one of the vacancies I was approached byone of the principals for the Non-trading party to stand forelection. I was then told how the ratepayers had been cajoled for a large number of years, how mem- bers of the Council had abused the trust entrusted to them how the financial state of the borough, was a sort of total paralysis, how indeed, it had been quite easy for our local legislators to work in their own interests at the expense of the ratepayers, and, then among other things if I only knew half these gentlemen contained up their sleeve, together with what\ they had already charged in public and a great deal more, which they could adduce if only an inquiry were granted, I should not hesitate for one moment to accept their offer, and throw in my share along with them. I must confess before he had finished,my armour was half on, and like the "man in the street" I was taken in, although I was not taken on. Therefore refused the kind invitation, and here I may say that do think that events have proved justification for my action in refusing to comply with their request, inas- much, that, aii inquiry has been granted, and an oppor- tunity has been given them of providing their mytterions evidence, and of fulfilling the charges which they have made; with what result. That owing to this action ,of the Council, they call a mass meeting of their followers in the Parr Hall to move a resolution of no confidence in them, and very kindly ask them to resign. Now although I predicted .in my last letter, -that they would hold such a meeting, yet the arrogant assumption contained in their invitation never occurred to me, and I must say eclipses anything which they . have yet ati empted. But. sir, where is all this going to 'land us. Are the non-traders desirous that any inquiry shall take place at all, or are they wishful only that certain men shall be moved out of the council, or is it that they want to make up a party of themselves. Have they got any 'information which will convince the rate- payers of the justice of their claims and who are the transgressors and what have they done ?, These are the questions which must be answered before they cancount upon the entire support of the ratepayers, or in other words, as conveyed by one of our poets (I can't say
Oh that this wicked trading crew Were all reduced to one or two Sod these were painted red or blue That everyone might know them! Thanking -you for insertion, I beg to remain yours faithfully,

div.head: THOMAS KNOWLES, 36, Gieen-street, Warrington. January 27th, 1903._ 'rhe Unionist Demonstration, -- The " Cowardice " of Giadstone and Chamberlain.
div.p: THOMAS KNOWLES, 36, Gieen-street, Warrington. January 27th, 1903._ 'rhe Unionist Demonstration, -- The " Cowardice " of Giadstone and Chamberlain.

The Unionist Demonstration held last Friday in the Parr Hail, in numbers and enthusiasm gave healthy evi- dence of the interest the people of Warrington take in imperial politics, and it is all the more noteworthy since so tnnch energy has been of late taken up as Mr. Hall put it, by the "squabbles round the parish pump." Although on the opposite side in politics I rejoice in the enthusiasm of so many young men of the town in their desire to consolidate what they deem to be the

better ,party. I bare no desire to detract from the effect of this meeting, but simply to offer some criticism of the speech of Mr. W. Joynson- liick9 which in .some respects was as unworthy of the meeting, as it was of the speaker. Mr. Hicks tried to traCe the cause of the war to "cowardice" on ..he part of Mr. Gladstone and his Government in making peace with the Boers shortly after the battle of Majuba in 1881. He contrasted the action of Mr. Glad- stone in 1881 with the action of the present Govern- ment after the reverses of Colenso, etc. "Did they, (with emphasis on the they) haul down the Hag, and enter into negotiations with the enemy, etc"? Now Mr. Hicks knows full well, or if he does not know he , ought to know, that the petty reverse of Majuba had othing whatever to do with the peace made with the noers. The absurd contention that men like Bladstone, Chamberlain, Hartington, and Rose- Gry, wen who bad the power and might beE ngland at their call, should turn cowards because ew hundred men were captured on the top of Majuba,

is too absurd to be entertained by any sensible man. I would commend to Mr. Hicks' attention the eulogy pro- nounced by Mr. Marshall Hall on Mr. Chamberlain,and would ask him if he finds in such a man any of the elements of which a coward is made. Mr. Chamberlain in 1881 eloquently defended the policy adopted by Mr. Gladstone's Government, the government of which he was an active member, and showed that it was a braver thing to do the right in face of a reverse than it would have been if there had been no set, back at Majnba. Whatever Mr. Hicks may say against either Mr. Glad- stone or Mr. Chamberlain, the charge of cowardice is • not one that he will get any Englishman, whatever his politics may be, to endorse. That the Government of that day may, as Mr. Chamberlain now ! thinks, have been too magnanimous, is an open question into which Ido not here intend to enter. Mr. Cham- berlain thinks that the Boers were not capable of appre- ciating the high standard of righteousness and magnan- imity which the Government manifested to them, and put it down to cowardice. lam not prepared to take this for granted, but if it be correct it is very plain that the Boers are not alone in this, but have an associate in Mr. Hicks, who with them fails in understanding high motives of political action, and unworthily puts it down to cowardice, and in so doing seeks to blacken the char- acter of the living, and the memory of the dead. There are some political speakers, and Mr. Hicks appears to belong to this class, who will use any weapon and use it unfairly, if by so doing he can damage the other side and extol his own. Mr. Hicks finds fault with Mr. Crosfield in finding in the Jameson Raid a strong reason for the conduct of the Boers in regard to the war. Mr. Hicks is careful to emphasize the fact that he does not know Mr. Crosfield, e thanks God lor that." I notice that he uses this expression several times- and each time very inappropri- ately. It would show better judgement on the part of Mr. Hicks if he omitted the name of the Deity in his partisan speeches. The habit is neither reverent nor in good taste, and perhaps if he knew Mr. Crosfield he might learn from him some much needed lessons on these points. Few men who take an unbiased view of the deplorable Raid will deny that its influence was bound to make for war. If it be true that the action of the Government in 1881 made war possible, the Jameson Raid converted this possi- bility into a probability while the way the enquiry dealt with the Raid increased this probability. I do not quite see why Mr. Hicks should be anxious to minimise the effect of the Raid on the Boer feeling toward England. It was no Conservative Raid. The only reason lean find is that Mr. Hicks is so anxious to discredit the statesmen of 1881 that he is prepared to ; whitewash and minimise the effect of a rebellious act as wicked and stupid as any Englishman ever plotted. Any ! dirt seems good enough if it will only tarnish the memory of Gladstone. With a speaker of this type•we are not surprised to hear him say Mr. Gladstone sent his (Mr. Hicks') namesake, Hicks Pasha, into the desert •to be destroyed. Mr. Hicks probably knows, or if he , does not ha ought to know, that Mr. Gladstone had i nothing to do with the sending of Hicks Pasha into the i desert. Of course Gordon's sad end is too good ! a point to be missed by a man of the style of Mr. Joynson-Hicks, this too must be raked up to support the Unionist cane. In the regret we must ever feel at the loss of that heroic spirit in lonely Kar- toum, it is well that we temper our condemnation with . justice and discrimination. I trust that in time to ' come, when the present Conservative veteran, Lord Salisbury, will have passed over to the great majority, that no Liberal of the time of Mr. Hicks will ever try , to tarnish his memory by attributing to him the lives of the brave. men who perished at Colenso. Tt was gener- ally acknowledged thatas far as those at home were in any way responsible for the reverse in South Africa that it was the war office and its chief who were to blame, and not primarily Lord Salis- bury. If anyone at home was to be blamed for the failure of the expedition to relieve • General Gordon it was the War Office and its chief Lord Hartington. I well remember the sympathy that Lord Hartington evoked when with a very heavy heart, he had to defend the action of the Government, and especially of the War Office after -Gordon's death. Whether that defence was a complete one or not is now of little consequence. But it is somewhat strange that at a Unionist Demonstration a speaker should be so far carried away by his desire to throw discredit on the Liberal Party, that he should overlook the fact that the fate of Gordon, if it does reflect on the memory of Gladstone does so equally, if not more so on the War Minister of that day who is now the official head of the Liberal Unionist Party,and also the Government Leader in the House of Lords.
CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketh, January 29th, 1903.
